Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 4, verse 1 (part 1 of 2):

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted and glorified, saying: ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord, who created you from a single soul﴾

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: By His saying, may His mention be exalted, "O mankind, fear your Lord, who created you from a single soul," He means: Beware, O mankind, of your Lord, lest you oppose Him in what He has commanded you and what He has forbidden you, so that there befalls you of His punishment what you have no power to withstand.

Then He, may His mention be exalted, described Himself as the One who alone created all of mankind from a single person, informing His servants how the beginning of His creation of that was from the single soul [[In the printed edition and the manuscript: "wa-'arrafa 'ibadahu ..." — I have adopted "wa-'arrafa" from the manuscript, and I have deduced from the method of Abu Ja'far in his exposition, and from his later saying "wa-manabbihahum" then "wa-'atifan," that the correct reading is "wa-mu'arrifan," which is what the flow of the whole discourse requires.]] and alerting them by that to the fact that all of them are the children of one man and one mother, and that some of them are from others, and that the right of some of them over others is obligatory like the right of a brother over his brother, because they are joined in descent from one father and one mother, and that what is incumbent upon them of caring for one another's rights, even if the meeting in descent to the common father is distant, is like what is incumbent upon them of that in the nearer descent [[His saying "wa-'atifan" is a continuation of His saying "mu'arrifan 'ibadahu ... wa-manabbihahum ..."]] and bringing them together in compassion for one another, so that they may act equitably and not wrong one another, and so that the strong may give the weak his right in accordance with what God has obliged him to give, and He said: "who created you from a single soul," meaning: from Adam, as:

8400 - Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: As for "created you from a single soul," it is from Adam, peace be upon him.

8401 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zuray' narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: "O mankind, fear your Lord, who created you from a single soul," meaning Adam, peace be upon him.

8402 - Sufyan ibn Wakee' narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to us, from Sufyan, from a man, from Mujahid: "created you from a single soul," he said: Adam.

* *

Similar to His saying "from a single soul," where what is meant is a man, is the poet's verse:

"Your father is a successor, and another bore him, and you are a successor; that is perfection."

He said "another bore him," meaning "the man," and so made the feminine agree with the word "successor." And He, may His mention be exalted, said "from a single soul" because "soul" is feminine, and the meaning is: from a single man. If it were said "from a single one," bringing the wording into the masculine in accordance with the meaning, it would be correct. [[This is the view of al-Farra' in Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1: 252.]]

* *

The interpretation of His, may His praise be exalted, saying: ﴿And from it He created its mate, and dispersed from the two of them many men and women﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, may His praise be exalted, "And from it He created its mate," and from the single soul He created its mate. By "mate" (zawj) He means the second of her [[See the explanation of "zawj" previously at 1: 514 / 2: 446. By his saying in explaining "zawj," "the second of her," he means that "zawj" is "the single one who has a partner," so each of the two partners is called "zawj," and then it was said of a man's wife, and of a woman's husband, "zawj."]] and it is, as the people of interpretation have said, her wife, Eve.

Those who said so:

8403 - Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid regarding His saying: "And from it He created its mate," he said: Eve, from the lower rib of Adam while he was asleep, so he awoke and said: "Atha," meaning in Nabataean, woman.

8404 - Al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

8405 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah: "And from it He created its mate," meaning Eve, she was created from Adam, from one of his ribs.

8406 - Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: 'Amr ibn Hammad informed us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, who said: He made Adam dwell in the Garden, and he would walk in it solitary, having no mate to find rest with. He slept a sleep, then awoke, and there beside his head was a woman sitting, whom God had created from his rib. He asked her, "What are you?" She said, "A woman." He said, "Why were you created?" She said, "So that you may find rest in me."

8407 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, who said: Sleep was cast upon Adam, peace be upon him, as we have been informed from the People of the Book, from the People of the Torah and others, from the people of knowledge, from 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas and others. Then He took one of his ribs, from his left side, and closed up the place with flesh, while Adam was asleep and did not stir from his sleep, until God, blessed and exalted, created from that rib his wife Eve, and shaped her as a woman so that he might find rest in her. When the sleep was lifted from him and he stirred from his sleep, he saw her beside him, and he said, as they claim, and God knows best: "Flesh of my flesh, blood of my blood, and my wife!" So he found rest in her.

8408 - Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to me, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "And from it He created its mate." He made Eve from Adam.

* *

As for His saying, "and dispersed from the two of them many men and women," it means: and He spread from them, that is, from Adam and Eve, "many men and women," whom He has seen, as He, may His praise be exalted, said: ﴿like scattered moths﴾ [Surah al-Qari'ah: 4]. [[See al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1: 252.]]

* *

It is said of it: "Allah dispersed (baththa) the creation, and dispersed them (abthahum)." [[See the explanation of "bath" previously at 3: 275.]]

* *

The people of interpretation have said in agreement with what we have said on this.

Those who said so:

8409 - Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "And dispersed from them many men and women," and "dispersed" means "created."

* *

The interpretation of His, may His praise be exalted, saying: ﴿And fear God, by whom you ask one another, and the wombs﴾

Abu Ja'far said: The readers differed regarding the recitation of this.

The majority of the readers of Madina and Basra recited "tasa'alūna" with the shadda, meaning "tatasa'alūna," then assimilated one of the two "t"s into the "s," making it a doubled "s."

* *

And some readers of Kufa recited "tasa'alūna" without the shadda, on the pattern of "tafa'alūna."

* *

Both are well-known recitations and eloquent dialects—I mean the lightening and the doubling in His saying "tasa'alūna bihi." Whichever of them a reader recites, he has hit the correct form, because the meaning, in whichever of its two forms it is recited, does not differ.

* *

As for its interpretation: "And fear God, O people, by whom, when one of you asks another, he asks by Him," so the questioner says to the one questioned, "I ask you by God, I adjure you by God, and I bind you by God," and what is similar to that. He, may His mention be exalted, says: Just as you, O people, exalt your Lord with your tongues, so that you see that whoever gives you his covenant and you break it treacherously [[akhfara al-dhimma wa-l-'ahd: to break faith with a protection or covenant, to betray it and not fulfil one's pledge.]] has committed a grave deed, so likewise exalt Him by your obedience to Him in what He has commanded you and your avoidance of what He has forbidden you, and beware His punishment by opposing Him in what He has commanded you or forbidden you, as:

8410 - Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abu Zuhayr narrated to us, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak regarding His saying: "And fear God by whom you ask one another," he said: He says: Fear God, by whom you make covenants and pledges.

8411 - Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi': "And fear God by whom you ask one another," he says: Fear God, by whom you make covenants and pledges.

8412 - Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Abi Ja'far, from his father, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, the like of it.

8413 - Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj informed us, from Ibn Juraij, who said: Ibn 'Abbas said: "tasa'alūna bihi," he said: you incline toward one another by it.

* *

As for His saying, "and the wombs," the people of interpretation differed in its interpretation. Some of them said: its meaning is: And fear God, by whom, when you ask one another, the questioner says to the one questioned, "I ask you by Him and by the womb."

Those who said so:

8414 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Hakkam narrated to us, from 'Amr, from Mansur, from Ibrahim: "Fear God by whom you ask one another and the wombs," he says: Fear God by whom you incline toward one another, and the wombs. He says: the man asks by God and by the womb.

8415 - Yaqub ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, from Mughirah, from Ibrahim, who said: It is like the saying of a man: "I ask you by God, I ask you by the womb," meaning His saying: "And fear God by whom you ask one another and the wombs."

8416 - Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Mansur, from Ibrahim: "Fear God by whom you ask one another and the wombs," he said: he says: "I ask you by God and by the womb."

8417 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, from Mughirah, from Ibrahim: It is like the saying of a man: "I ask you by the womb."

8418 - Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "Fear God by whom you ask one another and the wombs," he said: he says: "I ask you by God and by the womb."

8419 - Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Al-Hammani narrated to us, saying: Sharik narrated to us, from Mansur, or Mughirah, from Ibrahim regarding His saying: "And fear God by whom you ask one another and the wombs," he said: It is the saying of a man: "I ask you by God and the womb."

8420 - Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Suwayd narrated to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak informed us, from Ma'mar, from al-Hasan, who said: It is the saying of a man: "I adjure you by God and the womb."

* *

Muhammad said: [[His saying "Muhammad said" means Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari, Abu Ja'far, the author of the commentary. This is the first time that al-Tabari, or one of his students, or some copyist of his commentary, writes "Muhammad said" rather than his kunya "Abu Ja'far." See what follows at p. 569, note 2.]] This interpretation is also the view of those who read His saying "wa-l-arḥāmi" with the genitive, as a conjunction with the "hā'" in His saying "bihi," as though he meant: "And fear God by whom you ask one another and by the wombs," thus conjoining an apparent noun to a pronominal suffix in the genitive. That is not eloquent speech among the Arabs, for they do not coordinate an apparent noun with a pronoun in the genitive, [[His saying "tansuq," meaning "ta'tif" (conjoins). "Naseq" means conjunction; see the glossary of technical terms in these volumes of the commentary. "Mukanna" means the pronoun; see the glossary of technical terms.]] except in a poetic necessity, and that is due to the constraint of verse. [[This is the view of al-Farra' in Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1: 252, 253; he mentioned this recitation with its chain to Ibrahim ibn Yazid al-Nakha'i, and it is the recitation of Hamzah and others.]] As for ordinary speech, nothing compels the speaker to choose what is disliked in speech and the poor in its grammar. Among what has come in poetry of conjoining an apparent noun to a pronoun in the genitive case is the poet's saying: [[He is Miskin al-Darimi.]]

"We hang our swords on pillars like these, and between them and the Ka'b are open, wide plains."

So he conjoined "al-Ka'b," which is an apparent noun, to the "hā' and alif" in His saying "baynahā," which is a pronoun. [[Ma'ani al-Qur'an of al-Farra' 1: 253; al-Hayawan 6: 493, 494; al-Insaf: 193; al-Khizana 2: 338; al-'Ayni (in the margin of al-Khizana) 4: 164. It is among verses that al-Jahiz mentioned and al-'Ayni completed, praising himself and his people, saying: ...]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 4, verse 1 (part 2 of 2):

8434 - Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words, "And fear God, by whom you ask one another," [and fear the ties of kinship (al-arham), lest you sever them]. He then recited: ﴿And those who join what God has commanded to be joined﴾ [Surah al-Ra'd: 21].

* *

Abu Ja'far said: In accordance with this interpretation, whoever reads it in the accusative (nasb) has read it with the meaning: "And fear God, by whom you ask one another, and fear the ties of kinship, lest you sever them," coordinating "al-arham" (the ties of kinship) with the name of God, may He be exalted, in its i'rab (grammatical inflection, case-marking) as accusative.

He said: The recitation (qira'a) that we do not permit any reader to recite other than it in this regard is the accusative: ﴿And fear God, by whom you ask one another, and the wombs﴾, meaning: "and fear the ties of kinship, lest you sever them." This is because we have already shown that the Arabs do not coordinate a noun in the apparent form with a pronoun in the genitive case, except in cases of poetic necessity, as I described earlier. [[See what has passed shortly before, pp. 519, 520.]]

* *

On the interpretation of His words: ﴿Indeed, God has ever been over you an Watcher (raqib)﴾ (1).

Abu Ja'far said: He, may He be exalted, means: Indeed God has never ceased to be a watcher over you.

* *

By His words "over you," He means over the people to whom He, may His praise be exalted, said: "O mankind, fear your Lord." When the addressee and the absent party are combined in a report, the Arabs shift the speech into the form of address. So they say, when addressing one man or a group, and others who are absent are with them: "You (plural) did such-and-such, and you (plural) made such-and-such."

By His words "raqiban," He means: a guardian, one who counts your deeds against you, one who watches closely over your guarding of the sanctity of your ties of kinship and your maintaining them, and your severing them and neglecting their sanctity, as related:

8435 - Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding "Indeed God has ever been over you a watcher (raqib)": a guardian (hafiz).

8435 (repeated) - Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: I heard Ibn Zayd regarding His words, "Indeed God has ever been over you a watcher": over your deeds, He knows them and recognizes them.

From this is the saying of Abu Du'ad al-Iyadi:

Like the seats of the watchmen (ruqaba') for the gamblers (dariba'), their hands outstretched [[Tahdhib al-Alfaz: 475; al-Ma'ani al-Kabir: 1148; Majaz al-Qur'an 1: 113; al-Maysir wa'l-Qidah: 133; and others. It is one of the fine verses describing a white bull. I have not found them all together. Among them:

And hooves (qawa'im) thrown forward (khudhuf), behind them tufts (zamaʿ) that are extra,
Like the seats of the watchmen for the gamblers, their hands outstretched, with the arrows (nawahid),
A whiteness like the fire on the head, on the height, which the worshippers (al-a'abid) kindle,
And he sometimes pricks up his ears, as the one who has lost (al-mudill) listens to the voice of one who announces (nashid).

He describes the legs of this bull. "Khudhuf" is the plural of "khadhuf," which is one that moves swiftly and runs quickly, throwing pebbles with its legs, that is, flinging them. "Zamaʿ" is the plural of "zamaʿah," a protruding extra growth above the hoof of a sheep or bull, hanging down with hair on it. Then he describes these protruding tufts behind the bull's hooves, comparing their projecting above the hooves to the watchmen overseeing the gamblers, with their hands outstretched. This is a description of utmost skill and beauty. "Ruqaba'" is the plural of raqib, the trustee of the gamblers, who guards their casting of the arrows and watches them. "Dariba'" is the plural of darib, the one who casts the arrows. Ibn Qutaybah claimed that his words "their hands" refers to the hands of the gamblers, and he was mistaken; he meant the hands of the watchmen, not of the gamblers. And his words "lahaq" refer to whiteness, that is, the whiteness of the bull; he compares its whiteness to the whiteness of fire on the head of a shining hill, which the worshippers kindle. Then he describes the bull when alarmed, saying that it "yusikh," that is, it listens attentively, inclining its head to one side out of fear. "Al-mudill" is one who has lost something, so he awaits finding it. "Al-nashid" is one who seeks a lost thing, that is, one who describes it and identifies it. So the bull listens to the voice of the announcer who identifies it, listening as one who hopes that it is his lost thing. This is from fine and excellent poetry.]]

Commentary on the interpretation of His saying: ﴿And give the orphans their property, and do not substitute the bad [property] for the good﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By this, may His mention be exalted, He means the guardians of orphans. He says to them: "Give, O assembly of the guardians of orphans, [the orphans] their property when they reach maturity [[In the manuscript and the printed edition, what I have placed between the brackets has been dropped, but the context requires it, and it seems the copyist was misled by the repetition and dropped one of them, so he erred.]] and find them to be of sound judgement [[See the explanation of "give" (ātā) in the lexical indices, and the explanation of "orphans" in what has preceded: 2:292 / 3:345 / 4:295.]]" = "and do not substitute the bad for the good," meaning: do not substitute for their property, which is lawful for you, your own property that is lawful for you, as:

8436 - Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to us, he said: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, he said: 'Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding the saying of God, exalted is He: "and do not substitute the bad for the good," he said: the lawful for the unlawful.

8437 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, he said: Abu Huthayfa narrated to us, he said: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

8438 - Sufyan narrated to me, he said: my father narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, his saying: "and do not substitute the bad for the good," he said: the unlawful in place of the lawful.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: Then the people of interpretation differed concerning the manner of their substitution of the bad for the good, which they were forbidden, and its meaning.

Some of them said: The guardians of orphans would take the best and choicest of his property and put in its place the inferior and worthless [property] for the orphan; that is their substitution which God, exalted is He, forbade them.

Those who said this:

8439 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, he said: Ibn Yaman narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Mughira, from Ibrahim: "and do not substitute the bad for the good," he said: Do not give counterfeit and take good.

8440 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, he said: Ibn Yaman narrated to us, from Sufyan, from al-Suddi, and from Yahya ibn Sa'id, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, and Ma'mar from al-Zuhri, they said: He gives the emaciated and takes the fat.

8441 - And with the same chain, from Sufyan, from a man, from al-Dahhak, he said: Do not give the corrupt and take the good.

8442 - Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to us, he said: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, he said: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "and do not substitute the bad for the good," one of them would take a fat sheep from the orphan's flock and put in its place a lean sheep, saying: "A sheep for a sheep!" And he would take the good dirham and cast in its place the counterfeit, saying: "A dirham for a dirham!!"

* *

Others said: The meaning of that is: Do not hasten to the unlawful sustenance and eat it before what has been decreed for you of the lawful comes to you.

Those who said this:

8443 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, he said: Ibn Yaman narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "and do not substitute the bad for the good," he said: Do not hasten to the unlawful sustenance before the lawful that has been decreed for you comes to you.

8444 - And with the same chain, from Sufyan, from Isma'il, from Abu Salih, the like of it.

* *

Others said: The meaning of that is, as in what:

8445 - Yunus ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to me, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying: "and do not substitute the bad for the good," he said: The people of the Jahiliyya did not give inheritance to women nor to small children; the eldest would take it. And he recited: ﴿and you desire to marry them﴾ and: ﴿and the weak among the children﴾ [Surah al-Nisa: 127], [if they had nothing], they would not give inheritance to them. He said: So his share of the inheritance is good, and this which he took is bad.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The most probable of these sayings as the interpretation of the verse is the saying of the one who said: The interpretation of that is: Do not substitute the property of your orphans—O guardians—which is unlawful for you, the bad for you, so that you take its choicest and best, for the good that is lawful for you from your own property [i.e., do not take] the inferior and worthless in its place. [[What I added between the brackets is an inference from his later interpretation. Without this addition the sentence can hardly be made coherent.

Then see the explanation of "the bad" (al-khabith) in what has preceded: 5:559 / 7:424, and the explanation of "the good" (al-tayyib) in what has preceded: 3:301 / 5:555 / 6:361 / 7:424.]]

This is because "tabaddul al-shay' bi-al-shay'" in the speech of the Arabs means taking one thing in place of another, giving it to the one from whom it is taken, or putting it in place of what was taken. [[See the explanation of "tabaddul" and "istabdal" in what has preceded: 2:112, 130, 494.]]

* *

Since that is the meaning of "tabaddul" and "istibdal" [[In the printed edition: "al-tabdil", and I have restored the correct reading from the manuscript.]], it is known that what Ibn Zayd said, that its meaning is that the eldest son of the deceased takes all the property of his deceased father and parent, to the exclusion of their younger children, [is] a saying with no meaning. For if the eldest of his children takes all his property to the exclusion of the younger ones, he has not substituted anything for what he took. So what is the "substitution" which He, may His praise be exalted, mentioned: "and do not substitute the bad for the good," when the taker has not substituted in place of the taken anything in exchange?

* *

As for what Mujahid and Abu Salih said, that its meaning is: Do not hasten the unlawful sustenance before the lawful comes— even if they did not intend by that something like the saying transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "A man is indeed deprived of sustenance by the sin he commits," its corruption is similar to the corruption of Ibn Zayd's saying. For whoever hastens to the unlawful and eats it, then God gives him his lawful sustenance, has not substituted anything in place of anything. But if they both intended by that that God, may His praise be exalted, forbade His servants to hasten to the unlawful and eat it before the lawful comes, so that their eating of it becomes a cause of depriving them of the good, then that is a known aspect and an intelligible course, which the interpretation can bear. However, the more fitting of the two sayings as the interpretation of the verse is what we have said; [[In the printed edition: "however, the more fitting in that as the interpretation of the verse is what we said," which is not good; in the manuscript: "however, more fitting in that as the interpretation of the verse is what we said," which shows the copyist again erred, dropping "the two sayings," which I have restored within the brackets.]] because that is the more apparent of its meanings, since God, may His praise be exalted, mentioned that only in the context of the orphans' property and its rulings. So for that to be of the same kind as the ruling at the beginning and end of the verse is [more fitting] than for it to be of a different kind. [[In the printed edition: "so that is not of the same kind as the ruling at the beginning of the verse, which removes it from being of a different kind," having put "wa-akhiraha" and "fa-akhrajaha," reducing the sentence to something unintelligible. As for the manuscript, its context reads: "fa-la yakun dhalika min jins hukm awwal al-ayah wa-akhiriha min an yakun min ghayr jinsihi," which is a slip by the copyist; the correct reading is "fa-la yakun" and "fa-la'anna yakun," and the correct addition of "awla" is what I have placed between the brackets.]]

* *

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿And do not consume their property along with your property﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By this, may His mention be exalted, He means: Do not mix their property—meaning the property of the orphans—with your property, so that you consume it together with your property [[See the explanation of "consuming property" in what has preceded: 3:548, 549 / and the explanation of "ila" in the sense of "ma'a" (with) in what has preceded: 1:299 / 6:443, 444.]], as:

8446 - Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, he said: Sufyan narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying: "and do not consume their property along with your property," he said: Do not consume your property and their property, mixing them and consuming them all together.

8447 - al-Muthanna narrated to us, he said: Ishaq narrated to us, he said: Abu Zuhayr narrated to us, from Mubarak, from al-Hasan, who said: When this verse about the orphans' property was revealed, they disliked mixing with them, and the guardian of the orphan would separate the orphan's property from his own. They complained of that to the Prophet ﷺ, and God revealed: ﴿They ask you about orphans. Say: Setting things right for them is best; and if you mix with them, they are your brothers﴾ [Surah al-Baqarah: 220]. He said: So mix with them and fear God. [[The report 8447: this report Abu Ja'far did not transmit in his explanation of the verse of Surat al-Baqarah, 4:349–355, and this is among the indications of the brevity of this tafsir.]]

* *

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿Indeed, that is a great sin (ḥawban kabīran)﴾ (2)

Abu Ja'far said: He means, may His mention be exalted, [by His saying] : [[What is between the brackets is an addition without which the sentence cannot stand.]] "Indeed, that was a great sin": indeed, your consuming the property of your orphans is a great sin.

* *

The "hā'" in His saying "innahu" refers to the noun of the act, I mean "the consuming."

* *

As for "ḥawb," it means sin. It is said of it: "ḥāba al-rajul yaḥūbu ḥawban and ḥūban and ḥiyābah," and it is said: "tahawwaba al-rajul min kadhā," when he regarded it as a sin, and from it is the saying of Umayya ibn al-Askar al-Layth: [[In the printed and manuscript editions: "ibn al-Askan," which is a clear error.]]

"And indeed two emigrants surrounded him... that morning, they had surely erred and sinned (ḥābā)"

[[The line has passed with its takhrij at 2:110, and will come at 13:37 (Bulaq). See Majaz al-Qur'an of Abu 'Ubayda 1:13. I did not record there the places where it recurs in the tafsir, so let it be noted there. Its narration there is: "by the life of God, they have surely erred and sinned" with the khā'; and I think that the better of the two narrations is its narration in this place, with the unpointed ḥā'; although most books have recorded it with the pointed khā', and I also think it is an ancient misreading; and the meaning of Abu Ja'far's narration is more fitting to the context of the poetry, God willing.]]

From it comes the saying: "We alighted in a ḥawbah of the land and a ḥībah of the land," when they alighted in a bad place of it.

* *

As for "kabīr," it means great.

* *

So the meaning of that is: indeed, your consuming the property of the orphans along with your property is a sin, great in the sight of God.

* *

Those who expounded the interpretation said in accordance with what we have said.

Those who said this:

8448 - Muhammad ibn 'Amr and 'Amr ibn 'Ali narrated to me, both said: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, from 'Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding God's saying: "a great sin (ḥawban kabīran)," he said: a sin.

8449 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, he said: Abu Huthayfa narrated to us, he said: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

8450 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, he said: Abu Salih narrated to us, he said: Mu'awiya narrated to me, from 'Ali ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn 'Abbas, his saying: "Indeed, it was a great sin," he said: a great sin.

8451 - Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to us, he said: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, he said: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "it was a sin" — as for "ḥawban," it is a sin.

8452 - al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, he said: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, he said: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatada, regarding His saying: "ḥawban," he said: a sin.

8453 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, he said: Yazid ibn Zurayʿ narrated to us, he said: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada: "Indeed, it was a great sin," he says: a great wrong.

8454 - Yunus narrated to me, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: I heard Ibn Zayd say regarding His saying: "Indeed, it was a great sin," he said: a great sin= and it is for the people of Islam.

8455 - 'Amr ibn 'Ali narrated to us, he said: Yahya ibn Sa'id narrated to us, he said: Qurra ibn Khalid narrated to us, he said: I heard al-Hasan say: "a great sin (ḥawban kabīran)," he said: a great sin, by God.

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on Surah 4, Verse 3 (Part 1 of 3)**

On the interpretation (*ta'wil*) of His saying: ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphans, then marry what seems good to you of women, two, three, or four. And if you fear that you will not be just, then (marry) one, or what your right hands possess﴾.

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: The people of interpretation differed regarding the interpretation of this.

Some of them said: The meaning of this is: "And if you fear, O guardians of orphans, that you will not act justly regarding their dowries, so that you do not give them their proper dowries equal to the dowries of women like them, then do not marry them. Rather, marry other foreign women whom God has made lawful to you and made good for you, from one up to four. And if you fear that you will act unjustly (if you marry more than one of the foreign women), then do not be equitable, but marry only one of them, or what your right hands possess."

Mention of those who said this:

8456 – Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from al-Zuhri, from 'Urwa, from 'A'isha: "And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphans, then marry what seems good to you of women." She said: "O son of my sister, it is the orphan girl who is in the custody of her guardian, who desires her wealth and her beauty, and wants to marry her for less than the customary dowry (*sunna*). So they were forbidden to marry them unless they act justly toward them in completing the dowry, and they were commanded to marry other women besides them."

[[Hadith 8456: al-Tabari narrates this hadith, in full and abridged forms, through seven chains: 8456–8461 and 8477. It is authentic and sound, found in the two Sahihs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and other collections.
This chain is the narration of Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak, from Ma'mar, from al-Zuhri. Hadith 8460 will come, from the narration of 'Abd al-Razzaq, from Ma'mar, without mention of its wording, referring back to this narration.
Al-Bukhari narrated it in his Sahih twelve times, which we will indicate, God willing.
Al-Bayhaqi narrated it in al-Sunan al-Kubra (7:141–142) through multiple chains and routes.]]

8457 – Yunus ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Yunus ibn Yazid informed me, from Ibn Shihab, who said: 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr informed me that he asked 'A'isha, the wife of the Prophet ﷺ, about the saying of God, Blessed and Exalted is He: "And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphans, then marry what seems good to you of women." She said: "O son of my sister, this is the orphan girl who is in the custody of her guardian, who shares with him his wealth, and he is pleased with her wealth and her beauty. So her guardian wants to marry her without acting justly regarding her dowry, giving her the same as what others would give her. So they were forbidden to marry them unless they act justly toward them and give them their highest customary dowry (*sunna*), and they were commanded to marry other women besides them who seem good to them." Yunus ibn Yazid said: Rabi'a said regarding the saying of God, "And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphans": he said, it means: leave them, for I have made four women lawful to you.

[[Hadith 8457: This is through the narration of Ibn Wahb, from Yunus ibn Yazid, from al-Zuhri.
Hadith 8459 will come, from the narration of al-Layth ibn Sa'd, from Yunus, from al-Zuhri, without mention of its wording, referring back to this narration. Al-Bukhari narrated it in his Sahih (5:94–95, Fath al-Bari), through the route of al-Layth, from Yunus, from al-Zuhri.
Muslim narrated it (2:398–399), through the route of Ibn Wahb, from Yunus, longer than what is here. However, it does not contain what is mentioned at its end here, from the saying of Rabi'a which Yunus narrated from him. That is not part of the core of the hadith.
Al-Bukhari narrated it (9:91, Fath al-Bari) through the narration of Hassan ibn Ibrahim, from Yunus, from al-Zuhri, similar to what is here with slight abridgment. It does not contain the words of Rabi'a.
As for his saying "a'la sunnatihinna fi al-sadaq" (their highest customary dowry): this is what is established in Sahih Muslim as well. In the manuscript it reads "sabiluhunna" (their way) instead of "sunnatihinna." The apparent reading is that it is a scribal error by the copyist.]]

8458 – Al-Hasan ibn al-Junayd narrated to us, and Sa'id ibn Muslima informed us, both saying: Isma'il ibn Umayya informed us, from Ibn Shihab, from 'Urwa, who said: I asked 'A'isha, the Mother of the Believers, and I said: "O Mother of the Believers, what do you say about the saying of God: 'And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphans, then marry what seems good to you of women'?" She said: "O son of my sister, it is the orphan girl who is in the custody of her guardian, who desires her beauty and her wealth, and wants to marry her for less than the customary dowry of her kind. So they were forbidden from that: that they marry them unless they act justly and complete the dowry for them. Then they were commanded to marry other women besides them if they do not complete the dowry for them."

[[Hadith 8458: Al-Hasan ibn al-Junayd ibn Abi Ja'far al-Bazzar al-Baghdadi: trustworthy (*thiqa*). Ibn Khuzayma narrated from him in his Sahih. Ibn Abi Hatim included him (1/2/4) and mentioned no criticism of him, and al-Khatib (7:292) did likewise; both under the entry "al-Hasan." Al-Hafiz al-Mizzi listed him in al-Tahdhib al-Kabir under "al-Husayn." Al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar followed him in Tahdhib al-Tahdhib, following the arrangement of the book, but he stated explicitly that it is "with a fatha on the ha' and the sin," meaning "al-Hasan," which is correct.
Sa'id ibn Muslima ibn Hisham ibn 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan: weak (*da'if*). Al-Bukhari said in al-Kabir (2/1/473): "There is something questionable about him." He mentioned that he had "munkar" narrations. He said in al-Du'afa' (p. 15): "munkar" (rejected). Ibn Ma'in said: "He is not worth anything." Abu Hatim said: "He is weak in narration, rejected in narration" (Ibn Abi Hatim 2/1/67).
In the printed edition here it reads: "al-Hasan ibn Junayd and Abu Sa'id ibn Muslima," which is an error; "wa-Abu" was written instead of "wa-Anba" (wa-akhbarana), an abbreviation of "and informed us."
Isma'il ibn Umayya al-Umawi: his biography has passed at 2615. The weakness of this chain, because of Sa'id ibn Muslima, does not prevent the authenticity of the hadith in itself through other routes, as has passed and will come.]]

8459 – al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Salih narrated to us, saying: al-Layth narrated to me, saying: Yunus narrated to me, from Ibn Shihab, who said: 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr narrated to me: that he asked 'A'isha, the wife of the Prophet ﷺ, and he mentioned a hadith similar to the hadith of Yunus from Ibn Wahb.

8460 – al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from al-Zuhri, from 'Urwa, from 'A'isha, similar to the hadith of Ibn Humayd from Ibn al-Mubarak.

[[The two hadiths 8459 and 8460 are repetitions of the two hadiths 8457 and 8456. We have indicated each of them in its place.]]

8461 – al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, from Hisham, from his father, from 'A'isha, who said: "It was revealed" (she meant the saying: "And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphans," the verse) "concerning the orphan girl who is with a man, and she has wealth, so he may marry her for her wealth, though she does not please him; then he beats her and treats her badly. So he was admonished for that."

[[Hadith 8461: al-Qasim is Ibn al-Hasan. "al-Husayn" is Ibn Dawud, known as "Sunayd." See what has passed in the chain at 8398.
Hajjaj is Ibn Muhammad al-Misisi al-A'war. His biography has passed at 1691. My brother, al-Sayyid Mahmud, translated him in vol. 6, p. 548, note 3.
This hadith through this route was narrated by al-Bukhari (8:179, Fath al-Bari) through the route of Hisham ibn Yusuf, from Ibn Juraij, similarly. However, its wording gives the impression that the verse was revealed concerning a specific person. Al-Hafiz said: "What is known from Hisham ibn 'Urwa is the generalization (*tamim*) of the ruling." Likewise al-Isma'ili narrated it through the route of Hajjaj ibn Muhammad from Ibn Juraij, and its wording is: "It was revealed concerning the man who has an orphan girl with him," etc.
I say: the narration of Hajjaj is the one in al-Tabari as well.
Al-Bukhari also narrated it (8:199, Fath al-Bari) through the route of Abu Usama, from Hisham ibn 'Urwa, correctly.
Muslim likewise narrated it, similar in wording (2:399), through the route of Abu Usama, from Hisham.
Al-Bukhari also narrated it, similar in wording (9:119), through the route of 'Abda, that is Ibn Sulayman, from Hisham ibn 'Urwa.
It will come at 8477 through the narration of Waki', from Hisham. We will takhrij it there, God willing.
We mention here the rest of its routes in the two Sahihs, apart from the narration of Waki', as a benefit:
Al-Bukhari (5:94–95, Fath al-Bari) and Muslim (2:399) both narrated it through the route of Salih, from al-Zuhri, from 'Urwa.
Al-Bukhari (5:292, Fath al-Bari; 9:169–170; and 12:298) narrated it through the route of Shu'ayb, from al-Zuhri.
He also narrated it (9:117, 169–170) through the route of 'Uqayl, from al-Zuhri.
He also narrated it (9:162) through the route of Abu Mu'awiya, from Hisham ibn 'Urwa, abridged.
Ibn Kathir mentioned the hadith of 'A'isha (2:342–343) from two of al-Bukhari's narrations, and did not add anything to its takhrij.
Al-Suyuti mentioned it in three wordings, long and short (2:118), and attributed it additionally to 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Nasa'i, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim.]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: According to this interpretation, the answer (*jawab*) to His saying "And if you fear that you will not act justly" is His saying "then marry."

* *

Others said: Rather, the meaning of this is: the prohibition of marrying more than four, out of concern for the wealth of orphans that their guardians might destroy it. [[In the printed edition: "hadhran 'ala amwal al-yatama" (out of caution for the wealth of orphans). I have adopted what is in the manuscript.]] This is because the Quraysh, a man among them would marry ten women, or more, or fewer. When he became destitute, he would turn to the wealth of the orphan in his custody and spend it or use it for marriage. So they were forbidden from that, and it was said to them: "If you fear for the wealth of your orphans that you will spend it, then do not be just with it, because of your need for it for the expenses of your wives. So do not exceed four in the number of women you marry. And if you also fear, regarding the four, that you will not be just with their wealth, then limit yourselves to one, or to what your right hands possess."

Mention of those who said this:

8462 – Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, saying: Shu'ba narrated to us, from Simak, who said: I heard 'Ikrima say regarding this verse: "And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphans": "A man of Quraysh would have women with him, and he would have orphans with him, and his wealth would be depleted, so he would turn to the wealth of the orphans." He said: "Then this verse was revealed: 'And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphans, then marry what seems good to you of women.'"

8463 – Hannad ibn al-Sari narrated to us, saying: Abu al-Ahwas narrated to us, from Simak, from 'Ikrima, regarding His saying: "And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphans, then marry what seems good to you of women, two, three, or four. And if you fear that you will not be just, then (marry) one, or what your right hands possess." He said: "A man would marry four, five, six, or ten, and a man would say: 'What prevents me from marrying as so-and-so married?' So he would take the wealth of his orphan and marry with it. So they were forbidden to marry beyond four."

8464 – Sufyan ibn Waki' narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Habib ibn Abi Thabit, from Tawus, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The men were restricted to four, because of the wealth of the orphans."

8465 – Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: "And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphans": "A man would marry with the wealth of the orphan whatever God willed, so God forbade that."

* *

Others said: Rather, the meaning of this is: the people used to be cautious (*yatahawwabun*) regarding the wealth of orphans, lest they not act justly with it, but they were not cautious regarding women, lest they not act justly with them. So it was said to them: "Just as you fear that you will not be just with the orphans, so likewise fear that you will not be just with the women, and do not marry from them except one up to four, and do not exceed that. And if you also fear that you will not be just in exceeding one, then do not marry except those whom you do not fear you will act unjustly with, one, or what your right hands possess."

Mention of those who said this:

8466 – Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Ibn 'Ulayya narrated to us, from Ayyub, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: "The people were upon their ignorance, unless they were commanded with something or forbidden from something. He said: So the orphans were mentioned, and this was revealed: 'And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphans, then marry what seems good to you of women, two, three, or four. And if you fear that you will not be just, then (marry) one, or what your right hands possess.' He said: Just as you fear that you will not act justly with the orphans, likewise fear that you will not act justly with the women."

8467 – Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphans" to "or what your right hands possess." "They used to be strict regarding the orphans but not strict regarding the women. One of them would marry several wives and not be just among them. So God, Blessed and Exalted, said: 'Just as you fear that you will not be just among the orphans, so fear regarding the women. So marry one up to four. And if you fear that you will not be just, then (marry) one, or what your right hands possess.'"

8468 – Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zurai' narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding His saying: "And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphans, then marry what seems good to you of women," until: "that you may not be unjust" (adna alla ta'ulu). He says: "Just as you feared injustice toward the orphans and it troubled you, so likewise fear regarding the gathering of wives. In the Jahiliyya, a man would marry ten or fewer. So God, may His praise be majestic, permitted four, then the one who restricted them to four (said): 'two, three, or four. And if you fear that you will not be just, then one.'" He says: "If you fear that you will not be just among four, then three; otherwise, two; otherwise, one. And if you fear that you will not be just with one, then what your right hand possesses."

[[In the manuscript: "jami' al-nisa'" (the gathering of women); the printed edition reads "jami' al-nisa'" as well, and the correct reading is what is in the printed edition.]] (Note: this is as recorded in the text, which reads "jami' al-nisa'"; the manuscript reads "jumi' al-nisa'," and the printed text reads "jami' al-nisa'," which is the correct form.) [[In the printed edition: "thumma al-ladhi sayyarahunna ila arba'" (then the one who restricted them to four), adding "al-ladhi" (the one who), while what is in the manuscript is a good reading.]]

8469 – al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Ayyub, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr regarding His saying: "And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphans, then marry what seems good to you of women." He says: "What has been made lawful for you of women, 'two, three, or four.' So be fearful regarding women just as you feared regarding the orphans: that you not act justly with them."

8470 – al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: al-Hajjaj ibn al-Minhal narrated to us, saying: Hammad narrated to us, from Ayyub, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: "Islam came while the people were upon their ignorance, unless they were commanded with something and followed it, or forbidden from something and avoided it, until they asked about the orphans. So God, Blessed and Exalted, revealed: 'then marry what seems good to you of women, two, three, or four.'"

8471 – al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Abu al-Nu'man 'Arim narrated to us, saying: Hammad ibn Zayd narrated to us, from Ayyub, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: "God, Blessed and Exalted, sent Muhammad ﷺ while the people were upon the matter of their ignorance, unless they were commanded with something or forbidden from it. And they used to ask him about the orphans, so God, Blessed and Exalted, revealed: 'And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphans, then marry what seems good to you of women, two, three, or four.'" He said: "Just as you fear that you will not act justly with the orphans, so fear that you will not act justly, and be equitable, with the women."

8472 – al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiya ibn Salih narrated to me, from 'Ali ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: "And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphans," he said: "In the Jahiliyya they would marry ten women who were without husbands, and they used to greatly honor the status of the orphan. So they were careful about the orphan's status as part of their religion, but they abandoned what they used to marry in the Jahiliyya. So He said: 'And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphans, then marry what seems good to you of women, two, three, or four,' and He forbade them from what they used to marry in the Jahiliyya."

[[Hadith 8472: Abdullah ibn Salih, the scribe of al-Layth ibn Sa'd: his biography and authentication have passed at 186.
Mu'awiya ibn Salih al-Hadrami: his authentication has passed at 186. He is mentioned in al-Tahdhib, in al-Bukhari's al-Kabir (4/1/335), al-Saghir (p. 193), Ibn Sa'd (7/2/207), and Ibn Abi Hatim (4/1/382–383), and in Tarikh Qudat Qurtuba (pp. 30–40) and Qudat al-Andalus by al-Nabahi (p. 43).
'Ali ibn Abi Talha: we have explained at 1833 that he did not hear from Ibn 'Abbas. Therefore this chain is disconnected (*munqati'*), weak because of its disconnection.
The hadith was narrated by al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan al-Kubra (7:150), through the route of 'Uthman ibn Sa'id, from Abdullah ibn Salih, with this chain.
The hafiz referred to it in Fath al-Bari (8:179–180) in explaining the hadith of 'A'isha, saying: "This interpretation of 'A'isha's was also reported from Ibn 'Abbas, similar to it. Al-Tabari narrated it."
Al-Suyuti mentioned it (2:118), attributing it only to Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 4, verse 3 (part 2 of 3):

8473 - I was told on the authority of al-Husayn ibn al-Faraj, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: ʿUbayd ibn Sulayman related to us, who said: I heard al-Dahhak say, concerning His words: ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly toward orphans, then marry what seems good to you of women﴾. They, in their pre-Islamic time of ignorance, would not take anything from the property of an orphan, yet they would marry ten women and marry the wives of their fathers. So they neglected their religion regarding women, and God admonished them concerning orphans and concerning women. Regarding orphans He said: ﴿And do not exchange the bad for the good﴾ up to ﴿Indeed, it is a great sin﴾. And He admonished them regarding women, saying: ﴿then marry what seems good to you of women﴾, the verse, and He said: ﴿And do not marry those whom your fathers married of women﴾ [Surah an-Nisa, 22].

8474 - I was told on the authority of ʿAmmar, from Ibn Abi Jaʿfar, from his father, from al-Rabiʿ, concerning His words: ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly toward orphans﴾ up to ﴿what your right hands possess﴾: He says: If you fear injustice toward orphans and that troubles you, then likewise be wary regarding the multitude of women [in the manuscript and the printed edition here reads "جميع النساء" (all women), and the correct reading is what I have written; see the earlier note, p. 536, note 1]. He said: In the pre-Islamic period a man would marry ten or fewer, and God permitted four and restricted them to four. He says: ﴿But if you fear that you will not be just, then one﴾, and if you fear that you will not be just even with one, then what your right hand possesses.

* *

Others said: The meaning of that is: Just as you feared regarding orphans, so likewise be wary regarding women, lest you commit fornication with them; rather, marry what seems good to you of women.

Those who said this:

8475 - Muhammad ibn ʿAmr related to us, who said: Abu ʿAsim related to us, who said: ʿIsa informed us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, concerning His words: ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly toward orphans﴾, he says: If you were scrupulous in the guardianship of orphans and in consuming their wealth, out of faith and conviction, then likewise be scrupulous regarding fornication, and marry women in a good marriage ["mathna wa thulatha waruba"] ... ﴿two, three, or four; but if you fear that you will not be just, then one, or what your right hands possess﴾.

8476 - Al-Muthanna related to me, who said: Abu Hudhayfa related to us, who said: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

* *

Others said: Rather, the meaning of that is: And if you fear that you will not act justly toward the orphans whose guardians you are, then do not marry them; and marry, yourselves, what is lawful for you of them.

Those who said this:

8477 - Sufyan ibn Waki' related to us, who said: My father related to us, from Hisham ibn ʿUrwa, from his father, from ʿA'isha: ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly toward orphans﴾, she said: It was revealed concerning the orphan girl who is in a man's care, he being her guardian, with no guardian other than him, and no one contesting him over her, and he marries her for her wealth, then beats her and treats her badly.
[Note on the hadith: This chain is weak, due to the weakness of Sufyan ibn Waki', whose weakness we have explained many times, the first being at 142, 143. But the hadith itself is sound, as has passed at 8456–8461, and in the reports we have taken from the two Sahihs. Moreover, it is established and sound through the narration of Waki' himself, not through the narration of his son Sufyan from him. Al-Bukhari narrated it (9:160, Fath), more extensively than here, from Yahya, from Waki', with this chain. Yahya, the teacher of al-Bukhari in this chain, al-Hafiz said in al-Fath: "He is Ibn Musa, or Ibn Ja'far, as I have explained in the introduction." What is in the introduction of al-Fath, p. 236, is that Ibn al-Sakan attributed him as "Yahya ibn Musa."]

8478 - Humayd ibn Mas'ada related to us, who said: Yazid ibn Zurayʿ related to us, who said: Yunus related to us, from al-Hasan, concerning this verse: ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly toward orphans, then marry what seems good to you﴾, meaning: what is lawful for you of your orphans who are your relatives; ﴿two, three, or four; but if you fear that you will not be just, then one, or what your right hands possess﴾.

* *

Abu Jaʿfar said: The most preferable of the statements we have mentioned regarding the interpretation of this verse is the statement of the one who said its interpretation is: "And if you fear that you will not act justly toward orphans, then likewise be wary regarding women, so marry from them only those of whom you do not fear injustice, from one up to four. And if you fear injustice even regarding one, then do not marry her; rather, [have recourse to] what your right hands possess, for it is more fitting that you not be unjust toward them."

We only said that this is the more preferable interpretation of the verse because God, may His praise be majestic, began the preceding verse by forbidding the consumption of orphans' wealth unjustly and mixing it with other property. He, may He be exalted and remembered, said: ﴿And give the orphans their property, and do not exchange the bad for the good, and do not consume their property along with your property; indeed, it is a great sin﴾. Then He informed them that if they feared God in that matter and were scrupulous about it, then the obligation upon them of fearing God and being scrupulous regarding women is like the obligation upon them of scrupulousness regarding orphans. He informed them how to escape injustice toward them, as He had shown them the means of escape from injustice in orphans' property, saying: Marry, if you are secure from injustice toward women in your own selves, what I have permitted and made lawful for you of them: two, three, or four. And if you also fear for yourselves injustice in the matter of one, such that you cannot do justice to her, then do not marry her, but take concubines from the slave-women, for you are more likely not to be unjust toward them, because they are your possessions and your property, and the rights you owe them are not like those owed to free women; so that will be closer for you to safety from sin and injustice.

In the speech, since the meaning is what we have said, something has been omitted, the sufficiency being in what has appeared of the speech, so its mention is dispensed with. The meaning of the speech is: And if you fear that you will not act justly regarding the property of orphans, so that you deal fairly with it, then likewise fear that you will not act justly regarding the rights of women which God has obligated upon you; so do not marry from them except those with whom you are secure from injustice: two, three, or four. And if you also fear regarding that, then one. And if you fear regarding one, then what your right hands possess. The mention of His words "then likewise fear that you will not act justly regarding the rights of women" is thus omitted, the sufficiency being in what has appeared from His words, may He be exalted: "But if you fear that you will not be just, then one, or what your right hands possess."

* *

If someone says: Where is the answer to His words: "And if you fear that you will not act justly toward orphans"?

It is said: It is His words "then marry what seems good to you," but the meaning that indicates that what we have stated is intended is His words: "But if you fear that you will not be just, then one, or what your right hands possess; that is more suitable so that you do not incline toward excess."

* *

We have already shown earlier that the meaning of "al-iqsat" (acting justly) in the speech of the Arabs is justice and fairness, and that "al-qist" is injustice and wrongdoing, which suffices so as not to repeat it in this place. [See what has passed, 6:77, 270.]

* *

As for "al-yatama" (orphans), it is the plural of both male and female orphans in this place. [See the explanation of "al-yatama" earlier, shortly before, p. 524, note 3, and the references there.]

* *

As for His words: "then marry what seems good to you of women," He means: then marry what is lawful for you of them, not what is forbidden to you of them, as:

8479 - Ibn Humayd related to us, who said: Ibn al-Mubarak related to us, from Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid, from Abu Malik concerning His words: "then marry what seems good to you of women": what is lawful for you.

8480 - Al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, who said: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, who said: Ma'mar informed us, from Ayyub, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr concerning His words: "then marry what seems good to you of women," he says: what is lawful for you.

* *

If someone says: How was it said, "then marry what seems good to you of women," and not "then marry whoever seems good to you"? "Ma" is only used for other than people.

It is said: The meaning of that is other than the way you have supposed; rather its meaning is: marry in a good marriage, as:

8481 - Muhammad ibn ʿAmr related to me, who said: ʿIsa related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "then marry what seems good to you of women": marry women in a good marriage.

8481m - Al-Muthanna related to me, who said: Abu Hudhayfa related to us, who said: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

* *

So what is intended by His words "what seems good to you" is the act, not the persons and individuals of the women; therefore it is said "ma" and not "man," as one says: "Take from my slaves what you wish," meaning: take from them your desire. If you intended: "Take whom you wish from them," you would say: "Take from my slaves whom you wish from them." [See al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:253, 254.] Likewise His words "or what your right hands possess," meaning: or the right hands' possession.

* *

The meaning of His words "then marry what seems good to you of women, two, three, and four" is: let each one of you marry two, three, or four, as it is said: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women and then do not produce four witnesses, lash them eighty lashes﴾ [Surah an-Nur, 4].

* *

As for His words "two, three, and four" (mathna wa thulatha wa ruba'), their inflection has been left off because they are deviated from "ithnan," "thalatha," and "arba'a," just as "Umar" is deviated from "Amir," and "Zufar" from "Zafir," so his inflection is left off. Likewise "ahad," "thana," "mawhad," "mathna," "mathlath," and "marba'" are not inflected, all of that for the reason mentioned, the deviation from its forms. What indicates that this is so, and that the masculine and feminine are equal in it, is what has been said in this surah and in "Surat Fatir" [1]: "mathna wa thulatha wa ruba'" is meant to refer to "wings," and "wings" is masculine. Also it is not annexed to what "thalatha" and "thalath" are annexed to, and "al" (the definite article) does not enter it. This is evidence that it is a name for a number that is definite; had it been indefinite, "al" would have entered it and it would have been annexed as "thalatha" and "arba'a" are annexed. [See al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:254, 255.] What clarifies this is the statement of Tamim ibn Ubayy ibn Muqbil:

You see the blue gadflies beneath its chest,
single and in pairs, their neighing has struck them down.

[From a long qasida of his which I transmitted long ago; Ma'ani al-Qur'an of al-Farra 1:255, 345; al-Hayawan 7:233; al-Lisan (n-ʿ-r, f-r-d, ṣ-ʿ-q, th-n-y). It is found also later in the tafsir 7:184 (Bulaq). He describes his horse, and after the line: "Prostrate and fallen, as if it were / threads of a woven garment that its weaver twisted." The line is also narrated as "al-nuʿarat al-khudr" and "fard wa mathna." Al-Nuʿarat is the plural of nuʿra: a large gadfly, blue-eyed, green, with a sting at the tip of its tail with which it stings solid-hoofed animals, harming them, and sometimes enters a donkey's nose and makes it rear its head so nothing turns it back. "Al-labān": the chest of a solid-hoofed animal. "Asʿaqatha": killed them. "Sawahiluhu" is the plural of sahila, a verbal noun of the form fa'ila meaning neighing, as one says "rawaghi al-ibil," meaning its roaring. His saying in the second line "fariswan" means slain, that he has preyed upon it, crushed and destroyed it. "Al-khayyuta" is the plural of khayt, like fuhula and bulha, plurals of fahl and ba'l. "Al-mari": a worn-out garment. He describes the gadflies that have fainted, as if from their softness in their exhaustion they were threads that a twisting spinner twisted out of a worn cloth.]

He made "ahad wa mathna" refer to "al-nuʿarat," which is definite. The Arabs may make them indefinite and then inflect them, as the poet said: [I do not know who said them.]

Indeed the youth who is smitten with its remembrance,
we slew him with it, between the twofold and the single...

[Ma'ani al-Qur'an of al-Farra 1:254. In the printed and manuscript editions the verse read: "we slew him with it, between the twofold and the single / with four of you and a fifth other / and a sixth with the darkness in Ma'bad's spear." As you see, it is patched together from the two verses I have set down from Ma'ani al-Qur'an, and what al-Tabari says here is the exact statement of al-Farra in his Ma'ani. "Sad" means sixth; they say "jaʾa sadisan wa sadiyan wa satan."]

with four of you, and another fifth,
and a sixth with the darkness in Ma'bad's spear.

What makes it clear that "thana" and "ahad" are not inflected is the statement of a poet: [He is Sakhr ibn ʿAmr al-Sulami, brother of al-Khansa.]

Indeed I have slain you, two by two and singly,
and left Murra like yesterday's retreating one.

[Majaz al-Qur'an 1:115; al-Aghani 13:139; al-Mukhassas 7:124; Sharh Adab al-Katib of al-Jawaliqi: 394; al-Battalyusi: 466; al-Khizana 4:474. It will also come in the tafsir 22:76 (Bulaq) and elsewhere, except that Ibn Qutayba in Adab al-Katib narrated it as "ka-amsi al-dabir," and the editor of the tafsir in this place followed him writing "ka-amsi al-dabir," but in the manuscript and in the other place in the tafsir it came correctly. They are two verses he said concerning his killing of Duraid ibn Harmala al-Mari, in a report mentioned, and after it: "And I struck Duraid with a spear-thrust, wide, spurting like a rent garment at the throat." "Al-tanja al-najla'": wide. "Azghalat" the spear-thrust with blood: it gushed out in gushes, i.e., gush by gush. "ʿAtta al-thawb" means he tore it. "Al-manhar" is the base of the throat of a camel, the upper part of its chest where it is slaughtered, i.e., one stabs it in its throat so the blood gushes out. As for the narration "ka-amsi al-dabir," al-Jawaliqi mentioned verses by Yazid ibn ʿAmr al-Sa'iq al-Kilabi: "You have hamstrung my camel under my saddle while it stood, and you struck my neighbor with a piercing arrow. When you ride, then wear your armor; indeed spears are discerning of the unarmored. When you wrong and devour your friend, injustice will leave you prostrate, stumbling. Indeed I will slay you two by two and singly, and I will leave your helper like yesterday's retreating one."]

And the statement of a poet: [He is ʿAmr Dhu al-Kalb, brother of Banu Kahil, who was a neighbor of Hudhayl. Abu ʿUbayda attributed it in Majaz al-Qur'an to Sakhr al-Ghayy al-Hudhali, which is a mistake.]

Death has decreed for you that it meet me,
one by one, one by one, in a lawful month.

[Diwan al-Hudhaliyyin 3:117; Majaz al-Qur'an of Abu ʿUbayda 1:115; al-Maʿani al-Kabir: 2840; al-Mukhassas 17:124; al-Aghani 13:139. The diwan's version is "fi al-shahr al-halal," and the author of al-Aghani erred in attributing the verse to Sakhr ibn ʿAmr, and narrated it as "fi al-shahr al-haram." His saying "manat lak" means: death has decreed for you that you meet me in a lawful month, alone, myself and you alone, so I will fell you without doubt. That is because he had met him before that in a sacred month and could not raise a weapon against him. He says after it: "And the duration of the fight when we meet is only the turning of a right hand to a left," meaning the fight between me and you lasts only as long as it takes to turn the right hand to the left.]

Nothing has been heard from the Arabs deflecting what exceeds "rubaʿ" and "marbaʿ" from its form: "khamas" and "mukhmas" are not heard from them, nor "sabaʿ" and "musbaʿ"; likewise what is above "rubaʿ," except in a verse of al-Kumayt. [In the printed edition: "in the verse of al-Kumayt," the correct reading being from the manuscript.] For it is narrated for him in "ten," "ʿishar," which is his saying:

So they did not wait for you until you threw
above the men qualities, ʿishar (tens).

[Majaz al-Qur'an of Abu ʿUbayda 1:116; al-Aghani 3:139; al-Lisan (ʿ-sh-r); al-Mukhassas 17:125; al-Jawaliqi 292, 293; al-Battalyusi: 467; al-Khizana 1:82, 83, from a qasida of al-Kumayt praising Aban ibn al-Walid ibn ʿAbd al-Malik, and before it: "They hoped for you before your years were complete, ten, and no teeth grew for you in succession (ittigar)." "For an early tooth or a pair, of your years, then they waited for you with expectation." His saying "wa la nabta fika ittigaran": ittigar means the child's teeth fell out and others replaced them. His saying "khasa aw zaka": singly or as a pair. His saying "fa-baqawka" from the phrase "baqaytu fulanan baqyan," meaning I waited for him and watched him. "Istaraythahu": he found him slow. He says: they discerned in you nobility for a year or two from your birth, and hoped that you would be an obeyed lord of high renown, but you had hardly reached ten before your qualities exceeded those of the lords among men. As for Abu Jaʿfar's saying "he means ten by ten," it seems he means the great number of qualities by which he surpassed men.]

He means: "ʿashran, ʿashran" (ten by ten). It is said that nothing else has been heard. [See this whole section in al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:254, 255, and Abu ʿUbayda's Majaz al-Qur'an 1:114–116.]

* *

And as for His saying, "But if you fear that you will not be just, then [marry only] one," the accusative in "one" (wāḥidah) is read with the sense: "If you fear that you will not be just" in what is required of you regarding justice toward the women beyond one whom you take in marriage, "then marry one of them." [[In the printed edition and manuscript: "fīmā yalzimukum min al-'adl mā zād 'alā al-wāḥidah ..." which does not make sense; the correct reading is "fīmā zād" as I have established it.]] in what God has made obligatory for them upon you.

Had the reading come in the nominative (rafʿ) in this place, it would be permissible, with the sense: "then one is sufficient," or "then one is adequate," as the Exalted said: ﴿And if they are not two men, then a man and two women﴾ [Surat al-Baqarah: 282]. [[See al-Farrā's Maʿānī al-Qurʾān 1: 255.]]

* *

If someone says to us: You know that what is lawful for you from among all free women is marrying up to four, so how is it said: "Marry what seems good to you of women, two, three, or four," when that makes nine?¹ [[See al-Nāsikh wa-l-Mansūkh by Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās: 92.]]

It is said: The interpretation of that is: "Marry what seems good to you of women: either two, if you are secure from injustice from yourselves in what is owed to them upon you; or three, if you do not fear that; or four, if you are secure from that regarding them."

What confirms the correctness of this is His saying: "But if you fear that you will not be just, then [marry only] one," for the meaning is: If you fear [injustice] regarding the two, then marry one. Then He said: And if you fear that you will not be just even with the one, then [take] what your right hands possess.

* *

If someone says: Since the command and prohibition of God are for obligation and binding, until there is proof that it is for instruction, guidance and information, and the Exalted said: "Marry what seems good to you of women," which is a command, is there any evidence that it is among the commands that are not in the manner of binding obligation?

It is said: Yes. The evidence for that is His saying: "But if you fear that you will not be just, then [marry only] one." Thus it is known by that that His saying: "Marry what seems good to you of women," although its form is that of a command, its meaning is an indication of a prohibition against marrying those women regarding whom the one marrying fears injustice in number, not the meaning of a command to marry. For what is intended is: "And if you fear that you will not act justly toward orphans, then you feel scrupulous about them, so likewise be scrupulous regarding women, and do not marry except those regarding whom you are secure from injustice, from one up to four, which I have made lawful for you."

We have already explained in another place that the Arabs express speech in the form of a command while its meaning is a prohibition, or a threat and warning, as the Exalted said: ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾ [Surat al-Kahf: 29], and as He said: ﴿Let them disbelieve in what We have given them, and enjoy yourselves; but you will soon know﴾ [Surat al-Naḥl: 55; Surat al-Rūm: 34]. That came in the form of a command, while what is meant is a threat, warning, deterrence and prohibition. Likewise His saying: "Marry what seems good to you of women" means, as a prohibition: "Do not marry except what seems good to you of women."

* *

Upon the manner we have described regarding the meaning of His saying "or what your right hands possess," the people of interpretation (ahl al-taʾwīl) have said.

Those who said that:

8482 – Bishr ibn Muʿādh related to us, saying: Yazīd related to us, saying: Saʿīd related to us, from Qatādah: "But if you fear that you will not be just, then [marry only] one, or what your right hands possess," he says: If you fear that you will not be just with one, then what your right hand possesses.

8483 – Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn related to us, saying: Aḥmad ibn al-Mufaḍḍal related to us, saying: Asbāṭ related to us, from al-Suddī: "or what your right hands possess," the slave-concubines.

8484 – It was related to me from ʿAmmār, saying: Ibn Abī Jaʿfar related to us, from his father, from al-Rabīʿ: "But if you fear that you will not be just, then [marry only] one, or what your right hands possess," if you fear that you will not be just with one, then what your right hand possesses.

8485 – Yaḥyā ibn Abī Ṭālib related to me, saying: Yazīd related to us, saying: Juwaybir related to us, from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, regarding His saying: "But if you fear that you will not be just," he said: In intercourse and love.

* *

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying: ﴿That is more suitable that you not deviate﴾ (3).

Abū Jaʿfar said: By that the Exalted means: "And if you fear that you will not be just regarding two, three or four, and you marry one, or fear that you will not be just regarding the one, and so you take what your right hands possess, then that is 'more suitable' (adnā), meaning: closer, 'that you not deviate' (allā taʿūlū)," meaning: that you not act unjustly nor incline [unfairly].

* *

From it is said: "ʿāla al-rajul yaʿūlu ʿawlan wa-ʿayālah," when he inclined and acted unjustly. And from it: "ʿawl al-farāʾiḍ" (the increase of the shares in inheritance), because when their portions increased, deficiency entered them.

As for [ʿāla meaning] need, one says: "ʿāla al-rajul ʿaylah," when he became needy, as the poet said: [[He is Aḥīḥah ibn al-Julāḥ.]]

"The poor man does not know when his wealth will come, and the wealthy man does not know when he will become needy."

Meaning: he becomes impoverished.

* *

The people of interpretation have said in accordance with what we have said regarding that.

Those who said that:

8486 – Ḥumayd ibn Masʿadah related to us, saying: Yazīd ibn Zurayʿ related to us, saying: Yūnus related to us, from al-Ḥasan: "That is more suitable that you not deviate," he said: al-ʿawl is inclining regarding women.

8487 – Ibn Ḥumayd related to us, saying: Ḥakkām related to me, from ʿAnbasah, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, from al-Qāsim ibn Abī Bazzah, from Mujāhid regarding His saying: "That is more suitable that you not deviate," he says: Do not incline.

8488 – Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr related to me, saying: Abū ʿĀṣim related to us, saying: ʿĪsā related to us, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid regarding His saying: "That is more suitable that you not deviate," that you not incline.

8489 – al-Muthannā related to me, saying: Abū Ḥudhayfah related to us, saying: Shabl related to us, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, the same.

8490 – Muḥammad ibn al-Muthannā related to us, saying: Abū al-Nuʿmān Muḥammad ibn al-Faḍl related to us, saying: Hushaym related to us, saying: Dāwūd ibn Abī Hind informed us, from ʿIkrimah: "allā taʿūlū," he said: that you not incline. Then he said: Have you not heard the saying of Abū Ṭālib:

"By a balance of justice, its weight not inclining [ghayr ʿāʾil]." [[Sīrat Ibn Hishām 1: 296, and many others. From the poem which they claim Abū Ṭālib composed, in which he confronted the Quraysh regarding the matter of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and said in it that he would never abandon or leave the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for anything, until he perishes defending him. He says before the verse: "May God repay us, [regarding] ʿAbd Shams and Nawfal, with a swift punishment for evil, not delayed."
The verse is also transmitted in the version Abū Jaʿfar mentioned; and it is also transmitted: "lā yaḥiṣṣu shaʿīrah," from ḥiṣṣ al-shaʿr, when one removes it. "Shaʿīrah" in this version is a diminutive of "shaʿrah" (a hair); in the other versions it is "shaʿīrah" with a fatḥah on the shīn and a kasrah on the ʿayn, meaning one grain of barley (shaʿīr), the well-known seed, which is the smallest unit of weight for gold and silver, a grain of barley of medium size that has not been husked, from whose ends what has extended has been cut off; they also call it "ḥabbah" (a grain). See above 4: 586, note 2, regarding the explanation of "ḥabbah." This meaning was not specified by the lexicographers, so it was specified there. His saying "lā takhussu shaʿīrah" means: do not diminish the amount of a grain of barley. And his saying "taghull" is from the expression "ghalla yaghullu ghulūlan," when he betrayed or stole.]]

8491 – al-Muthannā related to me, saying: Ḥajjāj related to us, saying: Ḥammād ibn Zayd related to us, from al-Zubayr, from Ḥurayth, from ʿIkrimah regarding this verse: "allā taʿūlū," he said: that you not incline. He said: And he recited a verse of poetry which he claimed Abū Ṭālib had said:

"By a balance of justice that does not diminish a grain of barley, and a weigher of truthfulness whose weight is not inclining [ghayr ʿāʾil]." [[Sīrat Ibn Hishām 1: 296, and many others. From the poem which they claim Abū Ṭālib composed... (the same note as above, repeated in the printed text).]]

* *

Abū Jaʿfar said: This verse is also transmitted in a version other than this one:

"By a balance of truthfulness that does not cheat a grain of barley, for it there is a witness from itself, not inclining [ghayr ʿāʾil]." [[Sīrat Ibn Hishām 1: 296, and many others. (The same note as above, repeated in the printed text).]]

* *

8492 – Yaʿqūb ibn Ibrāhīm related to me, saying: Hushaym related to us, from Mughīrah, from Ibrāhīm regarding His saying: "allā taʿūlū," he said: that you not incline.

8493 – al-Muthannā related to me, saying: ʿAmr ibn ʿAwn related to us, saying: Hushaym informed us, from Mughīrah, from Ibrāhīm, the same.

8494 – al-Muthannā related to me, saying: ʿAmr ibn ʿAwn related to us, saying: Hushaym informed us, from Abū Isḥāq al-Kūfī, who said: ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān (may God be pleased with him) wrote to the people of Kufa regarding something they reproached him for: "Indeed I am not a balance that does not incline (lā aʿūl)."

8495 – Abū Kurayb related to us, saying: ʿUthhām ibn ʿAlī related to us, saying: Ismāʿīl ibn Abī Khālid related to us, from Abū Mālik regarding His saying: "adnā allā taʿūlū," he said: do not incline. [[Report 8495: In the printed edition: "ʿAbbād ibn ʿAlī," but the scribe of the manuscript had written "ʿAbbād" then changed the dāl into a mīm and did not dot the word, so the matter became confused for the editor; the correct reading is "ʿUthhām" (ʿAthām), namely "ʿUthhām ibn ʿAlī al-ʿĀmirī," the teacher of Abū Kurayb, whose biography was given under no. 337.]]

8496 – Bishr ibn Muʿādh related to us, saying: Yazīd related to us, saying: Saʿīd related to us, from Qatādah: "dhālika adnā allā taʿūlū," closer that you not incline.
