This is confusion and a wonder among wonders. I did not find anyone who mentioned this "Damrah," and al-Tabari did not mention her, as al-Hafiz erred in mentioning her and giving her a separate biography, and he was mistaken. This is among the proofs of al-Hafiz's haste in composing his book al-Isabah, and of the validity of what was said, that it was nothing but a draft that he did not finalize, so he did not refine it.

This difference requires lengthy discussion; I have limited myself to this extent of it.

As for "al-Aswad ibn Khalaf," he is "al-Aswad ibn Khalaf ibn As'ad ibn 'Amir ibn Bayadah al-Khuza'i," and he is not "al-Aswad ibn Khalaf ibn 'Abd Yaghuth," as al-Hafiz mentioned in al-Isabah, and Ibn Sa'd (5:339). If that is so, then he is the brother of "'Abd Allah ibn Khalaf ibn As'ad," the father of "Talhat al-Talhat." I did not find that Ibn Hajar pointed out in al-Isabah the report of his marrying his father's wife, although he mentioned it in the biographies of the women mentioned in the report, and in the biography of his father's wife "Humaynah bint Abi Talhah." Likewise Ibn al-Athir did not mention it at all, although he mentioned it in his biography of "Humaynah." In al-Isabah and Ibn al-Athir, it is "Khalaf ibn Asad ibn 'Asim ibn Bayadah," which is a scribal distortion; rather it is "As'ad ibn 'Amir."

This also requires more thorough investigation, which is not the place for it.

As for the report of "Manzur ibn Zabban ibn Sayyar al-Mazini," there is a difference about the account of his story which al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar mentioned in his biography and in the biography of "Mulaykah." He preferred that this incident took place in the era of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, and that 'Umar separated them, which was hard on him, for he loved her, and he said verses about her, from his own composition:

By the life of my father, a religion that separates us, between you and me, by force... indeed it is great.

His story is in al-Aghani (12:194) (Dar al-Kutub).

8941. Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraj, who said: I said to 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah: A man marries a woman, then does not see her until he divorces her; is she lawful for his son? He said: She is "mursalah" (dispatched). [[This is how it came in the manuscript and the printed edition here, and in number 8957 below and in al-Durr al-Manthur (2:134), "mursalah." What came in the lexicographical books is "imra'ah mirasil." They said: She is the one whom her husband has parted from in any manner, whether he died or divorced her. It was also said: She is the one whose husband has died, or who senses from him that he intends to divorce her, so she adorns herself for another. It was also said: She is the one who has been divorced several times. And it was said: She is the one who invites proposals. All of that is close to one another, for when a woman's husband dies or divorces her, she is apt to invite proposals and seek the path to marriage. In a hadith: "A man from the Ansar married a woman who was mirasil," meaning thayyib (previously married), and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Why not a virgin you can play with and who plays with you?!" The lexicographers said: "Al-mirasil is the one who has aged and still has some youthfulness left." It seems that explaining this term requires combining all these sayings, and it is said: she is the one who has left youthfulness, so her husband died or divorced her, and she is more in need than one in her youth of seeking adornment and inviting proposals, due to the scarcity of men's desire for her, compared to their desire for beautiful, youthful virgins.

As for this report, if the wording "mursalah" is correct, its interpretation is: she is the one whom her husband has dispatched, that is, divorced; and what is meant by it is the divorced virgin who is treated in judgment as a thayyib (previously married woman). If the correct reading is "hiya mirasil," then one should add to the meaning of "mirasil" that she is a virgin who has been divorced, so she is in the position of a thayyib. See the following report.]] Allah, the Exalted, said: "And do not marry those whom your fathers married of women." He said: I said to 'Ata': What is His saying: "except what has already passed"? He said: The sons used to marry the wives of their fathers in the Jahiliyyah. [[This report will come under number 8957, with a difference in its wording; see the note on it there.]]

8942. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah ibn Salih narrated to me, from 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: "And do not marry those whom your fathers married of women," the verse, he says: Every woman whom your father married and your son married, whether he consummated the marriage or not, she is forbidden to you.

\* \*

There is a difference concerning the meaning of His saying: "except what has already passed."

Some of them said: Its meaning is: "But what has already passed, leave it." And they said: This is an exceptive that is disconnected (istithna' munqati').

\* \*

Others said: The meaning of that is: "And do not marry the marriage of your fathers" = meaning: "And do not marry as they married," in the corrupt ways in which they married, which are not permissible in Islam like them: "Indeed it was an abomination and hateful and an evil way," meaning: the marriage of your fathers which they contracted in their Jahiliyyah was an abomination, hateful and an evil way, except what has already passed of marriage from you in your Jahiliyyah, of which the initiation of the like is not permissible in Islam; for it is pardoned for you.

They said: His saying: "And do not marry those whom your fathers married of women" is like one saying to a man: "Do not do what I did," and "Do not eat as I ate," meaning: "Do not eat as I ate, and do not do as I did."

\* \*

Others said: The meaning of that is: "And do not marry those whom your fathers married of women," by a permissible marriage whose contract was valid among them, "except what has already passed of them of the forms of fornication among them, for their marrying those women is lawful for you, because they were not their lawful wives, and what occurred from your fathers and them of that was an abomination, hateful and an evil way."

Mention of who said that:

8943. Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying: "And do not marry those whom your fathers married of women, except what has already passed," the verse: It is fornication. "Indeed it was an abomination and hateful and an evil way." So he added here "hateful" (al-maqt). [[He means by his saying "he added here," he added to what came in Surat al-Isra' (32): "And do not approach fornication; indeed it is an abomination and an evil way."]]

\* \*

Abu Ja'far said: The most correct of the sayings about this, in accordance with what the people of interpretation have said in its interpretation, is that its meaning is: "And do not marry from among women the marriage of your fathers, except what has already passed of you and went by in the Jahiliyyah; indeed it was an abomination, hateful and an evil way." So His saying "from among women" is connected to His saying "And do not marry," and His saying "what your fathers married" is in the sense of the verbal noun (masdar), and His saying "except what has already passed" is in the sense of the disconnected exception, because it is apt in its place: "But what has already passed and went by" = "indeed it was an abomination, hateful and an evil way."

\* \*

If one says: How can this view agree with the view of those whose opinion you mentioned from the people of interpretation, when you know that those whose opinion you mentioned on this said only: this verse was revealed concerning the prohibition of marrying the wives of fathers, and you mention that they were forbidden only to marry the marriage of them?

It is said to him: We only said that this is the interpretation that agrees with the apparent sense of the revelation, [[In the printed edition and the manuscript: "And if we say that this is the interpretation," a statement that does not stand with what follows, and the correct wording that fits the context is what I have established.]] since "ma" in the speech of the Arabs is for other than human beings; and if what was intended by it were the prohibition of the wives of fathers only, to the exclusion of all the marriages of their fathers that were forbidden, the initiation of their like in Islam through the prohibition of Allah, exalted is His remembrance, [[In the printed edition: "...forbidden, the initiation of their like was begun in Islam," and it did not properly read the manuscript's "ibtada'" and changed it into something that corrupts the sentence.]] it would have been said: "And do not marry those whom your fathers married of women, except what has already passed," for that is what is well known in the speech of the Arabs, since "man" is for human beings and "ma" for other than them, and it would not have been said: "And do not marry what your fathers married of women." [[In the manuscript and the printed edition: "since 'man' is for human beings, and 'ma' is for other than them, and do not say: and do not marry what your fathers married of women," a statement that does not stand at all. The correct wording of his saying is "wa-lam yuqal" (and it was not said), in the passive, and it is coordinated with his earlier saying: "it would have been said: and do not marry those whom your fathers married." The copyist was confused by the repetition of the verse twice, so his eye slipped, and he dropped from the sentence what I have placed between the parentheses above, which the sentence neither completes nor stands without, and I exercised judgment in restoring it from his speech and argument, as you see.]] [As for His saying, exalted is His remembrance: "And do not marry what your fathers married of women,"] it includes within "ma," [[In the manuscript: "it includes what was of the marriages of their fathers," which is a slip and error by the copyist, as the speech became confused for him; the correct wording is what the editor of the first printed edition inferred, as I have placed it.]] what was of the marriages of their fathers that they contracted in their Jahiliyyah. So He forbade them in Islam through this verse the marriage of the wives of fathers, and every marriage other than that which Allah, exalted is His remembrance, [forbade] the initiation of its like in Islam, [[What is between the brackets is an addition that is indispensable, dropped from the manuscript and the printed edition.]] of what the people of the Jahiliyyah used to marry in their polytheism.

\* \*

As for the meaning of His saying: "except what has already passed," it means: except what has already gone by. "Indeed it was an abomination": He says: indeed your marriage that has passed from you is like the marriage of your fathers, which is forbidden to you, the initiation of its like in Islam after My prohibition of that to you, "abomination," He says: disobedience [[See the interpretation of "fahishah" in what has passed: 115, note 2, and the references there.]] "and hateful and an evil way," [[Abu Ja'far did not explain "al-maqt" here, nor in the rest of the places where "al-maqt" is mentioned, except by implication. "Al-maqt" is the most intense hatred; then this marriage that they used to contract in the Jahiliyyah was named "the marriage of hatred" (nikah al-maqt), and the child born from it was called "al-maqta" by way of attribution.]] that is: an evil path and a method, [[See the interpretation of "al-sabil" in what has passed: 37, note 6, and the references there. As for "sa'a," Abu Ja'far did not clarify its meaning, and did not mention that the grammarians of Arabic consider it a rigid verb that runs in the manner of "ni'ma" and "bi'sa," although his interpretation included that. This is among the evidences that he abridged this interpretation in many places.]] of what you used to do in your Jahiliyyah of the marriages that you used to contract.

[[Abu Ja'far's argument in this place is the argument of a man who is discerning, knowledgeable of speech and its positions, capable of mastering the derivation of meanings that spread out, following the context of the rulings and reports in the Book of his Lord, and expert in what the Arabs were upon in their Jahiliyyah.

The scholars have responded to Abu Ja'far's view, and some of them said: it is a view that is not sound. They mentioned that "ma" may apply to kinds of rational beings, although it does not apply to individuals of rational beings, according to those who hold that position. They regarded al-Tabari's view that "ma" is verbal and remains in the sense of the verbal noun as a weak opinion. However, Abu Ja'far's position is sound and correct, and their argument against him does not harm it. What led them to that was Abu Ja'far's failure to clarify the argument for his view. And I am saying about that what will suffice, God willing.]]

That is because those who rejected Abu Ja'far's view (may Allah have mercy on him) held that this verse is an explicit text prohibiting only the marriage of a man to his father's wives, and it seems they reasoned that if "ma" were read as a verbal particle (*mașdariyyah*, a particle that turns the following clause into a verbal noun), then there would be no clear text in the verses prohibiting the wives of fathers apart from this. The correct view is otherwise. Allah, glorified and exalted, has prohibited the marriage of fathers' wives, which the people of the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period of ignorance) used to practise, in His saying in the nineteenth verse of Surah al-Nisa earlier: ﴿O you who believe, it is not lawful for you to inherit women against their will﴾. Abu Ja'far said in its explanation: "It is not lawful for you to inherit the marriage of the women of your relatives and fathers against their will," and he cited there the reports that describe the form of marrying fathers' wives and relatives in general. What he cited there contains an explanation of the form of marrying fathers' wives and relatives by inheritance, as the people of the Jahiliyyah knew it. Thus this verse is a decisive and clear text prohibiting the marriage of fathers' wives and relatives by inheritance, in the form known to the people of the Jahiliyyah, because they knew the marrying of fathers' wives only in this form which Allah explained in His Book, and whose description the reports agreed upon: that a man succeeds his father in marriage to his wife.

I incline to the view that Allah, blessed and exalted, said: "It is not lawful for you to inherit women against their will," mentioning their inheritance against their will, then He followed that with the prohibition of restraining women in general (*ʿaḍl*, preventing a woman from remarrying in order to keep her property), and with the explanation of their purpose in restraining women, which is to take away some of what they were given as their dowries. This is because the people of the Jahiliyyah only became entangled in marrying fathers' wives for one reason: taking what the fathers had given them of wealth, and so that the woman would not take away the wealth her fathers-in-law had left her. Therefore He followed it with the general prohibition of restraint, since their conduct towards their fathers' wives was also restraint, and their purpose in it was the same as their purpose in restraining their own women.

Moreover, the people of the Jahiliyyah did not engage in marrying paternal aunts, maternal aunts or sisters, as you will see later, but rather they disapproved of it. Their disapproval of marrying fathers' wives, who were in the position of their mothers during their fathers' lifetimes, should have been part of their practice and custom; but love of wealth led them to oppose that.

Then Allah followed that, as Abu Ja'far said, "with the prohibition of the marriages of their fathers that they used to contract in the Jahiliyyah. So by this verse He forbade them to marry fathers' wives and every marriage other than it, forbidding in Islam the beginning of the like of what the people of the Jahiliyyah used to contract." Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, has mentioned in the hadith of al-Bukhari (*al-Fath* 9:158) that the marriage of the Jahiliyyah was of four kinds, among them "the marriage of people today," and then she enumerated the types of marriage and described them. Islam confirmed from among them one kind only: a man proposes to another man for his ward or his daughter, he gives her a dowry, and then he marries her.

This verse therefore nullifies all the types of marriage of the Jahiliyyah, whatever was corrupt marriage, such as *al-istibḍāʿ* (a husband sending his wife to a man of noble stock to conceive from him), the marriage of prostitutes, the *nikāḥ al-badal* (exchange of wives), and *al-shighār* (a marriage where two men exchange their daughters or sisters without dowry). All of that was: "an indecency and hateful and an evil way," as you know from its description in the hadith of Aisha. It includes, as Abu Ja'far said, the marriage of fathers' wives.

Then Allah, glorified and exalted, followed this verse, which forbade all the marriages of the Jahiliyyah, with another verse that forbade every marriage that was known among other nations besides the Arabs, or among religious communities other than the religion of Islam. So He said: "Forbidden to you are your mothers, your daughters, your sisters, your paternal aunts, your maternal aunts," to the end of the verse. The Arabs never knew the marriage of mothers, daughters, sisters, paternal aunts or maternal aunts; rather that was found among others, such as the Egyptians, the Jews and their like, where a man marries his sister, his paternal aunt or his maternal aunt. Among the evidence that the Arabs did not know the marriage of sisters, nor the marriage of paternal aunts or maternal aunts, is that in their Jahiliyyah they used to swear to divorce their women or to forbid them to themselves, or to abandon them, by saying to the wife: "You are to me like the back of my sister," or "like the back of my paternal aunt," or "like the back of my maternal aunt." This was for them a prohibition upon themselves of approaching the wife. This is a topic that I have not found anyone to have given its due; perhaps I will be enabled to cover it fully in another place, if Allah wills. It is an important topic in the interpretation of these verses, and Allah is the One whose help is sought.

So this last verse is not specific to the marriages of the people of the Jahiliyyah; rather it is a prohibition of every marriage that Allah disliked for the believers, of what was among the nations before them either permitted or practised, or of which some was rare among them and not as well known as the marriages of the Jahiliyyah which Allah mentioned in the inheritance of fathers' and relatives' wives, and which Aisha mentioned in her hadith. Its prohibition came in general terms in His saying: ﴿And do not marry those women whom your fathers married﴾, with the meaning of "ma" as a verbal particle, as Abu Ja'far held.

Written by: Mahmud Muhammad Shakir.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 4, verse 23 (part 1 of 2):

The interpretation of His words: ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers, your daughters, your sisters, your paternal aunts, your maternal aunts, your brother's daughters, your sister's daughters, your mothers who have nursed you, your milk-sisters, your wives' mothers, and your stepdaughters under your guardianship, born of the wives with whom you have consummated the marriage; but if you have not consummated the marriage with them, there is no blame on you; and the wives of your sons who are of your loins; and that you combine two sisters, except for what has already passed. Indeed Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾ (23).

Abu Ja'far said: By this, may His remembrance be exalted, is meant: "Marriage to your mothers is forbidden to you." The word "marriage" is omitted, being sufficiently indicated by the context.

Ibn 'Abbas used to say concerning this:

8944 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Za'idah narrated to us, from al-Thawri, from al-A'mash, from Isma'il ibn Raja', from 'Umayr, mawla of Ibn 'Abbas, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Seven are forbidden by blood ancestry, and seven by marriage affinity." Then he recited: "Forbidden to you are your mothers," until he reached: "and that you combine two sisters, except for what has already passed." He said: "And the seventh is: 'And do not marry what your fathers married of women.'"

8945 - Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Mu'ammal narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Isma'il ibn Raja', from 'Umayr, mawla of Ibn 'Abbas, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Seven are forbidden by blood, and seven by marriage." Then he recited: "Forbidden to you are your mothers," up to His words: "and married women, except what your right hands possess."

8946 - Ibn Bashshar narrated to us again, saying: Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Isma'il ibn Raja', from 'Umayr, mawla of Ibn 'Abbas, from Ibn 'Abbas, the like of it. [[The narrations 8944–8946: Isma'il ibn Raja' ibn Rabi'ah al-Zubaydi, whom Muslim and the four compilers related from; he is trustworthy, and used to gather the children of his scribes and narrate to them so that his hadith would not be forgotten! And "'Umayr, mawla of Ibn 'Abbas" is 'Umayr ibn 'Abd Allah al-Hilali, mawla of Umm al-Fadl. Trustworthy.
Al-Hakim also transmitted the report of Ibn 'Abbas in al-Mustadrak 2: 304, by way of Muhammad ibn Kathir, from Sufyan, from al-A'mash, from Isma'il ibn Raja', and said: "This is a sound hadith according to the conditions of the two Shaykhs, though they did not record it," and al-Dhahabi agreed. The Hafiz referred to it in al-Fath 5: 133, attributing it to al-Tabarani. Also Ibn Kathir in his Tafsir 2: 390.]]

8947 - Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Dhi'b, from al-Zuhri, with something similar.

8948 - Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Habib, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Seven are forbidden to you by lineage, and seven by marriage." "Forbidden to you are your mothers," the verse. [[The report 8948: al-Bukhari related it in his Sahih by this chain (al-Fath 5: 132) with a different wording, and al-Bayhaqi related it in its wording in al-Sunan al-Kubra 7: 158. The wording of al-Bukhari: "Seven are forbidden by lineage, and seven by marriage," like the preceding report. See also Tafsir Ibn Kathir 2: 390.]]

8949 - Ibn Wakf' narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to us, from 'Ali ibn Salih, from Simak ibn Harb, from 'Ikrimah, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Forbidden to you are your mothers, your daughters, your sisters," and said: Allah forbade seven by lineage and seven by marriage. Then he recited: "and your wives' mothers and your stepdaughters," the verse.

8950 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Jarir narrated to us, from Mutarrif, from 'Amr ibn Salim, mawla of the Ansar, who said: Seven are forbidden by lineage, and seven by marriage: "Forbidden to you are your mothers, your daughters, your sisters, your paternal aunts, your maternal aunts, your brother's daughters, and your sister's daughters" — and by marriage: "your mothers who nursed you, your milk-sisters, your wives' mothers, and your stepdaughters under your guardianship, born of the wives with whom you have consummated the marriage; but if you have not consummated the marriage with them, there is no blame on you; and the wives of your sons who are of your loins; and that you combine two sisters, except for what has already passed" — then he said: "And married women, except what your right hands possess" — "and do not marry what your fathers married of women." [[The report 8950: "'Amr ibn Salim," is Abu 'Uthman al-Ansari, judge of Merv; there is much difference about him and about his father's name. It is said his name is his kunya, and he is well known by his kunya, but al-Tabari mentioned him without the kunya and without his father's name.]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: All those whom Allah, may He be exalted, named and whose prohibition He made clear in this verse are forbidden; their marriage is not permitted for the man upon whom Allah has forbidden it, by the consensus of the entire Ummah, with no disagreement among them on this, except regarding the mothers of our wives with whom their husbands have not consummated the marriage. Concerning marrying them there is a difference among some of the early Companions: if the daughter is separated from her husband before consummation, are they among the "unspecified" prohibitions (al-mubhamat), or are they among those for whom consummation is a condition regarding their daughters?

All the scholars, early and late, said: They are among the al-mubhamat [["al-mubhamat" (the absolutely prohibited) are those prohibitions that are never lifted in any way or for any cause, such as the prohibition of the mother and the sister and the like. al-Qurtubi said in his Tafsir (5: 107): "The prohibition of mothers is general in every case, not specified in any respect, and therefore the scholars call it (al-mubham), meaning there is no door to it and no path to it, due to the closing and strength of the prohibition." I will present to you what al-Azhari said in explaining it, saying: "I have seen many scholars take this to mean the matter being unspecified and ambiguous, meaning problematic — and this is an error." He said: "Many people of knowledge do not distinguish between the mubham and the non-mubham among horse colors, which is that which has no marking differing from the majority of its color."

He said: When Ibn 'Abbas was asked about His words, "and your wives' mothers," while Allah did not specify consummation with them, he answered: "This is of the unspecified prohibition, which has no aspect other than prohibition, whether you have consummated the marriage with the women or not. So the mothers of your wives are forbidden to you in every respect."

As for His words, "and your stepdaughters under your guardianship, born of the wives with whom you have consummated the marriage," the stepdaughters here are not among the unspecified, because they have two clarified aspects: they are permitted in one and forbidden in the other. So when one has consummated with the mothers of the stepdaughters, the stepdaughters are forbidden; and if one has not consummated with the mothers of the stepdaughters, they are not forbidden.

This is the explanation of the "mubham" which Ibn 'Abbas intended, so understand it.

Ibn al-Athir commented on this, saying: "This explanation from al-Azhari applies only to the stepdaughters and the mothers, not to the wives (halail), and in the beginning of the hadith he made Ibn 'Abbas's question concern the wives, not the stepdaughters," and this commentary is not good.

Then see al-Batalyawsi's "al-Insaf": 28, 29.] and it is forbidden for whoever marries a woman whose mother... [[Meaning: whoever marries a woman, her mother is forbidden to him.]] whether he has consummated the marriage with the wife he married or not. They said: The condition of consummation applies to the stepdaughter, not to the mother; as for the mother of the wife, the prohibition is absolute. They said: If it were permissible that the condition of consummation in His words, "and your stepdaughters under your guardianship, born of the wives with whom you have consummated the marriage," should refer back to "and your wives' mothers" as its connected clause, then it would be permissible for the exception in His words, "and married women, except what your right hands possess," to apply to all the prohibitions in His words, "Forbidden to you," the verse. They said: The consensus of all that the exception there refers only to what immediately precedes it, "and married women," is clearer evidence that the condition in "born of the wives with whom you have consummated the marriage" refers to what immediately precedes it in "and your stepdaughters under your guardianship, born of the wives with whom you have consummated the marriage," and not to the mothers of our wives.

* *

It is related from some of the early scholars that he used to say: The marriage to the mothers of our wives with whom we have not consummated is permitted, and their ruling in this is the ruling of the stepdaughters.

Mention of those who said so:

8951 - Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi 'Adi and 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, from Sa'id, from Qatadah, from Khallas ibn 'Amr, from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him: concerning a man who married a woman and divorced her before consummating with her, may he marry her mother? He said: She is in the position of the stepdaughter.

8952 - Hamid ibn Mas'adah narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zuray' narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, saying: Qatadah narrated to us, from Khallas, from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: She is in the position of the stepdaughter. [[The two reports 8951, 8952: Khallas ibn 'Amr al-Hajari is trustworthy, but scholars spoke about his hearing from 'Ali, and that his narration from him was from a written leaf he had; al-Bukhari stated this in al-Tarikh al-Kabir 2/1/208. For this reason al-Qurtubi said regarding this report: "The hadith of Khallas from 'Ali is not a valid proof, and its narration is not authentic according to the people of hadith knowledge; the authentic report from him is like the view of the majority."]]

8953 - Hamid narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, saying: Qatadah narrated to us, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, from Zayd ibn Thabit: that he used to say: If she dies while he is with her and he takes her inheritance, it is disliked that he marry her mother. And if he divorces her before consummating with her, then if he wishes, he may do so.

8954 - Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, from Zayd ibn Thabit, who said: If a man divorces his wife before consummating with her, there is no harm in his marrying her mother.

8955 - al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, saying: Ibn Jurayj said: 'Ikrimah ibn Khalid informed me that Mujahid said to him: "and your wives' mothers and your stepdaughters under your guardianship, born of the wives with whom you have consummated the marriage," both refer to consummation together. [[The report 8955: "'Ikrimah ibn Khalid ibn al-'As ibn Hisham al-Makhzumi," narrated from his father, Abu Hurayrah, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar and others. He is trustworthy. Some said: "munkar al-hadith," but they confused him with "'Ikrimah ibn Khalid ibn Salamah ibn al-'As ibn Hisham al-Makhzumi," and the two are different.
See what Ibn Kathir said on this subject in his Tafsir 2: 392–394, where he mentioned these reports.]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The first view is closer to the truth, namely the view of those who said: "The mother is among the unspecified (mubhamat)." Because Allah did not attach to them the condition of consummation with their daughters, as He attached that condition to the mothers of the stepdaughters, and because that is also the consensus of the authoritative body whose opposition is not permitted in what it has agreed upon. A report has also been related on this from the Prophet ﷺ, though there is doubt about its chain, namely:

8956 - al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Hibban ibn Musa narrated to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak informed us, saying: al-Muthanna ibn al-Sabah informed us, from 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "If a man marries a woman, it is not lawful for him to marry her mother, whether he has consummated with the daughter or not. And if he marries the mother and does not consummate with her and then divorces her, then if he wishes he may marry the daughter." [[The hadith 8956: al-Muthanna ibn al-Sabah al-Abna'i al-Makki, whose biography has passed at 4611. We add here that we consider his hadith to be good, because he became confused in later years, as we explained in the commentary on the Musnad, under hadith 6893.
Because of the discussion about him, al-Tabari held that there is doubt about the chain of this hadith.
Al-Bayhaqi also related it in al-Sunan al-Kubra 7: 160, by way of Ibn al-Mubarak, from al-Muthanna ibn al-Sabah. Then al-Bayhaqi said: "al-Muthanna ibn al-Sabah: not strong."
But al-Muthanna did not stand alone in narrating it. Al-Bayhaqi also related it, following the narration of al-Muthanna, by way of Ibn Lahi'ah, from 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, from the Prophet ﷺ, in similar wording. This is a strong follow-up to al-Muthanna, which removes what might be thought of as error in his narration. Ibn Kathir quoted this hadith from this narration of al-Tabari, 2: 394, within what he quoted from al-Tabari's words at this point.
al-Suyuti mentioned it, 2: 135, and added its attribution to 'Abd al-Razzaq and 'Abd ibn Humayd, and stated that al-Bayhaqi related it by the two routes we have mentioned.]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: This is a report, and although there is something in its chain, the consensus of the authoritative body upon the validity of this view makes us independent of supporting its soundness with other reports.

8957 - al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said to 'Ata': "A man marries a woman, has not seen her and has not had relations with her until he divorces her; is her mother lawful to him?" He said: "No, she is sent away." I said to 'Ata': "Did Ibn 'Abbas recite: 'and your wives' mothers to whom you have consummated'?" He said: "No," one after another [[The word "tatarra" means successive, one after another. The question about "tatarra" also came in a hadith related by Ibn Sa'd 2/2/131, from Qabath ibn Ushaym al-Laythi, where its explanation was "separately."]]. Hajjaj said: I asked Ibn Jurayj: "What is 'tatarra'?" He said: It is as if he said: "No! No!" [[The report 8957: This report has passed in brief with its chain, and with different wording, earlier at 8941; see the comment there.]]

* *

As for "al-rabā'ib" (stepdaughters), it is the plural of "rabībah," which is the daughter of a man's wife. She is called "rabībah" because of his raising her (tarbiyah), though she is originally "marbūbah," which was changed to "rabībah," just as it is said "hiya qatīlah" from "maqtūlah." [[In the print and manuscript: "qabīlah min maqbūlah" with a unified letter, which is not correct; the correct reading is as established here. The copyist may have written what he wrote because they say "rajul qatīl, and imra'ah qatīl," which is the well-known usage, but he overlooked that when they omit mention of the woman they say "hādhihi qatīlat banī fulān" and "marartu bi-qatīlah," and they did not say "marartu bi-qatīl" in this sense.]] It may also be said of the wife's husband: "huwa rabību ibn imra'atihi," meaning "huwa rābbuhu," just as one says "huwa khābir" and "khabīr," and "shāhid" and "shahīd." [[In the print: "jābir wa-jubayr" with a j, and in the manuscript the first lacks its dots and the second has a j, which is an error; nothing like that exists in Arabic. The correct form is as established, and "al-khābir wa-l-khabīr" means one who knows the news.]]

* *

The interpreters differed regarding the meaning of His words, "born of the wives with whom you have consummated the marriage."

Some of them said: The meaning of "consummation" (al-dukhūl) in this place is intercourse (al-jimā').

Mention of those who said so:

8958 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah ibn Salih narrated to me, from 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His words, "born of the wives with whom you have consummated the marriage," and that "consummation" means marriage.

* *

Others said: "Consummation" in this place means "the being alone" (al-tajrīd).

Mention of those who said so:

8959 - al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, saying: Ibn Jurayj said: I said to 'Ata': "His words, 'with whom you have consummated,' what is 'consummation with them'?" He said: That she is brought to him, and he uncovers her and examines her, and sits between her legs. [[In the print: "ya'us"; in the manuscript: "ya'īs"; the correct reading is as established. It is said "i'tassa al-shay'," meaning he touched and felt it to know its condition. This is among the words whose meaning the lexicons did not clarify, but its meaning is scattered throughout their discussions.]] I said: What if he does that in the house of her family? He said: It is the same, and that is enough! He has already made her daughter forbidden to him. I said: Is the stepdaughter forbidden on account of one who does this with her mother? Would my slave-girl not be forbidden to me if I did this with her mother? [[In the print and manuscript: "ala ma yahrum 'alayya min amati," which is not correct; the pure correct reading appears to be what I have established.]] He said: Yes, the same. 'Ata' said: If a man uncovers his slave-girl and sits between her legs, I forbid him her mother and her daughter.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The more correct of the two opinions in my view regarding the interpretation of this is what Ibn 'Abbas said, that the meaning of "al-dukhul" (consummation, sexual intercourse) is intercourse and marriage. For its meaning cannot be free of one of two matters: either it is in the apparent sense commonly understood for "dukhul" among people, which is reaching her by being alone with her, or it means sexual intercourse. And since there is consensus among all that a man's being alone with his wife does not make her daughter (from another marriage) forbidden to him if he divorces her before touching and intimacy with her, or before looking at her private part with desire, this indicates that the meaning of that is reaching her through intercourse.

Given that this is so, it is known that the correct interpretation of this is what we have stated.

* *

As for His saying: "And if you have not consummated with them, there is no blame upon you," it means: if you, O people, have not consummated with the mothers of your stepdaughters who are in your guardianship, by having intercourse with them until you divorced them, "then there is no blame upon you," meaning: there is no sin upon you in marrying those of your stepdaughters who are in such a state. [See the explanation of "al-junah" (blame, sin) previously: 3:230, 231 / 4:162, 566 / 5:70, 117, 138.]

* *

As for His saying: "And the wives of your sons who are from your loins," it means: and the wives of your sons who are from your loins.

* *

"Halā'il" is the plural of "halīlah," which is his wife. It has been said that a man's wife is called "halīlah" because she lawfully lies (yaḥull) with him on one bed.

* *

There is no disagreement among all the scholars that the wife of a man's son is forbidden to him to marry once his son has contracted marriage with her, whether he has consummated with her or not.

* *

If someone says: What do you say about the wives of sons by nursing (fosterage), since God Most High only forbade the wives of our sons from our loins?

It is said: The wives of sons by nursing and the wives of sons by birth are equal in prohibition. He only said, "And the wives of your sons who are from your loins," because its meaning is: the wives of your sons whom you have begotten, not the wives of your sons whom you have adopted, as:

8960 - Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to us, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: I said to 'Ata': Regarding His saying, "And the wives of your sons who are from your loins," he said: We were told, [In the manuscript and the printed edition: "kunna natahaddath" (we were narrating), which is an error; the correct reading is what is established, because 'Ata' narrates what he heard from the people of knowledge among his teachers. See Ibn Kathir 2: 396.] and God knows best, that it was revealed concerning Muhammad ﷺ when he married the wife of Zayd ibn Harithah, and the polytheists spoke about that, so it was revealed: "And the wives of your sons who are from your loins," and it was revealed: "And He has not made your adopted sons your sons" [Surah al-Ahzab: 4], and it was revealed: "Muhammad is not the father of any of your men" [Surah al-Ahzab: 40].

* *

As for His saying: "And that you combine two sisters," its meaning is: and it is forbidden for you to combine two sisters in your possession by marriage. So "an" (that) is in the nominative position, as if it were said: "And the combining of two sisters [is forbidden]."

[See the meanings of the Qur'an by al-Farra' 1: 260.]

* *

"Except what has already passed" — but what has passed of you. [See the explanation of "illa" and of "salafa" previously: 137, 138, footnote: 50.] "Indeed, Allah is ever Forgiving" — [In the manuscript and the printed edition: "fa-inna Allah," which I have adopted according to his method in tafsir, by mentioning the text of the verse.] of the sins of His servants if they repent to Him from them, "Merciful" toward them in what He imposed upon them of obligations, and He lightened for them and did not burden them beyond their capacity.

By this, He, mighty is His praise, informs that He is Forgiving toward whoever combined two sisters in marriage during his time of ignorance, before the prohibition of that, if he fears Allah, blessed and exalted, after its prohibition upon him, obeying Him by avoiding it; He is Merciful toward him and toward others among the people of obedience from His creation.

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on Surah 4, Verse 24 (Part 1 of 4)**

The exegesis (*ta'wil*, interpretation) of His words: ﴿And the married women, except those whom your right hands possess — the decree of Allah upon you﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By this, may His majesty be exalted, He means: Forbidden to you are the married women among the women, except those whom your right hands possess.

* *

The people of *ta'wil* differed concerning the "married women" (*al-muhsanat*) whom Allah intended in this verse.

Some of them said: They are the women who have husbands, excluding those among them who were taken captive. And "what the right hand possesses" refers to the captives whom the enemy separated from their husbands. They become lawful to whoever possesses them through the right hand, without a divorce having been pronounced by their husbands who are non-Muslim combatants (*harbi*).

*Those who said this, and their reports:*

8961 - Muhammad ibn Bashshar told us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman told us, saying: Isra'il told us, from Abu Husayn, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Every woman who has a husband, to have intercourse with her is adultery, except what you have taken captive.

8962 - Abu Kurayb told us, saying: Ibn 'Atiyyah told us, saying: Isra'il told us, from Abu Husayn, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, the like of it. [[The two reports 8961–8962: In the first chain, "'Abd al-Rahman" is 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi, who has been mentioned many times before. "Isra'il" is Isra'il ibn Yunus ibn Abi Ishaq al-Sab'i, trustworthy, mentioned before under nos. 1291, 1239 and others. "Abu Husayn" is 'Uthman ibn 'Asim ibn Husayn al-Asadi, trustworthy, mentioned before under nos. 642, 643. In the second chain, "Ibn 'Atiyyah" is al-Hasan ibn 'Atiyyah ibn Najih al-Kufi, mentioned before under nos. 1939, 4962.

This report was recorded by al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak 2: 304, through the chain of 'Abd al-Wahhab ibn 'Ata', from Shu'bah, from Abu Husayn, and he said: "This is a sound hadith according to the conditions of the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim), though they did not record it." al-Dhahabi agreed with him. It was also recorded through the same chain by al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan al-Kubra 7: 167.]]

8963 - al-Muthanna told me, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Salih told us, saying: Mu'awiyah told me, from 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His words: ﴿And the married women, except those whom your right hands possess﴾, he said: Every woman who has a husband is forbidden to you, except a slave-woman whom you own, who has a husband in the land of war; she is lawful to you once you have *istibra'* (ascertained, by a waiting period, that her womb is empty). [[In the manuscript: "idha istabri'tuha" (when you have *istabri'tuha*), as if the hamza was softened.]]

8964 - And al-Muthanna told me, saying: 'Amr ibn 'Awn told us, saying: Hushaym informed us, from Khalid, from Abu Qilabah concerning His words: ﴿And the married women, except those whom your right hands possess﴾, he said: Those women whom you have taken captive. If a woman is taken captive and she has a husband among her people, there is no harm in your having intercourse with her.

8965 - Yunus told me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said concerning His words: ﴿And the married women, except those whom your right hands possess﴾: Every married woman who has a husband is forbidden, except what your right hand possesses from among the captives, while she is married, and she is not forbidden to you because of him. He said: My father used to say this.

8966 - al-Muthanna told me, saying: 'Utbah ibn Sa'id al-Himsi told us, saying: Sa'id told us, from Makhul, concerning His words: ﴿And the married women, except those whom your right hands possess﴾, he said: The captives. [[Report 8966: "'Utbah ibn Sa'id ibn Hayyan ibn al-Rahd al-Sulami al-Himsi," who is also called "Wajin." Ibn Hibban mentioned him in al-Thiqat (the trustworthy). The "Sa'id" who narrates from Makhul appears to be Sa'id ibn 'Abd al-Aziz ibn Abi Yahya al-Tanukhi, a student of Makhul. His narration from him has been cited before under no. 3997.]]

* *

Those who held this view relied on reports which state that this verse was revealed concerning those taken captive at Awtas.

*The narration to that effect:*

8967 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh told us, saying: Yazid told us, saying: Sa'id told us, from Qatadah, from Abu al-Khalil, from Abu 'Alqamah al-Hashimi, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri: that the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ), on the day of Hunayn, sent an army to Awtas. They met an enemy, and they captured captives (*sabaya*) who had husbands among the polytheists. The Muslims were hesitant (*yata'thammun*) to have intercourse with them. So Allah, blessed and exalted, revealed this verse: ﴿And the married women, except those whom your right hands possess﴾, meaning: they are lawful to you once their waiting periods (*'iddah*) have ended. [[The hadiths 8967–8971: these are five chains for one hadith. Abu al-Khalil is Salih ibn Abi Maryam. His trustworthiness and biography have passed under no. 1899. The reports from him differ: between his narrating from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri directly, and his narrating from him through Abu 'Alqamah al-Hashimi as an intermediary. Indeed, the disagreement is on Qatadah, not on Abu al-Khalil, as will come, God willing.

Abu 'Alqamah al-Hashimi is al-Misri, client of the Banu Hashim. He is a trustworthy Successor (*tabi'i*).

Sa'id, in the first two chains, is Ibn Abi 'Arubah.

'Uthman al-Batti, in two of the chains, is 'Uthman ibn Muslim al-Basri. He is trustworthy; Ahmad, Ibn Ma'in, Ibn Sa'd and others declared him trustworthy. "al-Batti," with a fatha on the *ba'* and a shadda on the *ta'*, is a nisba to "al-Bat," the name of a place.

Al-Mizzi, in Tahdhib al-Kamal, and following him al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar in Tahdhib al-Tahdhib, decisively stated that Abu al-Khalil's narration from Abu Sa'id is *mursal* (a report whose chain omits a Companion), without any evidence! Yet Muslim recorded the hadith in both ways, which indicates its soundness in his view. For this reason al-Nawawi said in his commentary 10: 34–35, regarding the disagreement about including and omitting "Abu 'Alqamah": "It is possible that both its inclusion and its omission are correct, and that Abu al-Khalil heard it both ways, narrating it once like this and once like that." In my view this is the truth, and it would be an addition to a connected chain (*al-mazid fi muttasil al-asanid*). The hadith was transmitted by Ahmad (no. 11714; vol. 3, p. 72, Halabi edition), from 'Abd al-Razzaq, from Sufyan — that is al-Thawri — from 'Uthman al-Batti, from Abu al-Khalil, from Abu Sa'id, like the report here: 8970.

Likewise al-Tirmidhi recorded it, 4: 86, through the chain of Hushaym, from 'Uthman al-Batti. He said: "This is a *hasan* hadith. Thus al-Thawri narrated from 'Uthman al-Batti, from Abu al-Khalil, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, from the Prophet (ﷺ), similar to it, and in the hadith there is no mention of 'from Abu 'Alqamah'."

Muslim recorded it, 1: 417, through the chain of Shu'bah, from Qatadah, from Abu al-Khalil, from Abu Sa'id directly.

These narrations agree with the narrations here, 8969–8971, in which Abu 'Alqamah is not mentioned.

al-Tayalisi recorded it, no. 2239, from Hisham, from Qatadah, from Salih — that is Abu Khalil — from Abu 'Alqamah. Likewise Ahmad recorded it in al-Musnad, no. 11820, through the chain of Ibn Abi 'Arubah, and no. 11821, through the chain of Hammam — both from Qatadah, from Abu al-Khalil, from Abu 'Alqamah (vol. 3, p. 84, Halabi edition).

Likewise Muslim recorded it, 1: 416–417, in two chains, through the chain of Ibn Abi 'Arubah, from Qatadah; then through the chain of Shu'bah, from Qatadah — with the addition of "Abu 'Alqamah." From this it appears that Shu'bah narrated it from Qatadah in both ways: with the mention of Abu 'Alqamah and without it.

Likewise Abu Dawud recorded it, no. 2155, through the chain of Ibn Abi 'Arubah, from Qatadah.

Likewise al-Nasa'i recorded it, 2: 85, through the chain of Ibn Abi 'Arubah.

Likewise al-Bayhaqi recorded it, 7: 167, through the chain of Ibn Abi 'Arubah.

al-Tirmidhi also recorded it, 4: 86, through the chain of Hammam, from Qatadah. Then he said: "I do not know that anyone mentioned Abu 'Alqamah in this hadith, except what Hammam mentioned from Qatadah." Thus said al-Tirmidhi. But whatever he did not know, others knew: Sa'id ibn Abi 'Arubah and Shu'bah followed Hammam in this, as is clear from the narrations passed. Ibn Kathir criticized al-Tirmidhi for this, when he took out the hadith in his tafsir 2: 399. In any case, the hadith is sound through both routes — as we have said — and Muslim recorded it in his Sahih through both.

al-Suyuti mentioned it, 2: 137–138, without clarifying the disagreement in the chain, and he added its attribution to al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Ya'la, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tahawi and Ibn Hibban.

Note: We have added [from Abu al-Khalil] to the chain of 8970, because it is the correct reading, and it agrees with the narration of Ahmad, no. 11714, through the chain of al-Thawri. Its omission from the chain here is an error by the copyists.]]

Others who held that "the married women" in this place means "those who have husbands" said: Rather, they are every married woman among the women, forbidden to anyone other than their husbands, except that she be a slave-woman whom a buyer has purchased from her master. Others said: Rather, the meaning of "the *muhsanat*" in this place is: the chaste women. They said: The interpretation of the verse is: Chaste women are also forbidden to you, except what your right hands possess of them, by marriage, dowry, *sunnah* (prescribed practice) and witnesses, up to four. [[His words, "wa-sunnah" (and *sunnah*), appear this way in the manuscript and the printed edition, and likewise it occurs in the following report 8991. al-Suyuti cited it in al-Durr, similarly, with "wa-sunnah" as well. I am in doubt about this wording, and about the wording that will come in the two reports 9002 and 9008, which is "wa-bayyinah" (and evidence). Its occurrence in those two reports does not at all allow that it should be "bi-sunnah" or "bi-sunnah," so that I might say its correct form in them is "sunnah." As for "sunnah" in this place, the context allows it to be: "wa-sadaq wa-bayyinah wa-shuhud" (dowry, evidence and witnesses). Also, I do not know what "al-bayyinah" is in marriage, as you will see in the comment on the two reports 9002 and 9008.]]

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 4, verse 24 (part 2 of 4):**

As for "sunnah" in this place, and in the report (*athar*) 8991, I examined and did not find the pillars of marriage (*nikah*) other than the dower (*sadaq*), the guardian (*wali*) and the witnesses. The scholars have differed concerning the *wali*: Is it one of the conditions for the validity of the marriage or not? They differed as to whether it is a sunnah or an obligation (*fard*). They differed as to whether it is one of the conditions for the completion of the contract or for its validity. I saw the reason for their disagreement: no verse of the Qur'an that is an explicit text was revealed about the *wali* and its being a condition. Rather, it came in the Sunnah, the Sunnah of the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "There is no marriage except with a *wali*." They differed, however, about the interpretations (*mahmil*) of this hadith, and this is a detailed disagreement found in the books of jurisprudence (*fiqh*).

So it appeared to me that what came in the wording of Abu Ja'far, from the report of Abu al-'Aliyah number 8991, is that Abu al-'Aliyah called it "sunnah" while he meant the *wali*, because it came in the Sunnah, not in the apparent text of the Qur'an.

This is what I have deduced. Whoever is correct, or has a view other than this one, let him teach me, and may God reward him with good and thank him for what he has contributed. See the commentary on the two reports: 9002 and 9008.

He said: So He returned to the beginning of the surah, to four, and said: They are also forbidden, except with a dower, a sunnah and witnesses. [[The report 8991: al-Suyuti cited it in *al-Durr al-Manthur* 2:138, attributing it to Ibn Jarir and 'Abd ibn Humayd, and its wording is: "Except for one who marries with a dower..." See the earlier commentary.]]

Ma'mar said: Ibn Tawus informed me, from his father: "Except what your right hand possesses." He said: Your wife is from what your right hand possesses. Isa ibn Ubayd ibn Malik al-Marwazi al-Kindi narrates from Abu Mijlaz, but here he narrates from him through Ayyub ibn Abi al-'Awja'. Abu Tumaylah Yahya ibn Wadih narrated from him. Ibn Hibban mentioned him in *al-Thiqat*. He is biographied in *al-Tahdhib*.

Ayyub ibn al-'Awja' al-Qurashi narrated from Ikrimah and 'Ulba' ibn Ahmar. Al-Husayn ibn Waqid, al-Mubarak ibn Mujahid, Isa ibn Ubayd al-Marwazi and Ayyub narrated from him. He is counted among the Khurasanis, and he is from Marw. He is biographied in *al-Kabir* 1/1/421 and Ibn Abi Hatim 1/1/254. In the manuscript and the printed edition it was "Ayyub 'an Abi al-'Awja'," which is an error; the correct form is what I have written. Abu Mijlaz is Lahiq ibn Humayd, whose biography passed in number 2634.]]

* *

*Others said: "Rather, they are the free women."*

*Mention of those who said that:*

9010 - Ibn Bashshar told us, Hammad ibn Mas'adah told me, Sulayman told us, from 'Azrah, regarding His words: "And [forbidden to you are] married women," he said: The free women. [[Report 9010: Hammad ibn Mas'adah al-Basri, a trustworthy narrator, one of the shaykhs of Ahmad, passed as number 3056.

"Sulayman" is Sulayman al-Taymi.

"'Azrah" is 'Azrah ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Zurarah al-Khuza'i, passed as numbers 2752 and 2753. In the latter there is an error ("'Urwah"); the correct form is "'Azrah," so let it be corrected.

In the printed edition it was "Sulayman ibn 'Ar: 'arah," and I do not know where the editor got it, although "Sulayman ibn 'Ar'arah ibn al-Barnad" is biographied in Ibn Abi Hatim 2/1/134. The manuscript had "Sulayman ibn 'Azrah," and there is no "Sulayman ibn 'Azrah" among the narrators. It is apparent that it is "Sulayman ibn 'Azrah," and 'Azrah narrates from Sulayman al-Taymi and Qatadah.]]

* *

*Others said: "The married women (al-muhsanat) are the chaste women and women who have husbands, and it is forbidden to take either category except by marriage or by right-hand ownership."*

*Mention of those who said that:*

9011 - Al-Muthanna told me, Abdullah ibn Salih told us, al-Layth told me, Uqayl told me, from Ibn Shihab, who was asked about the words of God: "And [forbidden to you are] married women, except those whom your right hands possess," to the end of the verse. He said: We are of the view that in this verse He forbade married women who have husbands to marry while their husbands are still alive, and the *muhsanat* are the chaste women. They are not made lawful except by marriage or by right-hand ownership. *Ihsan* is of two kinds: *ihsan* of marriage, and *ihsan* of chastity, among free women and slave women. God forbade all of that, except by marriage or right-hand ownership.

* *

*Others said: "This verse was revealed about women who used to emigrate to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) while they had husbands. Some Muslims would marry them, and then their husbands would come as emigrants, so the Muslims were forbidden to marry them."*

*Mention of those who said that:*

9012 - Al-Qasim told us, al-Husayn told us, Hajjaj told me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Habib ibn Abi Thabit told me, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: "The women used to come to us, then their husbands would emigrate, so we prevented them." That is the meaning of His words: "And [forbidden to you are] married women, except those whom your right hands possess." [[Report 9012: Habib ibn Abi Thabit is Habib ibn Qays ibn Dinar; it is also said Habib ibn Qays ibn Hind, and also Habib ibn Hind. He narrated from Ibn Umar, Ibn Abbas, Anas ibn Malik, Zayd ibn Arqam, Mujahid, Ata' and Tawus. Abu Ja'far al-Tabari mentioned him in *Tabaqat al-Fuqaha*. He did not mention any narration from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri for him. He is trustworthy. He is biographied in *al-Tahdhib*, *al-Kabir* 1/2/311 and Ibn Abi Hatim 1/2/107. The report was cited by al-Suyuti in *al-Durr al-Manthur* 2:138, and he attributed it only to Ibn Jarir.]]

* *

*Ibn Abbas and a group of others besides him mentioned that the interpretation of this was obscure to them.*

9013 - Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna told us, Muhammad ibn Ja'far told us, Shu'bah told us, from Amr ibn Murrah, who said: A man said to Sa'id ibn Jubayr: Did you not see Ibn Abbas when he was asked about this verse: "And [forbidden to you are] married women, except those whom your right hands possess," and he said nothing about it? He said: He did not know it.

9014 - Al-Qasim told us, al-Husayn told us, Hushaym told us, Abd al-Rahman ibn Yahya informed us, from Mujahid, who said: If I knew whom to ask to explain this verse to me, I would ride camels' bellies to him, regarding His words: "And [forbidden to you are] married women, except those whom your right hands possess," up to His words: "So for what you enjoy from them" (Q 4:24), to the end of the verse. [[Report 9014: "Abd al-Rahman ibn Yahya." I do not know who this is.

This report was cited by al-Suyuti in *al-Durr al-Manthur* 2:139, and he attributed it only to Ibn Jarir.]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: As for *al-muhsanat*, it is the plural of *muhsanah*, and she is the one whose genitals have been protected by a husband. It is said of it: "*ahsana al-rajulu imra'atahu fa-huwa yuhsinuha ihsanan*" (the man protected his wife, and he protects her with protection), and "*husinat hiya fa-hiya tahsunu hasanah*" (she was protected, and she is protected with protection), when she is chaste. "*Wa-hiya hasinun min al-nisa'*" (and she is a chaste one among women) means: a chaste woman, as al-Ajjaj said:

*And a chaste woman among chaste women, smooth,*
*Protected from harm and from the contact of the sin,*

[[Diwan: 79; and *al-Lisan* (h-s-n), (q-n-s), and (w-q-s). Some lines of this poem have passed in 3:403, in which he mentions Abu al-Abbas al-Saffah and his caliphate. This poetry in his *Diwan* is compiled and not continuous, so I was unable to determine now who is meant by "wa-hasin," and it seems he meant the mother of Abu al-Abbas.

"Mulus" is the plural of "malsa'," and he meant by it being free from every blameworthy defect, like a smooth thing, which is free from roughness, defects and... And al-Mutalammis says, and he spoke the truth as a free Arab:

*So do not accept oppression for fear of death,*
*And die free by it, while your skin is smooth.*

By his words "harm" he means defect. It is also narrated as "min al-adha," which is also good. "Al-qiraf" is contact, the verbal noun of "qarafa al-shay' muqarafah wa-qiraf," meaning he approached it and mixed with it. So they said: "*qarafa al-jarab al-ba'ir*" (the mange approached the camel), meaning something of it touched him, and this is what is meant here, i.e., the contact of the disease. "Al-Waqs" is mange. The mange is used as a metaphor for sin and defect.]] It is also said, when she is chaste and protects her genitals from fornication: "*qad ahsanat farjaha fa-hiya muhsinah*" (she has protected her genitals, so she is protecting), as the Exalted One said: "And Mary, daughter of 'Imran, who guarded her chastity" (Q 66:12), meaning: she protected it from suspicion and kept it from fornication. Fortresses of cities and villages are called *husun* only because they prevent those who want to enter them and their people, and protect what is behind them from enemies who seek them. For this reason, a coat of mail is called "*dir' hasinah*" (a strong coat of mail).

* *

Since the root of *ihsan* is what we have mentioned, of prevention and protection, it is clear that the meaning of His words "and the married women from among women" is: the women who are prevented from you (i.e., forbidden to you) are unlawful to you, except what your right hands possess.

And since that is its meaning, and since ihsan (chastity/protection) may come from freedom, as His majesty and praise says: ﴿And the chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture before you﴾ [Surah al-Ma'idah: 5] = and it may come from Islam, as His exalted remembrance says: ﴿So when they are chaste [uhsinna], if they commit immorality, then for them is half the punishment for free [chaste] women﴾ [Surah an-Nisa: 25] = and it may come from chastity ('iffah), as His majesty and praise says: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women and then do not produce four witnesses﴾ [Surah an-Nur: 4] = and it may come from marriage = [[These are successive conjunctions, and the construction is: "And since that is its meaning, and ihsan may come from freedom ... and it may come from Islam ... and it may come from chastity ... and it may come from marriage ..."
= Then he returns again to the beginning of the speech, so its construction is: "And since that is its meaning ... and He, blessed and exalted, did not single out one chaste woman over another chaste woman."]] And He, blessed and exalted, did not single out one chaste woman over another chaste woman in His saying: "and chaste women from among the women" = [[This is the answer to "since" (idh), and the construction is: "And since that is its meaning ... it is obligatory that every chaste woman."]] so it is obligatory that every chaste woman, whatever meaning of ihsan applies to her, be forbidden to us for fornication or for marriage, except what your right hands possess of them by purchase, as the Book of God, majestic is His praise, has permitted us, or by marriage as the revelation of God has released for us.

What God, blessed and exalted, has permitted us in marriage from free women is four, apart from those who have been made forbidden to us by kinship and by marriage-relation. And from among the slave women: those whom we take captive from the enemy, apart from those whose meaning agrees with the meaning of what has been forbidden to us among the free women by kinship and by marriage-relation, for they and the free women are, in what is lawful and unlawful by that meaning, of one meaning = and apart from those women whom we have taken captive from the People of the Two Books who have husbands, for taking captives makes them lawful to whoever captured them after istibra' (waiting period to establish non-pregnancy), and after giving out the share of God, blessed and exalted, which He made for the people of the khums (one-fifth) from them. As for fornication, God, blessed and exalted, has forbidden it in all of them, so He has not made it lawful from a free woman or a slave woman, nor from a Muslim nor from a disbelieving idolatress.

As for a slave woman who has a husband, she is not lawful to her owner except after her husband divorces her, or his death and the completion of her waiting period from him. As for her master's selling her, it does not necessarily cause separation between her and her husband, nor make her lawful to her buyer, due to the sound report from the Messenger of God (ﷺ): [[The report of Barirah, in Muslim 10:139-148, and al-Bukhari also narrated it in several places in his Sahih.]] that he gave Barirah the choice when 'Aishah freed her, between remaining with her husband, whom her masters had married her to while she was enslaved, and separation from him. The Prophet (ﷺ) did not make 'Aishah's manumission of her a divorce. Had her manumission and the cessation of 'Aishah's ownership of her been a divorce, there would have been no meaning to the Prophet's (ﷺ) giving her the choice between remaining with her husband and separation. And separation would have become obligatory by the manumission, and divorce by the cessation of 'Aishah's ownership of her. [[In the manuscript: "and separation has become obligatory by manumission", which is a clear error; the correct reading is that of the printed edition.]] When the Prophet (ﷺ) gave her the choice between what we have mentioned and between remaining with her husband and separation, it was known that he gave her no choice in that except while the marriage contract remained valid as it was before 'Aishah's ownership ceased. So selling was the counterpart of manumission, which is the cessation of the ownership of the owner of a married female slave, namely selling, which is the cessation of its owner's ownership of her, since one of them is a cessation by sale and the other by manumission, in that separation does not become obligatory between her and her husband by either of them, nor by one of them [and divorce does not become obligatory by either of them or by one of them], [[In the printed edition: "in that separation does not become obligatory by it between them and her husband by them, nor by one of them, divorce" — a corrupt and disordered sentence, different from the manuscript, since the manuscript's version was also erroneous, and it added "by it" in "does not become obligatory by it", and I do not know what he intended by that!!
In the manuscript: "in that separation does not become obligatory between her and her husband by them, nor by one of them, and divorce." The first clause is sound; as for "and divorce", I believe the copyist became confused by repeating the clause as I have recorded it, so he wrote what he wrote. The correct reading, God willing, is what I have recorded between the brackets, and it is an inference from the context of the preceding argument, as you see.
Furthermore, Abu Ja'far's sentence from the beginning of the paragraph is very complex in structure, and therefore I placed the dividing lines to separate the exegesis from the flow of the speech; its flow is as follows: "it was a counterpart of manumission ... sale ... in that separation ...", meaning that sale is the counterpart of manumission, then within that he explained the meaning of "manumission" and the meaning of "sale".]] although they differ in other meanings: that for her in manumission there is the option of remaining with her husband or separation, for the reason of a divergence from the meaning of sale, and this option is not hers in sale.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: If someone says: How can it be that what is meant by the exception from "and chaste women from among the women" is what lies beyond the four, from five upward, by marriage, while those married by it are not owned?

It is said to him: God, exalted, by His saying "except what your right hands possess" did not single out the owned persons (the bodies), to the exclusion of those over whom authority is acquired by the marriage contract; rather He included by His saying "except what your right hands possess" both meanings: I mean ownership of the body and ownership of enjoyment through marriage, because all of that is possessed by our right hands. As for these, it is ownership of enjoyment; and as for those, it is ownership of service, enjoyment, and disposal in what is permitted to its owner from them. Whoever claims that God, blessed and exalted, meant by His saying "and chaste women from among the women" the chaste and the unchaste, apart from those we mentioned first by the exception in His saying "except what your right hands possess", [[His saying: "some" is in the accusative as the object of "meant by his saying".]] some of the kinds of what your right hands possess, but not others, which we have shown are not meant by it — let him be asked for proof of his claim from a principle or an analogy. For he will not say anything in that regard except that the same will be imposed on him in the other case.

* *

If one of them argues with the report of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that this verse was revealed concerning the captives of Awtas =

= It is said to him: The captives of Awtas were not made lawful by ownership and captivity apart from Islam. That is because they were idolatresses, worshippers of idols, and the proof has been established that the women of idol-worshippers are not made lawful by ownership apart from Islam, and that if they embrace Islam, Islam separates them from their husbands, whether they were captives or emigrants. However, when they are captives, they become lawful, if they embrace Islam, after istibra'. So there is no proof for one who argues that the chaste women whom He meant by "and chaste women from among the women" are the married captives to the exclusion of others, by the report of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that it was revealed concerning the captives of Awtas. For although it was revealed concerning them, it was not revealed to permit their intercourse by captivity specifically, to the exclusion of the other meanings we mentioned. Moreover, the verse is revealed with regard to one meaning, yet it includes what it was revealed about and other things, so its ruling applies to everything it includes, as we have explained concerning general and specific in our book "The Book of Clarification on the Principles of Rulings" (Kitab al-Bayan 'an Usul al-Ahkam).

* *

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying: ﴿the Book of God upon you﴾

Abu Ja'far said: He, exalted in remembrance, means: a decree from God upon you. So he brought "the Book" as a verbal noun (masdar) without its own verb. [[The "masdar" (with the mim vowelled and the sad open, the dal doubled and open), meaning an absolute object, from "tasdir", which is bringing out in the sense of the absolute object. See what has passed in 1:117, note 1, then p. 138, note 2/2:292 note 1, p. 500.]] This is permissible because His saying, "Forbidden to you are your mothers," through to "the Book of God upon you," means: God has written the prohibition of what He prohibited of that and the permission of what He permitted of that upon you, as a decree. [[See what has passed at 7:261.]]

* *

According to what we have said on this, the people of interpretation have spoken.
Mention of those who said that:

9015 - Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Mansur, from Ibrahim, who said: "the Book of God upon you": what He forbade to you.

9016 - al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, who said: I asked 'Ata' about it and he said: "the Book of God upon you": it is He who prescribed upon you the four, that you should not exceed them.

9017 - Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Ibn 'Ulayyah narrated to us, from Ibn 'Awn, from Muhammad ibn Sirin, who said: I said to 'Ubaydah: "and chaste women from among the women, except what your right hands possess, the Book of God upon you", and Ibn 'Awn indicated with his four fingers.

9018 - Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, saying: Hisham informed us, from Ibn Sirin, who said: I asked 'Ubaydah about His saying: "the Book of God upon you", and he said: four.

9019 - Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "the Book of God upon you": the four.

9020 - Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said about His saying: "the Book of God upon you": he said: this is the command of God upon you. He said: he means what He forbade them from these and what He permitted them. And he recited: "And lawful for you is what is beyond that, that you seek with your wealth," to the end of the verse. He said: "the Book of God upon you" is what He wrote and His command which He ordered you with. "The Book of God upon you" is the command of God.

* *

Some of the grammarians of Arabic used to claim that His saying "the Book of God upon you" is in the accusative in the manner of incitement (idra'), meaning: "Hold fast to the Book of God upon you."

= What he said of that is not common in the speech of the Arabs. That is because they [hardly] put it in the accusative with the particle by which they incite, [when they delay the incitement and place the object of incitement first]. [[This sentence in parentheses is necessary for the soundness of this view, and his saying "hardly" before it in parentheses is necessarily an addition too, otherwise his later saying "although it is permissible" would have no meaning, for he would have negated in one go that the Arabs put in the accusative with the particle by which they incite when they delay it, which is a contradiction. I deduced the second sentence from what has passed in his speech at 1:120 on incitement also.]] They hardly say: "your brother upon you, and your father behind you," although it is permissible.
And see also the Ma'ani al-Qur'an of al-Farra' 1:260.

What is more appropriate to the Book of God is that it be understood according to the known usage of the tongue in which it was revealed. This, together with what we have mentioned of the interpretation of the people of interpretation in accordance with the meaning of what we have said, and contrary to what he who claimed it is in the accusative in the manner of incitement directed it to.

* *

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying: ﴿And lawful for you is what is beyond that, that you seek with your wealth﴾

Abu Ja'far said: The people of interpretation differed in the interpretation of that.

Some of them said: The meaning of that is: And lawful for you is what is below the five, that you seek with your wealth in the manner of marriage.

Mention of those who said that:

9021 - Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "And lawful for you is what is beyond that," what is below the four, "that you seek your wealth."

9022 - Ibn WakI' narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Hisham, from Ibn Sirin, from 'Ubaydah al-Salmani: "And lawful for you is what is beyond that," meaning: what is below the four.

* *

Others said: Rather, the meaning of that is: And lawful for you is what is beyond that: those whom He named to you as forbidden from your relatives.

Mention of those who said that:

9023 - al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to us, from Ibn Juraij, who said: I asked 'Ata' about it, and he said: "And lawful for you is what is beyond that," he said: what is beyond the kinswomen, "that you seek with your wealth," the verse.

* *

Others said: Rather, the meaning of that is: "And lawful for you is what is beyond that": the number of what is lawful for you from the chaste women among the women, the free and the slave.

Mention of those who said that:

9024 - Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, concerning His saying: "And lawful for you is what is beyond that," he said: what your right hands possess.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The most correct of these sayings in interpretation is what we are going to explain. It is that God, exalted in remembrance, made clear to His servants the forbidden women by kinship and by marriage-relation, then the forbidden among the chaste women, then informed them, exalted is He, that He has permitted for them what is other than these forbidden ones made clear in these two verses, that we seek it with our wealth in marriage or by ownership of the right hand, not by fornication.

* *

If someone says: We know the permitted ones who are beyond the forbidden by kinship and marriage-relation, so what are the permitted ones among the chaste women, and what are the forbidden among them?

It is said: It is what is below the five, from one up to four, according to what we have mentioned from 'Ubaydah and al-Suddi, from the free women. As for what is other than the women who have husbands, there is no number restricted by the ownership of the right hand. We only said that it is so because His saying "And lawful for you is what is beyond that" is general in every permitted woman for us, that we seek her with our wealth. So directing the meaning of that to some of them is not more appropriate than to others, unless there is a proof establishing that it is so, which must be accepted. And there is no proof that it is so.

* *

The readers differed in the recitation of His saying: "And lawful for you is what is beyond that."

Some of them recited it: "wa-ahalla lakum" with the alif opened in "ahalla", meaning: God prescribed upon you, and made lawful for you what is beyond that.

Others recited it: ﴿wa-uhilla lakum ma wara'a dhalikum﴾, taking as a model His saying: ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers﴾, and "And lawful for you is what is beyond that."

* *

Abu Ja'far said: What we say about that is that both are two well-known, widely transmitted recitations among the readers of Islam, not differing in meaning. So whichever of the two a reader recites, he is correct in the truth.

* *
