"And man was created weak" means: He has made this easy for you if you are not able to afford marrying free women, because you were created weak, incapable of abstaining from intercourse with women, and of little patience in refraining from it. So He permitted you to marry your believing slave-women when you fear falling into sin (al-'anat) for yourselves and do not find the means to marry a free woman, lest you commit fornication, because of your scant patience in refraining from intercourse with women.

* *

Those of the interpreters (ahl al-ta'wil) said the same as what we have said concerning this.

Mention of those who said that:

9135 - Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, from 'Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "Allah desires to lighten [the burden] for you" — regarding marrying a slave-woman, and in everything in which there is ease.

9136 - Muhammad ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us, from Ibn Tawus, from his father: "And man was created weak," he said: In the matter of intercourse.

9137 - Ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us, from Ibn Tawus, from his father: "And man was created weak," he said: In the matter of women.

9138 - al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Ibn Tawus, from his father: "And man was created weak," he said: In the matter of women. A person is not weaker in anything than he is with women.

9139 - Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said concerning His saying: "Allah desires to lighten [the burden] for you," he said: He granted you a concession to marry these female slaves when you are compelled to them. "And man was created weak," he said: Had He not granted him a concession regarding them, there would have remained only the first ruling, namely, when he does not find a free woman.

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is His praise: ﴿O you who believe, do not consume one another's wealth unjustly, except that it be trade by mutual consent among you﴾

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: By His saying, exalted is His praise, "O you who believe," meaning: [[In the manuscript and printed edition: "He means by that, exalted is His praise," but the context requires what has been adopted.]] those who have believed, affirm Allah and His Messenger. "Do not consume one another's wealth unjustly," meaning: let none of you consume the property of another by means of what is forbidden to him, such as usury (ribā), gambling, and other matters which Allah has forbidden you. [[See the explanation of "consuming wealth unjustly" in what has preceded: 3:548, 549 / 7:528, 578.]] "Except that it be trade," as follows:

9140. Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbāt narrated to us, from al-Suddī, regarding "O you who believe, do not consume one another's wealth unjustly, except that it be trade by mutual consent among you": As for "their consuming one another's wealth unjustly," it is by usury, gambling, defrauding, and wrongdoing, "except that it be trade," so that one may profit a thousand for a dirham, if he is able. [[In the printed edition: "He forbade their consuming one another's wealth unjustly, by usury..." — I do not know why it was altered from the manuscript, though it agrees with what is in al-Durr al-Manthūr 2:143.]]

9141. Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Muhammad ibn al-Fadl Abū al-Nu'mān narrated to us, saying: Khālid al-Ṭaḥḥān narrated to us, saying: Dāwūd ibn Abī Hind informed us, from ʿIkrimah, from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His saying, "Do not consume your wealth among yourselves unjustly," he said: A man buys a commodity, then returns it and returns a dirham with it. [[The narrator: "Muhammad ibn al-Fadl Abū al-Nu'mān" is ʿĀrim, whose biography was previously given under no. 3387. The manuscript has "Muhammad ibn al-Mufaddal." The printed edition erred gravely, writing "Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal" and omitting "Abū al-Nu'mān." As for "Khālid al-Ṭaḥḥān," he is Khālid ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Wāsiṭī, whose biography was previously given under nos. 4433, 4434.]]

9142. Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Wahhāb narrated to us, saying: Dāwūd narrated to us, from ʿIkrimah, from Ibn ʿAbbās, concerning a man who buys cloth from another man, who says: "If I like it I will take it, and if not I will return it and return a dirham with it." He said: This is what Allah meant by "Do not consume your wealth among yourselves unjustly."

* *

Others said: Rather, this verse was revealed to forbid one of them from eating the food of another except by purchase. As for hospitality (qirā), it was forbidden by this verse, until it was abrogated (naskh) by His saying in Sūrat al-Nūr: ﴿There is no blame upon the blind, nor upon the lame, nor upon the sick, nor upon yourselves that you eat from your own houses...﴾ [Sūrat al-Nūr 24:61], to the end of the verse.

Those who said this:

9143. Muhammad ibn Humayd narrated to me, saying: Yaḥyā ibn Wāḍiḥ narrated to us, from al-Ḥasan ibn Wāqid, from Yazīd al-Naḥwī, from ʿIkrimah and al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, who both said, regarding His saying, "Do not consume your wealth among yourselves unjustly, except that it be trade by mutual consent among you," [the verse], that after this verse was revealed a man would feel scrupulous about eating at anyone's house; so this was abrogated by the verse in Sūrat al-Nūr, where He said: ﴿There is no blame upon the blind, nor upon the lame, nor upon the sick, nor upon yourselves that you eat from your own houses, or the houses of your fathers, or the houses of your mothers﴾ up to His saying: ﴿together or separately﴾. [[It is among the most wondrous things that the verse of Sūrat al-Nūr was quoted correctly a few lines earlier, yet both the manuscript and the printed edition agree in quoting it erroneously as: "There is no blame upon you that you eat from your houses..." This is a severe error, may Allah protect us and you from its like.]] So a wealthy man would invite a man from his family to a meal and say: "I am indeed scrupulous!" — and "tajannuḥ" means scrupulousness [["Tajannuḥ": scrupulousness. This is a good and ancient meaning in Arabic, which the lexicons did not record, so I have recorded it here.] — and he would say: "The needy have more right to it than I do!" [[In the printed edition: "more right to it than me," with the word order reversed; I have kept what is in the manuscript.]] Thus He permitted them to eat what has the name of Allah mentioned over it, and permitted the food of the People of the Book.

[[This narration seems to have some deficiency, and al-Suyūṭī abridged it very briefly in al-Durr al-Manthūr 2:143-144.]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: Of these two statements, the most correct is the statement of al-Suddī. This is because Allah, exalted is His remembrance, forbade consuming our wealth among ourselves unjustly, and there is no disagreement among the Muslims that consuming such is forbidden to us; Allah has never permitted the consumption of wealth unjustly.

Since this is so, there is no sense in the view of one who says: "That was a prohibition against a man eating the food of his brother as hospitality [in a manner that he had permission for], and then this was abrogated," [[This phrase between the brackets is clearly corrupted, and I have not found a meaning I accept, so I placed it between brackets; if it were removed, the speech would be sound.]] because the scholars of the entire Ummah and its common folk transmit that the hospitality of a guest and the feeding of food were among the praiseworthy deeds of both the people of polytheism and of Islam, for which Allah praised their doers and urged them toward them; and that Allah never forbade this in any era, but rather He encouraged His servants and urged them to it.

Since this is so, it lies outside the meaning of "consuming unjustly," and it is far from being either an abrogating or an abrogated ruling, because abrogation only occurs with something abrogated, and no prohibition of it has been established, so it could not be abrogated by permission.

Since this is so, the statement we have made is sound: that the falsehood by which Allah forbade consuming wealth is what we have described, of what He forbade His servants in His revelation or upon the tongue of His Messenger (ﷺ); and whatever contradicts it is an anomaly.

[[His saying "and whatever contradicts it is an anomaly" is coordinated with his saying "the statement we have made is sound."]]

The readers differed regarding the recitation of His saying: "except that it be trade by mutual consent among you."

Some recited it: ﴿illā an takūna tijāratan﴾ with a nominative (raf') ending, meaning: "except that trade exist, or occur, by mutual consent among you," so consuming it is then permitted to you, in that meaning. The one who recites in this manner takes "an takūn" as complete here (tāmmah), [[In the printed edition: "...in this manner, that 'an takūn' is complete..." I have returned it to what is in the manuscript, which is correct in its context.]] needing no predicate, as I have described. With this recitation, most of the people of the Ḥijāz and of Baṣra recited.

Others recited it — and they are the general readers of Kūfa: ﴿illā an takūna tijāratan﴾ with an accusative (naṣb) ending, meaning: "except that the wealth you consume among yourselves be trade by mutual consent among you," so consuming it is permitted to you at that point. Thus "the wealth" is implied in His saying "an takūn," and "trade" is in the accusative as the predicate. [[For a detailed discussion of these two readings, see the parallel of this verse in Sūrat al-Baqara 2:282 in 6:80-82, though the interpretation of the two verses differs, as is evident from reviewing it there.]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: Both recitations, in our view, are correct and permissible to recite, due to their being widely transmitted among the readers of the cities, along with the closeness of their meanings. However, even though this is so, reciting it with the accusative is more pleasing to me than reciting it with the nominative, due to the strength of the accusative on two counts:

The first: that in "takūn" there is a mention of the wealth. The second: that if no mention of it were made in it, and "trade" were singled out, being indefinite, the accusative would be eloquent in the speech of the Arabs, since it is constructed upon a subject and predicate. When only one indefinite noun appears with it, they use both the accusative and the nominative, as the poet said:

"When there is thrusting among them, and embracing..." [[This verse was quoted in full at 6:80, and I did not indicate its location here, because I did not find it during the verification of the poetry of the commentary, in order to integrate it into the body of the speech.]]

Abu Ja'far said: In this verse there is a clarification from Allah, exalted is His remembrance, refuting the statement of the ignorant among the Sufis who deny seeking sustenance through trade and crafts; and Allah, exalted, says: "O you who believe, do not consume one another's wealth unjustly, except that it be trade by mutual consent among you," [meaning] acquiring our livelihood through them [[In the printed edition: "acquisition permitted it for them," differing from the manuscript, as he did not read it well. It is as I have adopted, except that the copyist erred by writing "for them" (lahā); the correct is "by them" (bihā), i.e., by the trades and crafts.]] as follows:

9144. Bishr ibn Muʿādh narrated to us, saying: Yazīd narrated to us, saying: Saʿīd narrated to us, from Qatādah, regarding His saying: "O you who believe, do not consume one another's wealth unjustly, except that it be trade by mutual consent among you," he said: Trade is a provision from the provisions of Allah, and a lawful thing from the lawful things of Allah, for whoever seeks it with truthfulness and righteousness. We used to be told that the trustworthy, truthful merchant is with the seven [under the shade of the Throne on the Day of Resurrection]. [[He means the authentic hadith: "Seven will be shaded by Allah in His shade on a day when there is no shade but His: a just leader; a youth who grew up in the worship of Allah; a man whose heart is attached to the mosque whenever he leaves it until he returns to it; two men who love each other for the sake of Allah, gathering upon that and separating upon it; a man who remembers Allah alone and his eyes overflow; a man who is called by a woman of high station and beauty, and he says: 'Indeed I fear Allah, Lord of the worlds'; and a man who gives charity and conceals it, so that his left hand does not know what his right hand spends." Narrated by al-Tirmidhī from the hadith of Abū Hurayrah, and he authenticated it: 345.]]

* *

As for His saying: "by mutual consent," its meaning is as follows:

9145. Muhammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abū ʿĀṣim narrated to us, from ʿĪsā, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, regarding the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted: "by mutual consent among you," in a trade or sale, or a gift that one gives to another.

9146. Al-Muthannā narrated to me, saying: Abū Ḥudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid: "by mutual consent among you," in a trade, or a sale, or a gift one gives to another.

9147. Ibn Wakī' narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to us, from al-Qāsim, from Sulaymān al-Ju'fī, from his father, from Maymūn ibn Mihrān, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Sale is by mutual consent, and the option (khiyār) is after the transaction, and it is not lawful for a Muslim to cheat a Muslim." [[The narration 9147 is a mursal hadith. Ibn Kathīr cited it in his tafsīr 2:413, and al-Suyūṭī in al-Durr al-Manthūr 2:144, and he did not attribute it to anyone other than Ibn Jarīr.]]

9148. Al-Qāsim narrated to us, saying: Al-Ḥusayn narrated to us, saying: Ḥajjāj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: I said to ʿAṭāʾ: "Al-mumāsaḥah" (the handshake of the sale) — is it a sale? [["Tamāsaḥa al-rajulān": when two men transact and clasp hands, and one of them wipes the hand of his companion; this is among the forms of their sales in the Jāhiliyyah.]] He said: No, not until he gives him the option; the option is after the sale becomes obligatory; if he wishes he takes, and if he wishes he leaves.

* *

The scholars differed regarding the meaning of "mutual consent" (tarāḍī) in trade. Some of them said: It is that each of the two parties to the sale is given the option, after their contract, concerning what they have traded, whether to uphold the sale or cancel it, or until they separate from the meeting place in which they became bound to the sale by their bodies, by mutual consent regarding the contract they concluded between them before dissolving it.

Those who said this:

9149. Ibn Bashshār narrated to us, saying: Muʿādh ibn Hishām narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to me, from Qatādah, from Muḥammad ibn Sīrīn, from Shurayḥ, who said: Two men disputed, one of whom had sold a burnus (hooded cloak) to the other. He said: "I sold this man a burnus, and I asked him to be content, but he was not content with me!" He said: "Satisfy him as he satisfied you." He said: "I have given him dirhams, but he is not content!" He said: "Satisfy him as he satisfied you." He said: "I have satisfied him, but he is not content!" So he said: "The two sellers and buyers have the option as long as they have not separated." [[ "Al-bayyiʿ" (with a fatḥah on the bāʾ and a shaddah on the yāʾ), the seller or the buyer; and "al-bayyiʿān" are the two parties to the transaction.]]

9150. Ibn Bashshār narrated to us, saying: Mu'ammal narrated to us, saying: Sufyān narrated to us, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī al-Safar, from al-Shaʿbī, from Shurayḥ, who said: The two parties to the sale have the option as long as they have not separated. [[Narration 9150: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī al-Safar al-Hamdānī al-Thawrī; the name of Abū al-Safar is Saʿīd ibn Yaḥmad. ʿAbd Allāh narrated from his father, and from al-Shaʿbī and others. He is trustworthy, not a prolific narrator of hadith. He is biographed in al-Tahdhīb.]]

9151. Muhammad ibn al-Muthannā narrated to us, saying: Muḥammad ibn Jaʿfar narrated to us, from Shuʿbah, from al-Ḥakam, from Shurayḥ, the like of it.

9152. Ibn al-Muthannā narrated to us, saying: Muḥammad narrated to us, saying: Shuʿbah narrated to us, from Jābir, who said: Abū al-Ḍuḥā narrated to me, from Shurayḥ, that he said: The two parties to the sale have the option as long as they have not separated. Abū al-Ḍuḥā said: Shurayḥ used to narrate from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) something similar. [[The hadith "The two parties have the option..." is an authentic hadith narrated by al-Bukhārī, Muslim and others; see al-Bayhaqī's al-Sunan al-Kubrā 5:268-272.]]

9153. Al-Ḥusayn ibn Yazīd al-Ṭaḥḥān narrated to me, saying: Isḥāq ibn Manṣūr narrated to us, from ʿAbd al-Salām, from a man, from Abū Ḥawshab, from Maymūn, who said: I bought a Sābirī (a type of cloth) from Ibn Sīrīn; he haggled over its price with me, and I said: "Good!" He said: "Either you take it or you leave it." So I took it from him; when I weighed the price, he set down the dirhams, and said: "Choose: either the dirhams or the goods." So I chose the goods and took them. [[Narration 9153: al-Ḥusayn ibn Yazīd al-Ṭaḥḥān, previously mentioned with the nisbah "al-Subayʿī"; see what preceded under nos. 2892, 7863. In the printed edition and the manuscript here it reads "al-Ḥasan ibn Yazīd," which is an error. As for "Abū Ḥawshab," I did not find any narrator with this kunyah, and there is undoubtedly a corruption (taṣḥīf) in the isnād.]]

9154. Abū Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, from Ismāʿīl ibn Sālim, from al-Shaʿbī, that he used to say regarding the two parties to a sale: they have the option as long as they have not separated; so when they both leave (taṣādarā), the sale has become obligatory. [["Taṣādarā": this one departed and that one departed; it is said "ṣadara al-rajul fa huwa ṣādir," meaning he returned or departed.]]

9155. Muhammad ibn Ismāʿīl al-Aḥmasī narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn ʿUbayd narrated to us, saying: Sufyān ibn Dīnār narrated to us, from Ẓabyah, who said: I was in the market, and ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him) was in the market. A slave girl came to a fruit seller with a dirham, and said: "Give me this." He gave it to her, but she said: "I do not want it; give me my dirham!" He refused, so ʿAlī took it from him and gave it to her. [[Narration 9155: Muhammad ibn Ismāʿīl al-Aḥmasī, whose biography was given under no. 405, 718. Muhammad ibn ʿUbayd al-Ṭanāfisī, whose biography was given under no. 405. As for "Ẓabyah": this is how I have tentatively read it from the manuscript, and I do not know who he is. In the printed edition it reads "Ṭaysalah," a gross misreading of the manuscript. I have not found this narration elsewhere.]]

9156. Ibn Ḥumayd narrated to us, saying: Jarīr narrated to us, from Mughīrah, from al-Shaʿbī: that he was brought a case concerning a man who bought a mule (barādhawn) from another man, and it became binding upon him; then the buyer returned it before they separated. So he ruled that it had become binding upon him. Abū al-Ḍuḥā testified before him that Shurayḥ had ruled in a similar case that he should return it to its owner. So al-Shaʿbī returned to the judgment of Shurayḥ.

9157. Yaʿqūb ibn Ibrāhīm narrated to me, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, saying: Hishām narrated to us, from Ibn Sīrīn, from Shurayḥ, that he used to say regarding the two parties to a sale: If the buyer claims that the seller had made the sale binding for him, and the seller says: "I did not make it binding for him," then: two just witnesses that you both separated by mutual consent after a sale or option; otherwise the oath of the seller: that you both did not separate without a sale and without an option. [[The addition between the brackets is necessary for the context; see the narration that follows.]]

9158. Yaʿqūb narrated to me, saying: Ibn ʿUlayyah narrated to us, from Ayyūb, from Muḥammad, who said: Shurayḥ used to say: Two just witnesses that you both separated by mutual consent after a sale and option; otherwise his oath by Allah: that you did not separate by mutual consent after a sale or option.

9159. Ḥumayd ibn Masʿadah narrated to us, saying: Bishr ibn al-Mufaḍḍal narrated to us, saying: Ibn ʿAwn narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Sīrīn, from Shurayḥ, that he used to say: Two just witnesses that they separated by mutual consent after a sale or option.

* *

And the reason of the one who held this view is what:

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 4, verse 29 (part 2 of 2):

9160 - Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn Sa'id narrated to us, from Ubaydullah, who said: Nafi' informed me, from Ibn Umar, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Every two parties to a sale have no sale between them until they separate, except for an option (khiyar)." [[Hadith 9160: Yahya ibn Sa'id is al-Qattan. Ubaydullah is Ibn Umar ibn Hafs ibn Asim al-Umari. In the printed edition (and the manuscript) it reads "Abd Allah" with a takbir (not diminutive), which is the brother of "Ubaydullah". It is possible that this is so. But I see the correct reading as "Ubaydullah" in diminutive form, firstly because the hadith is well known from his transmission; and secondly because al-Hafiz al-Mizzi did not mention in Tahdhib al-Kamal a narration of Yahya al-Qattan from "Abd Allah", neither in the biography of Yahya nor in that of "Abd Allah". It is his habit to trace such matters and examine them thoroughly.
The hadith was also narrated by Ahmad in al-Musnad: 5158, from Yahya - who is al-Qattan - from Ubaydullah, with the same chain, similar in wording.
Ahmad also narrated it: 6193, from al-Fadl ibn Dukayn, from al-Thawri, from Abd Allah ibn Dinar, from Ibn Umar. Al-Bukhari (4: 280, Fath) narrated it from the narration of Abd Allah ibn Dinar, from Ibn Umar. Likewise Muslim (1: 447) narrated it through this route.
Ahmad also narrated it: 4566, with similar wording, from Ibn Uyaynah, from Abd Allah ibn Dinar.
It will also come later: 9164, from the narration of Ayyub, from Nafi', with the same meaning.
We have taken it out in many places in al-Musnad. It is a well-known, widely transmitted hadith.]]

9161 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Marwan ibn Mu'awiyah narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn Ayyub narrated to me, saying: Abu Zur'ah, whenever he made a sale with a man, would say to him: "Give me the option!" Then he would say: Abu Hurayrah said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Let no one separate [from a sale] except by mutual consent." [[Hadith 9161: Yahya ibn Ayyub ibn Abi Zur'ah ibn Amr ibn Jarir al-Bajali: trustworthy (thiqah). Ibn Ma'in said: "There is no harm in him." Some have reported from Ibn Ma'in that he was weak, but al-Bukhari included him in al-Kabir (4/2/260) and mentioned no criticism of him, and Ibn Abi Hatim included him (4/2/137).
Here he narrates from his grandfather "Abu Zur'ah ibn Amr ibn Jarir" - who was a trustworthy Successor (tabi'i).
The hadith was narrated by Abu Dawud (3485), from Muhammad ibn Hatim al-Jurjara'i, from Marwan - namely Ibn Mu'awiyah al-Fazari - with this chain.
Al-Bayhaqi narrated it in al-Sunan al-Kubra (5: 271), through the route of Abu Dawud. Al-Suyuti mentioned it (1: 144) and did not attribute it to anyone other than al-Tabari.]]

9162 - Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Ibn Ulayyah narrated to us, saying: Ayyub narrated to us, from Abu Qilabah, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "O people of al-Baqi'!" They heard his voice, then he said: "O people of al-Baqi'!" They craned their necks to look, until they recognized that it was his voice. Then he said: "O people of al-Baqi'! Let no two parties to a sale separate except by mutual consent." [[Hadith 9162: This is a mursal chain, since Abu Qilabah is a Successor. I do not know whether it is so in al-Tabari, or whether it was connected and the name of the Companion fell out through the copyists.
For al-Bayhaqi narrated it in al-Sunan al-Kubra (5: 271), through the route of al-Hasan ibn Makram, from Ali ibn Asim, from Khalid al-Hadhdha', from Abu Qilabah, from Anas, with similar wording. This is a good chain.
But al-Suyuti mentioned this narration of al-Tabari (1: 144), from Abu Qilabah, as mursal.]]

9163 - Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Tusi narrated to me, saying: Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi narrated to us, saying: Sulayman ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Simak narrated to us, from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas: that the Prophet ﷺ made a sale with a man, then said to him: "Choose." He said: "I have chosen." He said: "Thus is the sale." [[Hadith 9163: Sulayman ibn Mu'adh is Sulayman ibn Qarm - with a fatha on the qaf and sukun on the ra' - ibn Mu'adh, and he is trustworthy, as we preferred in our commentary on the Musnad: 5753.
The hadith is from the narration of al-Tayalisi, in his Musnad: 2675.
Likewise al-Bayhaqi narrated it in al-Sunan al-Kubra (5: 270), through the route of al-Tayalisi.
In al-Mustadrak of al-Hakim (2: 14) there is a hadith from Ibn Umar and Ibn Abbas together, traced to the Prophet, on the meaning of the option between the two parties to a sale. It is a strong corroboration of the meaning of this hadith.]]

* *

They said: "Trade by mutual consent" means what the Prophet ﷺ explained of giving each of the buyer and seller the choice to confirm the sale in what they transact between them, or to annul it after the contract of sale between them and before separation; or that they part from it bodily by mutual consent after the sale has been affirmed in their assembly. Whatever is contrary to that is not the trade between them by mutual consent.

* *

Others said: Rather, mutual consent in trade is the affirmation of the contract of sale in what the two parties transact between them by the consent of each of them: that which one of them has been made to own by the other and the other has been made to own by him, whether they separate from their assembly or do not separate, whether they exercised choice in the assembly after the contract or did not.

* *

The reason of those who said this view: The sale is only by speech, just as marriage is by speech, and there is no disagreement among the scholars on compulsion in marriage of one of the spouses over the other, whether they separate or do not separate from the assembly in which it took place. They said: So the ruling of sale is likewise. They interpreted the words of the Prophet ﷺ: "The two parties to a sale have the option as long as they have not separated," as meaning as long as they have not separated by speech. Among those who held this view were Malik ibn Anas, Abu Hanifah, Abu Yusuf, and Muhammad.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The more correct of the two views in our opinion is the view of the one who said: Trade which is by mutual consent between the two parties to a sale is that the two parties to a sale separate bodily from the assembly in which they have affirmed the bond of sale between them, by mutual consent to the contract that took place between them, and by the choice of each of them of the other = because of the soundness of the report from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, which is:

9164 - Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Ibn Ulayyah narrated to us, saying: Ayyub informed us = and Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Wahhab narrated to us, saying: Ayyub narrated to us = from Nafi', from Ibn Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The two parties to a sale have the option as long as they have not separated, or unless it is a sale of option" = and sometimes he said: "or one of them says to the other: Choose." [[Hadith 9164: This is one of the most authentic chains: "Ayyub, from Nafi', from Ibn Umar."
Al-Tabari narrated it here by two chains to Ayyub: through Ibn Ulayyah, and through Abd al-Wahhab, who is Ibn Abd al-Majid al-Thaqafi.
Malik narrated it in al-Muwatta, p. 671, with similar wording - from Nafi' from Ibn Umar: the golden chain.
Ahmad narrated it in al-Musnad: 4484, from Isma'il - who is Ibn Ulayyah - from Ayyub, with the same.
Al-Bukhari (4: 274, Fath) narrated it through Hammad ibn Zayd, from Ayyub.
Muslim (1: 447) narrated it from the narration of Malik, from the narration of Ubaydullah, and from the narration of Ayyub - and others - from Nafi'. Al-Bayhaqi (5: 268-269) narrated it with many chains.]]

* *

=Since this is authentically from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, the statement of one of the two parties to a sale to the other, "Choose," is either before the contract of sale, or with it, or after it.
=If it is before it, then that is an empty speech (khalf) that has no meaning, [["Khalf" (with fatha on the kha' and sukun on the lam): is bad, erroneous speech; one says "this is khalf min al-qawl" (this is faulty speech), and in the proverb: "He kept silent a thousand, then spoke khalf," said of one who is prolonged in silence, so that when he speaks he speaks in error.]] because neither of the two parties had made the other own what he did not yet own before the contract of sale, so that his giving the other choice over what he owned would have an understandable meaning; nor does anyone of the two lack knowledge that he has the option over making his companion own what is not yet his, in exchange for a compensation he takes from him; so it is said to him: "You have the option regarding what you wish to bring about, whether sale or purchase."
= Or it is - since this meaning is void [[In the manuscript and the print: "if it is void..." and the former is better.]] - that each of them gives the other choice together with the contract of sale. The meaning of choice in that state is similar to the meaning of choice before it, because it is a state in which neither of them had yet removed from himself what he had owned before, to the other, so the choice has an understandable meaning.
= Or it is after the contract of sale, since these two meanings are invalid. [[In the print: "if invalid..." and the correct reading is "since" as in the manuscript.]]
Since that is so, it is established that the other meaning of the words of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ - I mean his words "as long as they have not separated" - is only separation after the contract of sale, just as the choice was after it. Since that is established, the view of whoever claimed that its meaning is only separation by the speech by which the sale takes place is invalid. Since that is invalid, what we said is established: that choice and separation are the two meanings by which the completion of the sale after its contract occurs; and the interpretation of the one who said: the meaning of His words "except that it be trade by mutual consent among you" is: except that your eating of the property which some of you eat from others be by ownership from you of those whom you own it from, through a trade you have transacted between you, and you have separated from it by mutual consent of you after the contract of sale between you bodily, or by the choice of some of you to others, is correct. [[In the manuscript and the print: "or that some of you choose others," and I preferred what is written here.]]

* *

The discussion on the interpretation of His words: ﴿And do not kill yourselves; indeed Allah is ever Merciful to you﴾ (29)

Abu Ja'far said: By this, may His praise be exalted, He means: "And do not kill yourselves" — and let not some of you kill others, while you are one religion, one call, and one faith. So He, may His praise be exalted, made all the people of Islam part of one another, and made the killer among them as one who kills himself = in killing one of them = as killing himself, since the killer and the killed are one hand against those who oppose their creed. [[See the interpretation of "anfusakum" in this sense at 2: 301 / 6: 501 / 7: 454, 455.]]

And the people of interpretation said similarly to what we have said regarding this.

Mention of those who said that:

9165 - Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Ahmad ibn Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "And do not kill yourselves," he says: the people of your religion.

9166 - al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Ata' ibn Abi Rabah: "And do not kill yourselves," he said: some of you killing others.

* *

As for His words, may His praise be exalted: "Indeed Allah is ever Merciful to you," He means: Allah, blessed and exalted, has always been "Merciful" to His creation; and among His mercy to you is that some of you restrain from killing others, O believers, by forbidding the blood of some of you to others except by its right, and forbidding the consumption of the property of some of you by others in falsehood, except through trade by which it is owned from him with his consent and good pleasure; were it not for that, you would perish, and some of you would destroy others by killing, plundering, and seizing.

The commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on Surah 4, verse 30:

On the interpretation (*ta'wil*, the exegetical explanation) of His words: ﴿And whoever does that, in aggression and injustice, We will drive him into a Fire, and that is ever easy for God.﴾

Abu Ja'far said: The people of interpretation differed concerning the interpretation of His words, "And whoever does that in aggression."

Some of them said: The meaning of that is: whoever kills himself, meaning: whoever kills his believing brother, "in aggression and injustice, We will drive him into a Fire."

Those who said this:

9167. Al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Juraij, who said: I said to 'Ata': "Do you think His words, 'And whoever does that in aggression and injustice, We will drive him into a Fire,' refer to all of that, or to His words, 'And do not kill yourselves'?" He said: "Rather, to His words, 'And do not kill yourselves.'"

* * *

Others said: Rather, the meaning of that is: whoever commits what He has forbidden him from the beginning of this surah up to His words, "And whoever does that": marrying those whose marriage He has forbidden, transgressing His limits, consuming the wealth of orphans unjustly, and killing a soul whose killing is forbidden, unjustly and without right.

* * *

Others said: Rather, the meaning of that is: whoever consumes the wealth of his Muslim brother unjustly, without his genuine consent, and kills his believing brother unjustly, "We will drive him into a Fire."

* * *

Abu Ja'far said: The correct statement on this matter, in my view, is that it should be said: its meaning is: whoever does what God has forbidden him, from His words, ﴿O you who believe, it is not lawful for you to inherit women against their will﴾ up to His words, "And whoever does that," namely, marrying forbidden women, withholding a woman whose withholding is forbidden from women, consuming wealth falsely, and killing a believer whose killing is forbidden. This is because all of that is what God has promised punishment for its doers.

* * *

If someone says: What prevented you from making His words, "that," refer to everything for which God has threatened punishment from the beginning of the surah?

It is said: What prevented me is that each part of that has been coupled with a threat, up to His words, ﴿For those, We have prepared for them a painful punishment﴾, [[The end of the eighteenth verse of Surah al-Nisa'.]] and there is no mention of punishment after that for what God has forbidden in the verses that follow, up to His words, "We will drive him into a Fire." So His words, "And whoever does that," refer to what we have said, to what was not coupled with a threat, with the consensus (*ijma'*, scholarly agreement) of all that God the Exalted has threatened punishment for all of that, [[His words "more fitting" are the predicate of "was" in His words "So His words ..."]] is more fitting than that it refer to what had previously been stated with a threat coupled with the prohibition. [[This is a clear argument and proof of Abu Ja'far's sound understanding of the meanings and aims of the Qur'an, and a correct method of connecting the verses of the Clear Book, the like of which you will rarely find outside this tafsir (exegesis).]]

* * *

As for His words, "in aggression," it means transgressing from what God has permitted him to what He has forbidden him. "And injustice," meaning: he did that without what God has authorized, and embarked upon what God has prohibited him. [[See the explanation of "aggression" and "injustice" in the preceding language indexes, under the roots *'-d-w* and *z-l-m*.]] His words, "We will drive him into a Fire," mean: We will bring him to a Fire in which he will be burned and roast. [[See the explanation of "driving into" (*al-isla'*) earlier: 27–29.]] "And that is ever easy for God," meaning: the burning of the doer of that in the Fire and his being scorched in it is easy and simple for God, because he cannot resist his Lord's will for evil against him. The fulfillment of a threat is only difficult for the one who threatens when the one threatened is able to resist it. As for one who is in the grip of the one who threatens him, it is easy for him to carry out his judgment against him and to fulfill his threat, and what he intends against him is not difficult for him.

[[At this point, the sixth part of our manuscript ends, and at its end is the following text: "The sixth part of the book is complete, by God's praise, His aid, and His good success. May God bless our master Muhammad, his family, his companions, and grant them peace.

To follow in the seventh part, God willing:

On the interpretation of His words: ﴿If you avoid the major sins you are forbidden, We will remove from you your misdeeds and admit you to an honorable entrance﴾

"The completion of it was in some month of the year seven hundred and fifteen, may God make its conclusion and ending good, in goodness and well-being, by His grace and generosity. May God forgive its owner, its scribe, its author, and all Muslims. Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds." Then a scribe wrote beneath it, in a Maghribi hand, the following:

"Read by the poor one who depends on Him, Muhammad ibn Mahmud ibn Muhammad ibn Husayn al-Jaza'iri al-Hanafi, may He pardon them by His grace, and he completed it on the second of Rabi' al-Awwal in the year one thousand one hundred and thirty-nine. May God bless and grant peace to our master Muhammad and his family." This shaykh al-Jaza'iri, who wrote this colophon, is the one who previously wrote a gloss on a passage of the tafsir, which we have recorded in its place in the fifth part: 514, gloss: 2.

Then the seventh part of our manuscript began, and its opening reads: In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Lord, help me.]]

The discussion on the interpretation (ta'wil) of His words: ﴿If you avoid the major sins (kaba'ir) that you are forbidden, We will remove from you your misdeeds and admit you to a noble entrance﴾ [4:31]

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: The commentators (ahl al-ta'wil) differed about the meaning of "the major sins" (al-kaba'ir) which Allah, exalted is His praise, promised His servants would, if avoided, expiate all their other misdeeds for them.

Some of them said: The major sins that Allah, blessed and exalted is He, mentioned in His words, "If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden, We will remove from you your misdeeds," are those which Allah had prohibited to His servants from the beginning of Surat al-Nisa' up to the thirtieth verse of it.

Those who said this:

9168. Muhammad ibn Bashshar told us, saying: Abd al-Rahman told us, saying: Sufyan told us, from al-A'mash, from Abu al-Duha, from Masruq, from Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud), who said: "The major sins are from the beginning of Surat al-Nisa' up to the thirtieth (verse) of it."

9169. Ibn Bashshar told us, saying: Abd al-Rahman told us, saying: Sufyan told us, from Hammad, from Ibrahim, from Abdullah, with the like of it.

9170. Al-Muthanna told me, saying: Hajjaj told us, saying: Hammad told us, from Ibrahim, from Ibn Mas'ud, the like of it.

9171. Abu Hisham al-Rifa'i told us, saying: Waki' told us, saying: al-A'mash told us, from Ibrahim, who said: Alqamah told me, from Abdullah, who said: "The major sins are from the beginning of Surat al-Nisa' up to His words, 'If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden.'"

9172. Al-Rifa'i told us, saying: Abu Mu'awiyah and Abu Khalid told us, from al-A'mash, from Ibrahim, from Alqamah, from Abdullah, who said: "The major sins are from the beginning of Surat al-Nisa' up to His words, 'If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden.'"

9173. Abu al-Sa'ib told me, saying: Abu Mu'awiyah told us, from al-A'mash, from Muslim, from Masruq, who said: Abdullah was asked about the major sins, and he said: "What lies between the opening of Surat al-Nisa' and the thirtieth (verse)."

9174. Ibn Humayd told us, saying: Jarir told us, from Mughirah, from Hammad, from Ibrahim, from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The major sins are what lies between the opening of Surat al-Nisa' and thirty verses of it: 'If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden.'"

9175. Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim told me, saying: Hushaym told us, saying: Mughirah informed us, from Ibrahim, from Abdullah, that he said: "The major sins are from the beginning of Surat al-Nisa' up to the thirtieth of it: 'If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden.'"

9176. Ya'qub told me, saying: Ibn Ulayyah told us, from Ibn Awn, from Ibrahim, who said: "They used to hold that the major sins are what lies between the beginning of this surah, Surat al-Nisa', up to this point: 'If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden.'"

9177. Al-Muthanna told me, saying: Adam al-Asqalani told us, saying: Shu'bah told us, from Asim ibn Abi al-Najud, from Zirr ibn Hubaysh, from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The major sins are from the beginning of Surat al-Nisa' up to thirty verses of it." Then he recited: "If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden, We will remove from you your misdeeds and admit you to a noble entrance."

9178. Al-Muthanna told me, saying: Ibn Waki' told us, saying: Mis'ar told us, from Asim ibn Abi al-Najud, from Zirr ibn Hubaysh, who said: Abdullah said: "The major sins are what lies between the beginning of Surat al-Nisa' and the thirtieth (verse)." [[The narrations 9168–9178 are one report with many chains. Al-Haythami cited it in Majma' al-Zawa'id 7:4 and said: "Narrated by al-Bazzar, and its narrators are the narrators of the authentic (collections)."]]

* *

Others said: "The major sins are seven."

Those who said this:

9179. Tamim ibn al-Muntasir told me, saying: Yazid told us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ishaq informed us, from Muhammad ibn Sahl ibn Abi Hathmah, from his father, who said: "I was in this mosque, the mosque of Kufa, when Ali was giving a sermon to the people from the pulpit, [[In the printed edition and Ibn Kathir: "Ali (may Allah be pleased with him)." I have kept what is in the manuscript.]] and he said: 'O people, the major sins are seven.' The people paid attention, and he repeated it three times, then said: 'Will you not ask me about them?' They said: 'O Commander of the Faithful, what are they?' He said: 'Associating partners with Allah, killing a soul which Allah has forbidden, slandering a chaste woman, consuming the property of an orphan, consuming usury (riba), fleeing on the day of battle, and becoming a bedouin again after the migration (hijrah).' I said to my father: 'O father, what is becoming a bedouin after the migration? How could that apply here?' He said: 'O my son, what is greater than that a man migrates, then when his share of the spoils is given and jihad becomes obligatory upon him, he removes that from his neck and returns to being a bedouin as he was!!'" [[Ali's words: The narrator is Muhammad ibn Sahl ibn Abi Hathmah al-Ansari, who narrated from his father and paternal uncle. He is recorded in al-Kabir 1/1/107, Ibn Abi Hatim 3/2/277, and Ta'jil al-Manfa'ah: 365. al-Bukhari mentioned no criticism of him, and Ibn Hibban mentioned him in al-Thiqat.
This report was indicated by al-Bukhari in al-Tarikh al-Kabir in his biography, and Ibn Kathir cited it in his Tafsir 2:422, mentioning what Ibn Mardawayh narrated through Ibn Lahi'ah, from Ziyad ibn Abi Habib, from Muhammad ibn Sahl ibn Abi Hathmah, from his father, "I heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say," and he related the report as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet). Then he said: "Its chain is questionable, and its being traced to the Prophet is a gross error. The correct version is what al-Tabari narrated," and he related the report.]]

9180. Muhammad ibn Ubayd al-Muharibi told me, saying: Abu al-Ahwas Sallam ibn Sulaym told us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Ubayd ibn Umayr, who said: "The major sins are seven, none of which is a major sin except that there is a verse of the Book of Allah concerning it. Associating partners with Allah is among them: 'Whoever associates partners with Allah, it is as if he had fallen from the sky' [22:31]; and 'Those who consume the property of orphans unjustly, they only consume fire into their bellies' [4:10]; and 'Those who consume usury do not stand except as one stands whom Satan has driven mad by his touch' [2:275]; and 'Those who accuse chaste, unwary, believing women' [24:23]; and fleeing from battle: 'O you who believe, when you meet those who disbelieve advancing, do not turn your backs to them' [8:15]; and becoming a bedouin after migration: 'Indeed, those who turned back on their heels after guidance had become clear to them' [47:25]; and killing a soul." [[Ibn Ishaq's report 9180 and 9181: In the first report, Muhammad ibn Ubayd ibn Muhammad ibn Waqid al-Muharibi, Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas al-Kufi, is the teacher of al-Tabari. Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, al-Tirmidhi, Abu Hatim and others narrated from him. al-Nasa'i said: "There is no harm in him," and Ibn Hibban mentioned him in al-Thiqat. His narrations from him appear in many places: 1952, 3167, 3366, 4292, 8756.
And "Abu al-Ahwas, Sallam ibn Sulaym," whose biography appears under nos. 2058, 3167, 6170, 7216.
And "Ibn Ishaq" is Muhammad ibn Ishaq, whose biography has appeared many times.
And "Ubayd ibn Umayr ibn Qatadah ibn Sa'id al-Laythi," who narrated from his father, and had companionship (with the Prophet), and narrated from Umar, Ali, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Abu Musa, and Abu Hurayrah. He is a reliable Successor and among the senior Successors. His biography is in al-Tahdhib. In the printed edition here it read "Ubaydah ibn Umayr," which is an error; the correct reading is in the manuscript.
See the following report, no. 9189, and the commentary on it.]]

9181. Ibn Humayd told us, saying: Jarir told us, from Mansur, from Ibn Ishaq, from Ubayd ibn Umayr al-Laythi, who said: "The major sins are seven: associating partners with Allah: 'Whoever associates partners with Allah, it is as if he had fallen from the sky and the birds snatched him away, or the wind threw him into a far place' [22:31]; and killing a soul: 'Whoever kills a believer deliberately, his recompense is Hell' [4:93], and the verse; and consuming usury: 'Those who consume usury do not stand except as one stands whom Satan has driven mad by his touch' [2:275], and the verse; and consuming the property of orphans: 'Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly' [4:10], and the verse; and slandering a chaste woman: 'Indeed, those who accuse chaste, unwary, believing women' [24:23], and the verse; and fleeing from battle: 'And whoever turns his back to them that day, unless it is in maneuvering for battle or joining a company' [8:16], and the verse; and the apostate who becomes a bedouin after his migration: 'Indeed, those who turned back on their heels after guidance had become clear to them' [47:25], and the verse."

9182. Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim told us, saying: Ibn Ulayyah told us, from Ibn Awn, from Muhammad, who said: "I asked Ubaydah about the major sins, and he said: associating partners with Allah, killing a soul which Allah has forbidden without right, fleeing on the day of battle, consuming the property of an orphan without right, consuming usury, and slander (buhtan)." He said: "And they say: becoming a bedouin after migration." Ibn Awn said: "I said to Muhammad: 'And sorcery?' He said: 'Slander includes much evil.'"

9183. Abu Kurayb told us, saying: Hushaym told us, saying: Mansur and Hisham informed us, from Ibn Sirin, from Ubaydah, that he said: "The major sins: associating partners, killing a forbidden soul, consuming usury, slandering a chaste woman, consuming the property of an orphan, fleeing from battle, and the apostate who becomes a bedouin after his migration."

9184. Ya'qub told me, saying: Hushaym told us, saying: Hisham told us, from Ibn Sirin, from Ubaydah, with something similar.

* *

The reason for those who held this view is what follows:

9185. Al-Muthanna told me, saying: Abu Salih told us, saying: al-Layth informed me, saying: Khalid told me, from Sa'id ibn Abi Hilal, from Nu'aym al-Mujmir, who said: Suhayb, client of al-Utwari, informed me that he heard from Abu Hurayrah and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, both saying: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) addressed us one day and said: 'By Him in whose hand is my soul' (three times), then he bowed his head, and every man among us bowed his head weeping, not knowing what he swore by. Then he raised his head, and joy was in his face, and it was more beloved to us than red camels, and he said: 'No servant prays the five prayers, fasts Ramadan, gives zakat, and avoids the seven major sins, except that the gates of Paradise are opened for him, and it is said: Enter in peace.'" [[Hadith 9185: This is a sound chain.
Khalid is Ibn Yazid al-Misri, whose reliability was established at no. 5465. Nu'aym ibn Abdullah al-Mujmir (with the first letter of the name pointed with a dammah, the second with a kasrah, with a silent jim between them), al-Madani, client of the family of Umar ibn al-Khattab: a reliable, well-known Successor. The whole group narrated from him. Suhayb, client of al-Utwari, is a reliable Madinan Successor. al-Bukhari recorded him in al-Kabir 2/2/317, and Ibn Abi Hatim 2/1/444.
"Al-Utwari" is pointed with an unpointed ayn and a silent unmarked ta. It refers to "Utwarah," a clan of Kinanah, as Ibn al-Athir said. The printed edition of Ibn Kathir reads "al-Sawari" in this hadith, which is a foolish printing error. al-Bukhari narrated this hadith briefly in his al-Kabir, in the biography of Suhayb, as is his habit, through al-Layth, that is Ibn Sa'd, with this chain.
al-Nasa'i narrated it in 1:332 through Shu'ayb, from al-Layth, with it.
Ibn Kathir mentioned it at this place in 2:415 and said: "Thus al-Nasa'i narrated it, and al-Hakim in his Mustadrak, from the hadith of al-Layth ibn Sa'd, with it. al-Hakim also narrated it, and Ibn Hibban in his Sahih, from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Wahb, from Amr ibn al-Harith, from Sa'id ibn Abi Hilal, with it." Then al-Hakim said: "Sahih according to the conditions of the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim), though they did not record it."
al-Suyuti mentioned it at 2:145 and attributed it additionally to Ibn Majah, Ibn Khuzaymah and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan.]]

9186. Al-Muthanna told me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah told us, saying: Shibl told us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Ata', who said: "The major sins are seven: killing a soul, consuming usury, consuming the property of an orphan, accusing a chaste woman, false testimony, disobedience to parents, and fleeing on the day of battle."

* *

Others said they are nine.

Those who said this:

9187. Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim told me, saying: Ibn Ulayyah told us, saying: Ziyad ibn Mikhraq informed us, from Taysalah ibn Mayyas, who said: "I was with the Najadat (Kharijite group), and I committed sins which I considered to be major sins! So I met Ibn Umar and said: 'I committed sins which I consider to be major sins!'" [[In the printed edition and the manuscript it reads: "I commit sins," and in the manuscript "I commit" appears in three places; in the first place in the manuscript it reads "I committed." I lean toward this being correct, so I applied it to all three places, making them "I committed," as it better fits the meaning of the report and matches Ibn Kathir.]] He said: "And what are they?" I said: "I committed such and such." [[In the printed edition the words "I committed" were omitted at this point; I have restored them from the manuscript.]] He said: "That is not a major sin" = he said: "For something Taysalah did not name" = [[In the printed edition: "for something Tuysalah did not hear," the correct reading is in the manuscript. It means this sin, or these sins, he did not name or mention, and they are not major sins.]] = he said: "They are nine, and I will count them for you: associating partners with Allah, killing a soul without right, fleeing from battle, accusing a chaste woman, consuming usury, consuming the property of an orphan unjustly, violating sanctity in the Sacred Mosque, the one who seeks sorcery, [[In the printed edition, in al-Adab al-Mufrad of al-Bukhari and in Ibn Kathir: "the one who mocks" with a kha'. The meaning of "yastaskhir" is to mock and ridicule, and that is not a major sin, and I have not found it mentioned in any report.
In the manuscript and al-Durr al-Manthur 2:146, it reads "yastashir" with an unpointed ha', and reading it with the unpointed ha' is what I consider correct, though "istashar, yastashir" is not mentioned in any lexicon available to us today. I consider it correct, because what is mentioned in the reports and hadiths as a major sin is "sorcery" (sihr), and forming "istasahar" from "sihr" is sound in derivation and sound in meaning. I consider its meaning to be: asking a sorcerer to perform sorcery for you, or asking him to teach you the knowledge of sorcery. This agrees with what comes in the hadith of Taysalah that follows this report, in which it says: "and sorcery." It also appears in some reports: "and learning sorcery" (Ibn Kathir 2:418), and in the report of Ibn Abbas from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) concerning one who is forgiven: "and he was not a sorcerer who follows the sorcerers" (Majma' al-Zawa'id 1:104), and others.
Its soundness in terms of derivation is that they said regarding "tarq" (divination by pebbles, a kind of soothsaying): "istatraqa," meaning he asked the soothsayer to cast pebbles for him and to look into them for him. Similar examples are numerous, and there is no point in exhausting them here.]] and weeping of parents as disobedience" = Ziyad said: Taysalah said: "When Ibn Umar saw my fear, he said: 'Are you afraid the Fire will enter you?' I said: 'Yes!' He said: 'And do you want to enter Paradise?' I said: 'Yes!' He said: 'Are your parents alive?' I said: 'My mother is with me.' He said: 'By Allah, if you speak gently to her, and feed her, you will certainly enter Paradise as long as you avoid the damning acts.'" [[The report 9187: This is a sound chain.
Ziyad ibn Mikhraq al-Muzani al-Basri is reliable; Ibn Ma'in, al-Nasa'i and others declared him reliable. His biography is in al-Tahdhib. al-Bukhari recorded him in al-Kabir 2/2/339, and Ibn Abi Hatim 1/2/545.
Taysalah ibn Mayyas, and in the next chain it is "Taysalah ibn Ali al-Nahdi," and they are one person. His father's name was "Ali" and his nickname "Mayyas." al-Bukhari, in al-Kabir 2/2/368, affirmed that they are one, and mentioned that the correct attribution is "al-Bahdali," and said: "Bahdalah is from Bani Sa'd, and 'al-Nahdi' is not sound." Ibn Abi Hatim likewise affirmed in 2/1/501 that they are one, and that the attribution is "al-Bahdali," and it is said: "al-Sulami." He narrated from Yahya ibn Ma'in, who said: "Taysalah ibn Ali al-Bahdali al-Yamami: reliable."
The hadith was narrated by al-Bukhari in al-Adab al-Mufrad, p. 4, from Musaddad, from Isma'il ibn Ibrahim (that is, Ibn Ulayyah), with this chain.
Ibn Kathir mentioned it at this place in 2:417.]]

Al-Suyuti mentions it in abridged form, 2:146, but the text of his version contains a distortion. He also attributes it to Ibn Rahawayh, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Qadi Isma'il in *Ahkam al-Qur'an*.

As for his saying "with the Najdat": they are a group of the Kharijites, of the Harurites, attributed to Najda ibn 'Amir al-Haruri al-Hanafi, a man among them. It is said: "These are the Najdat." This is stated in *al-Lisan*. In the printed edition it read "al-Hadathan," which is a pure scribal error. In the manuscript it was written without diacritical dots in a form close to the word "al-Najdat." It is correctly given in *al-Adab al-Mufrad* and in the Azhar manuscript of Ibn Kathir's tafsir.

9188 - Sulayman ibn Thabit al-Kharraz al-Wasiti narrated to us, saying: Salm ibn Salam informed us, saying: Ayyub ibn 'Utba informed us, from Tuwaysila ibn 'Ali al-Nahdi, who said: I came to Ibn 'Umar while he was in the shade of an arak tree on the day of 'Arafa, pouring water over his head and face. He said: I said, "Tell me about the major sins (al-kaba'ir)." He said: "They are nine." I said: "What are they?" He said: "Associating partners with God, slandering chaste women," — he said: I said, "Before killing?" He said: "Yes, and humiliating..." — "and killing a believing soul, fleeing from the battlefield, sorcery, consuming usury, consuming the wealth of orphans, disobedience to Muslim parents, and desecrating the Sacred House, [your qibla, both living and dead]."

[Note: In the printed edition it reads "wal-ilhad" with the definite article; in the manuscript it reads "wal-hala." It is clear that the copyist joined the dal to the alif with a single stroke of the pen. Compare the similar case in the earlier report.]

[Note on the hadith 9188: This is another chain for the previous hadith, with similar wording.
Sulayman ibn Thabit al-Kharraz al-Wasiti, teacher of al-Tabari: I do not know who he is, and I have found no biography of him. In Ibn Kathir it reads "al-Jahdari" instead of "al-Kharraz."
Salm ibn Salam is Abu al-Muhdhdhib al-Wasiti. He is biographed in *al-Tahdhib* 4:131 and in Ibn Abi Hatim 2/1/268, and no criticism is mentioned of him.
Ayyub ibn 'Utba, Abu Yahya, judge of al-Yamama: weak, declared weak by Ahmad, al-Bukhari, and others.
Ibn Kathir mentions this hadith, 2:417, from this place. Then he mentions that 'Ali ibn al-Ja'd narrated it from Ayyub ibn 'Utba, giving it in full, and said: "Likewise al-Hasan ibn Musa al-Ashyab narrated it from Ayyub ibn 'Utba al-Yamami, and there is weakness in it."
The hafiz (memorizer of hadith) indicated in *al-Tahdhib* 5:36-37, in the biography of Tuwaysila, that "al-Baghawi recorded it in *al-Ja'diyyat* from 'Ali ibn al-Ja'd, from Ayyub ibn 'Utba, from Tuwaysila ibn 'Ali. al-Khatib in *al-Kifaya*, al-Kharaʼiti in *Masawi' al-Akhlaq*, and al-Bardijji in *al-Asma' al-Mufrada* recorded it by another route, from Ayyub ibn 'Utba, from Tuwaysila ibn Mayyas."
But Ayyub ibn 'Utba was not alone in narrating it from Tuwaysila. 'Ikrima ibn 'Ammar al-'Ijli also narrated it from him, and he is trustworthy:
al-Bukhari indicated it, as is his custom, in a brief reference in the biography of Tuwaysila 2/2/368. He said: "al-Nadr ibn Muhammad said: 'Ikrima ibn 'Ammar narrated to us, saying: Tuwaysila ibn 'Ali al-Bahdali told me, that he heard Ibn 'Umar.' Wakis said, from 'Ikrima: Tuwaysila ibn 'Ali al-Nahdi, that Ibn 'Umar used to stop at the arak tree on the day of 'Arafa." This is a fragment of this hadith.
This fragment was narrated by Abu Dawud in *Masa'il al-Imam Ahmad*, p. 118: "Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Wakis narrated to us, from 'Ikrima ibn 'Ammar, from Tuwaysila ibn 'Ali: that Ibn 'Umar stopped at the arak tree on the day of 'Arafa."
al-Suyuti was very brief when he mentioned this hadith, 2:146, and he attributed it only to "'Ali ibn al-Ja'd in *al-Ja'diyyat*."]

9189 - Sulayman ibn Thabit al-Kharraz narrated to us, saying: Salm ibn Salam informed us, saying: Ayyub ibn 'Utba informed us, from Yahya, from 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, from his father, from the Prophet (ﷺ), with its like, except that he said: "He began with killing before slander."

[Note on the hadith 9189: Yahya is Ibn Abi Kathir. In the manuscript and the printed edition it reads here "Yahya ibn 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr," through a corruption of "'an" into "ibn." This is a mistake by the copyists. Also, 'Abd al-Hamid ibn Sinan has dropped out of the chain here, between "Yahya ibn Abi Kathir" and "'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr." This is not the copyists' fault; it is an error of Ayyub ibn 'Utba.
'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr al-Laythi: a well-known Successor (tabi'i) of the great Successors. He has been mentioned many times.
His father, 'Umayr ibn Qatada al-Laythi: a Companion, who witnessed the conquest of Makka and the Farewell Pilgrimage.
The hadith was narrated by al-Hakim in *al-Mustadrak* 1:59, in full, by way of Harb ibn Shaddad, from Yahya ibn Abi Kathir, from 'Abd al-Hamid ibn Sinan, from 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, from his father. al-Hakim said: "The two shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) relied upon the narrators of this hadith, except 'Abd al-Hamid ibn Sinan. As for 'Umayr ibn Qatada, he is a Companion. And his son 'Ubayd is agreed upon as having been recorded and used as evidence." al-Dhahabi responded to him in his abridgement, saying that they did not rely on 'Abd al-Hamid because of his obscurity, though Ibn Hibban declared him trustworthy.
Then al-Hakim narrated it again, 4:259-260, by way of Harb ibn Shaddad also, in full. Then he said: "This hadith has a sound chain, but the two did not record it." Here al-Dhahabi agreed with his authentication and did not object to it.
The hafiz al-Mizzi narrated it in *Tahdhib al-Kamal*, p. 769 (photographed manuscript) in full, with two chains, by way of Harb ibn Shaddad, from Yahya.
Abu Dawud narrated it, 2875, by way of Harb ibn Shaddad, but did not give its whole wording.
Ibn 'Abd al-Barr narrated it in *al-Isti'ab*, in the biography of 'Umayr ibn Qatada, p. 439, with a chain by way of Abu Dawud. He gave its wording, but it is a summary of al-Hakim's two narrations.
al-Nasa'i narrated it, 2:165, in abridged form, by way of Harb ibn Shaddad. But in his version it reads "seven" instead of "nine."
Ibn Kathir mentioned it, 2:416, from al-Hakim's first narration. Then he said: "Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i recorded it in abridged form... Likewise Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it from his version in full. Then al-Hakim said: 'All its narrators are relied upon in the two Sahihs, except 'Abd al-Hamid ibn Sinan.' I say: He is a Hijazi, known only for this hadith, and Ibn Hibban mentioned him among the trustworthy. al-Bukhari said: 'There is something to consider in his hadith.'"
Then Ibn Kathir pointed to this narration of al-Tabari. Then he said: "He did not mention 'Abd al-Hamid ibn Sinan in the chain." This shows that the omission of "'Abd al-Hamid ibn Sinan" from the chain is not a copyists' error, but comes from the confusion of Ayyub ibn 'Utba.
'Abd al-Hamid ibn Sinan: Ibn Abi Hatim gave his biography, 3/1/13, and mentioned no criticism of him. This is therefore an authentication of him by Ibn Abi Hatim. The hadith was mentioned by al-Suyuti, 2:146, and he added its attribution to al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh.]

* *

Others said: they are four.

Those who said this:

9190 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Hakkam ibn Salm narrated to us, from 'Anbasa, from Mutarrif, from Wabra, from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The major sins are: associating partners with God, despair of God's mercy, losing hope in God's comfort, and feeling secure from God's plan.

9191 - Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, saying: Mutarrif informed us, from Wabra ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, from Abu al-Tufayl, who said: 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud said: The greatest of the major sins: associating partners with God, losing hope in God's comfort, despair of God's mercy, and feeling secure from God's plan.

9192 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Abu Mu'awiya narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from Wabra ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, who said: 'Abd Allah said: The major sins are: associating partners with God, despair of God's mercy, feeling secure from God's plan, and losing hope in God's comfort.

9193 - Abu Kurayb and Abu al-Sa'ib narrated to us, both saying: Ibn Idris narrated to us, saying: I heard Mutarrif, from Wabra, from Abu al-Tufayl, who said: 'Abd Allah said: The major sins are four: associating partners with God, despair of God's mercy, despair of God's comfort, and feeling secure from God's plan.

9194 - Muhammad ibn 'Ammara al-Asadi narrated to me, saying: 'Abd Allah narrated to us, saying: Shayban informed us, from al-A'mash, from Wabra, from Abu al-Tufayl, who said: I heard Ibn Mas'ud say: The greatest of the major sins is associating partners with God.

9195 - Muhammad ibn 'Ammara narrated to me, saying: 'Abd Allah narrated to us, saying: Isra'il informed us, from Abu Ishaq, from Wabra, from Abu al-Tufayl, from 'Abd Allah, with its like.

9196 - Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Wahb ibn Jarir narrated to me, saying: Shu'ba narrated to us, from 'Abd al-Malik, from Abu al-Tufayl, from 'Abd Allah, who said: The major sins are four: associating partners with God, feeling secure from God's plan, losing hope in God's comfort, and despair of God's mercy.

[Note on the report 9196: "'Abd al-Malik" is 'Abd al-Malik ibn Sa'id ibn Hayyan ibn Abjar, known as Ibn Abjar. He was a trustworthy and firm narrator of hadith, a follower of the Sunna. He narrates from Abu al-Tufayl 'Amir ibn Wathila. In the printed edition and the manuscript it read "'Abd al-Malik ibn Abi al-Tufayl," which is an obvious error.]

9197 - And with this chain he said: Shu'ba narrated to us, from al-Qasim ibn Abi Bazza, from Abu al-Tufayl, from 'Abd Allah, with its like.

9198 - Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, saying: Shu'ba narrated to us, from al-Qasim ibn Abi Bazza, from Abu al-Tufayl, from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, with its like in substance.

9199 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Jarir narrated to us, from 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Rufay', from Abu al-Tufayl, from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The major sins are four: associating partners with God, killing a soul which God has forbidden, feeling secure from God's plan, and losing hope in God's comfort.

9200 - Ibn Wakī' narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to us, from al-Mas'udi, from Furat al-Qazzaz, from Abu al-Tufayl, from 'Abd Allah, who said: The major sins: despair of God's mercy, losing hope in God's comfort, feeling secure from God's plan, and associating partners with God.

[Note on the reports 9190-9200: "Furat al-Qazzaz" in the last report is Furat ibn Abi 'Abd al-Rahman al-Qazzaz al-Tamimi. He narrated from Abu al-Tufayl and others, and from him narrated his son al-Hasan ibn al-Furat, Shu'ba, al-Mas'udi, and others. He is trustworthy. He is biographed in *al-Tahdhib*. This report from Ibn Mas'ud was transmitted by al-Tabari by many routes, one of which Ibn Kathir mentioned in his tafsir 2:422, and said: "Then he narrated it by several routes, from Abu al-Tufayl, from Ibn Mas'ud, and it is sound up to him without doubt." al-Suyuti recorded it in *al-Durr al-Manthur* 2:147, and attributed it also to 'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Abi al-Dunya in *al-Tawba*.
Ibn Kathir also recorded it in his tafsir 2:421-422, from a hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, traced to the Prophet, and said: "There is something to consider in its chain, and it is more likely to be a statement of Ibn 'Abbas (mawquf)."]

* *

Others said: everything God has forbidden is a major sin.

Those who said this:

9201 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, from Mansur, from Ibn Sirin, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The major sins were mentioned in his presence, and he said: Everything God has forbidden is a major sin.

9202 - Yahya ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Ibn 'Ulayya narrated to us, saying: Ayyub informed us, from Muhammad, who said: I was told that Ibn 'Abbas used to say: Everything God has forbidden is a major sin. And the "glance" was mentioned, and he said: It is the look.

9203 - Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to me, saying: Mu'tamir narrated to us, from his father, from Tawus, who said: A man said to 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas: "Tell me of the seven major sins." He said: Ibn 'Abbas said: "They are more than seven and seven..." [Note: In the manuscript and Ibn Kathir 2:425: "from seven and seven," and in the printed edition: "from seven and nine." I have adopted what is in the manuscript. See report no. 9204.] So I do not know how many times he said it.

9204 - Yahya ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Ibn 'Ulayya narrated to us, from Sulayman al-Taymi, [Note: In the printed edition: "Sulayman al-Tamimi," an error; the correct form is from the manuscript,] from Tawus, who said: They mentioned the major sins in the presence of Ibn 'Abbas, and they said: They are seven. He said: They are more than seven and seven! Sulayman said: So I do not know how many times he said it.

9205 - Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far and Ibn Abi 'Adi narrated to us, from 'Awf, who said: Abu al-'Aliya al-Riyahi stood over a circle in which I was, and said: People say: "The major sins are seven." I fear that the major sins are seventy, or that they exceed that.

9206 - 'Ali narrated to us, saying: al-Walid narrated to us, saying: I heard Abu 'Amr relate, from al-Zuhri, from Ibn 'Abbas, that he was asked about the major sins: "Are they seven?" He said: "They are nearer to seventy."

9207 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Qays ibn Sa'd, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, that a man said to Ibn 'Abbas: "How many are the major sins? Are they seven?" He said: "They are nearer to seven hundred than to seven, except that there is no major sin with seeking forgiveness, and no minor sin with persistence."

9208 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Jarir narrated to us, from Layth, from Tawus, who said: A man came to Ibn 'Abbas and said: "Tell me about the seven major sins which God mentioned: what are they?" He said: "They are nearer to seventy than to seven."

9209 - al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Ibn Tawus, from his father, who said: It was said to Ibn 'Abbas: "The major sins are seven?" He said: "They are nearer to seventy."

9210 - Ahmad ibn Hazim narrated to us, saying: Abu Nu'aym informed us, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Sa'dan narrated to us, from Abu al-Walid, who said: I asked Ibn 'Abbas about the major sins, and he said: Everything in which God is disobeyed is a major sin.

[Note on report 9210: I have not known or found "'Abd Allah ibn Sa'dan," nor have I found "Abu al-Walid." I fear there is a distortion or omission in both. In Ibn Kathir 2:425, however, it is written "'Abd Allah ibn Ma'dan," which I have also not found.]

* *

Others said: they are three.

Those who said this:

9211 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The major sins are three: despair of God's comfort, despair of God's mercy, and feeling secure from God's plan.

[Note on report 9211: See the earlier reports from Ibn Mas'ud, 9190-9200.]

* *

Others said: every sin that brings a binding consequence, and everything for which God has promised its people the Fire, is a major sin.

Those who said this:

9212 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiya narrated to me, from 'Ali ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning God's words: "If you avoid the major sins of what you are forbidden," he said: "The major sins" are every sin which God concluded with a Fire, or wrath, or a curse, or a punishment.

9213 - Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Ibn 'Ulayya narrated to us, saying: Hisham ibn Hassan informed us, from Muhammad ibn Wasi', who said: Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: Every binding consequence (mujiba) in the Qur'an is a major sin.

9214 - Ibn Wakī' narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Mihzam al-Sha'ab, from Muhammad ibn Wasi' al-Azdi, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: Every sin which God attributes to the Fire is among the major sins.

[Note on report 9214: "Muhammad ibn Mihzam al-Sha'ab," and it is said "al-Rammam," because he used to repair and split plates (al-qisa'). Ibn Ma'in and Ibn Hibban declared him trustworthy, and Abu Hatim said: "There is nothing wrong with him." He is biographed in *al-Kabir* 1/1/230, Ibn Abi Hatim 4/1/102, and *Ta'jil al-Manfa'a*: 379. In the manuscript and the printed edition it read "Muhammad ibn Mahram," but "Mihzam" (with a kasra on the mim, a sukun on the ha, and a fatha on the zay) is what the editor of *al-Tarikh al-Kabir* stated: "This is how it is vocalized in (Qaf), and this is how 'Abd al-Ghani vocalized it in *al-Mu'talif*: 421, and others. In (Kaw) it is vocalized like Mu'allim."
This report was recorded by al-Bukhari in his biography in *al-Tarikh al-Kabir*.]

9215 - 'Ali ibn Sahl narrated to us, saying: al-Walid ibn Muslim narrated to us, from Salim: that he heard al-Hasan say: Every binding consequence in the Qur'an is a major sin.

9216 - Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, from 'Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, concerning God's words: "If you avoid the major sins of what you are forbidden," he said: "The binding consequences."

9217 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, with its like.

9218 - Yahya ibn Abi Talib narrated to me, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Juwaybir narrated to us, from al-Dahhak, who said: The major sins: every binding consequence which God made necessary for its people, the Fire. And every act for which the prescribed punishment (hadd) is carried out is among the major sins.

* *

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: What we hold concerning this matter is what has been established by a report from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and that is what:

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 4, verse 31 (part 3 of 4):

9219 - Ahmad ibn al-Walid al-Qurashi narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, saying: Shu'bah narrated to us, saying: 'Ubaydullah ibn Abi Bakr told me, saying: I heard Anas ibn Malik say: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) mentioned the major sins (al-kaba'ir) — or: he was asked about the major sins — and said: "Associating partners with Allah, killing a soul, and disobedience to parents." Then he said: "Shall I not inform you of the greatest of the major sins?" He said: "False speech" — or he said: "false testimony" — Shu'bah said: "My greater assumption is that he said: false testimony."

[[Hadith 9219: 'Ubaydullah ibn Abi Bakr ibn Anas ibn Malik: a trustworthy Successor (tabi'i). He narrates from his grandfather, and also narrates from his father from his grandfather. "'Ubaydullah" is the diminutive form. In Ibn Kathir's citation of this hadith, "'Abdullah" appears, which is a pure error.
The hadith was transmitted by Ahmad in al-Musnad: 12363 (3: 131, Halabi) from Muhammad ibn Ja'far, with this isnad.
It was also transmitted by al-Bukhari 10: 345-346 (Fath) and Muslim 1: 37, both via Muhammad ibn Ja'far, with the same isnad.
Al-Bukhari also transmitted it 5: 192 (Fath), via Wahb ibn Jarir and 'Abd al-Malik ibn Ibrahim, both from Shu'bah, with the same isnad.
Ibn Kathir mentions it 2: 418, from the Musnad version, then attributes it to the two Sahihs.
al-Suyuti mentions it 2: 146-147 and adds attribution to 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, and Ibn Abi Hatim.
A later hadith will come, with two isnads, similar, via Shu'bah.]]

9220 - Yahya ibn Habib ibn 'Arabi narrated to us, saying: Khalid ibn al-Harith narrated to us, saying: Shu'bah narrated to us, saying: 'Ubaydullah ibn Abi Bakr informed us, from Anas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding the major sins, he said: "Associating partners with Allah, disobedience to parents, killing a soul, and false speech."

9221 - Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn Kathir narrated to us, saying: Shu'bah narrated to us, from 'Ubaydullah ibn Abi Bakr, from Anas, who said: They mentioned the major sins in the presence of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said: "Associating partners with Allah, disobedience to parents, and killing a soul. Shall I not inform you of the greatest of the major sins? False speech."

9222 - Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, saying: Shu'bah narrated to us, from Firas, from al-Sha'bi, from 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The greatest of the major sins: associating partners with Allah, and disobedience to parents" — or: "killing a soul" (Shu'bah being uncertain) — "and the perjurious oath (al-yamin al-ghamus)."

9223 - Abu Hisham al-Rifa'i narrated to us, saying: 'Ubaydullah ibn Musa narrated to us, saying: Shaybān narrated to us, from Firas, from al-Sha'bi, from 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr, who said: A Bedouin came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "What are the major sins?" He said: "Associating partners with Allah." He said: "Then what?" — He said: "And disobedience to parents." He said: "Then what?" "And the perjurious oath." I said to al-Sha'bi: "What is the perjurious oath?" He said: "The one who seizes the property of a Muslim man by his oath while he is lying in it."

[[Hadiths 9222 and 9223: they are two isnads for one hadith, with the same meaning.
"Firas" (with a kasra on the fa' and a light ra'): he is Ibn Yahya al-Hamdani al-Kharifi. He is trustworthy, and the Jama'ah (compilers of the six books) narrated from him.
'Ubaydullah ibn Musa in the second isnad is al-'Absi al-Hafiz; his biography has passed (2092). In the printed edition it is given as "'Abdullah" with a takbir, which is an error.
His shaykh Shaybān is al-Nahwi Abu Mu'awiyah, Ibn 'Abd al-Rahman; his biography has passed (2340).
The hadith was transmitted by Ahmad in al-Musnad: 6884, from Muhammad ibn Ja'far, from Shu'bah, like the first isnad here.
Al-Bukhari transmitted it 12: 170 (Fath), from Muhammad ibn Bashshar, from Muhammad ibn Ja'far, with the same isnad.
He also transmitted it 11: 482-483, via al-Nadr ibn Shumayl, from Shu'bah.
The second version here, the narration of 'Ubaydullah ibn Musa, was pointed to by al-Hafiz in Fath 11: 483, from the narration of Ibn Hibban in his Sahih.
The hadith was also transmitted by al-Tirmidhi 4: 87-88, al-Nasa'i 2: 165, 254, and Abu Nu'aym in al-Hilyah 7: 202. Ibn Kathir mentions it 2: 419, from the Musnad version, and attributes it to al-Bukhari, al-Tirmidhi, and al-Nasa'i.
al-Suyuti mentions it 1: 147, attributing it to these, and to Ahmad and al-Tabari.]]

9224 - al-Muthanna told me, saying: Ibn Abi al-Sarri Muhammad ibn al-Mutawakkil al-'Asqalani narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn Sa'id narrated to us, from Khalid ibn Ma'dan, from Abu Ruhm, from Abu Ayyub al-Ansari, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever establishes the prayer, gives the zakat, fasts Ramadan, and avoids the major sins, for him is Paradise."
