That is a public mention of evil, except by one who has been wronged, in that he did not give him hospitality.

10761. Al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, who said: Ibn Jurayj said, Mujahid said: "except one who has been wronged and takes his revenge," publicly speaking evil. Mujahid said: It was revealed concerning a man who was a guest of a man in a wilderness, and he did not host him; so it was revealed: "except one who has been wronged," mentioning that he did not host him, and no more than that.

* *

Others said: The meaning is: except one who has been wronged and takes revenge on his wrongdoer, for Allah has permitted him to do so.

Mention of those who said this:

10762. Muhammad ibn al-Husayn related to us, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi: "Allah does not like the public mention of evil speech except by one who has been wronged," he says: Allah does not like the public mention of evil speech from anyone among creatures, but one who has been wronged and takes revenge with the like of what was done to him, there is no blame upon him.

= Thus, "man," according to these statements which we have mentioned, apart from the statement of Ibn 'Abbas, is in the accusative position as a disjunctive exception from the first. The Arabs' practice is to put in the accusative what follows "illa" in a disjunctive exception.

* *

So the meaning of the speech, according to these statements apart from the statement of Ibn 'Abbas, is: Allah does not like the public mention of evil speech, but one who has been wronged has no blame upon him for informing of what was inflicted upon him, or for taking revenge on the one who wronged him.

* *

Others read it: ﴿illā man ẓalama﴾, with a fatḥah on the "ẓā'", and interpreted it: Allah does not like the public mention of evil speech, except one who has wronged, so there is no harm in speaking evil of him publicly.

Mention of those who said this:

10763. Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: My father used to read: ﴿Allah does not like the public mention of evil speech except by one who has wronged﴾. Ibn Zayd said: He means: except one who persists in that hypocrisy, so evil is publicly spoken of him until he desists. He said: This is like: ﴿And do not insult one another by nicknames. Wretched is the name of defiance after faith. And whoever does not repent, it is those who are the wrongdoers﴾ [Surah al-Hujurat: 11]: that you name him with wickedness, "after faith," after he had been a believer, "and whoever does not repent," from that deed which was mentioned to him, "it is those who are the wrongdoers." He said: He is worse than the one who said that. [[In the printed edition: "He is worse than the one who said that to him," and what is in the manuscript is purely correct.]]

10764. Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His words: "Allah does not like the public mention of evil speech except by one who has wronged," then he recited: ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest depths of the Fire﴾ until he reached ﴿And Allah will give the believers a great reward﴾. Then he said, after what he had said: they are in the lowest depths of the Fire = ﴿What would Allah do with your punishment if you are grateful and believe? And Allah is ever Appreciative and Knowing﴾, ﴿Allah does not like the public mention of evil speech except by one who has been wronged﴾. He said: Allah does not like that one should say to this one: "Did you not become a hypocrite? Are you not the hypocrite who wronged and did such-and-such?" after he has repented. "Except one who has wronged," except one who persists in hypocrisy. He said: It seems my father would say that to him, and read it: ﴿illā man ẓalama﴾.

* *

= Thus, "man," according to this interpretation, is in the accusative, being governed by "al-jahr."

* *

The meaning of the speech, according to the one who says this statement, is: Allah does not like that anyone should publicly speak evil of any hypocrite, except one of them who has wronged and persists in his hypocrisy, for there is no harm in publicly speaking evil of him.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The more correct of the two readings is the reading of the one who reads ﴿illā man ẓulima﴾ with a ḍammah on the "ẓā'", due to the consensus of the authoritative reciters and the scholars of interpretation on its soundness, and the anomaly of the reading with fatḥah.

* *

Since that is the more correct of the two readings, the correct interpretation of it is: Allah does not like, O people, that anyone should publicly speak evil of anyone, "except one who has been wronged," meaning: except one who has been wronged, there is no blame upon him for informing of what was done to him wrongly.

And if that is its meaning, it includes the informing by one who was not hosted, or who was badly hosted, or who was harmed by wrong in his person or property, of others among the rest of people. [[In the printed edition: "by way of compulsion from the rest of people," which has no meaning. The correct reading is what is in the manuscript. His words "ghayrahu" (others) are an object of the verbal noun "ikhbār," and the context: "included in it is the informing ... others among the rest of people," i.e., he informs others among the rest of people of what befell him and was inflicted upon him.]] Likewise, his invoking curses upon one who harmed him by wrong: that Allah should help him against him, because in his invoking evil upon him there is an announcement by him to whoever hears his invocation of evil against him.

* *

Since that is so, "man" is in the accusative position, because it is disjunct from what precedes it, and there is no noun before it from which it is excepted; it is like His words: ﴿You are not over them a controller. Except one who turns away and disbelieves﴾ [Surah al-Ghashiyah: 22-23].

* *

As for His words: "And Allah is ever Hearing and Knowing," it means: "And Allah is ever Hearing" of what you utter of evil speech publicly to those to whom you speak it publicly, and other than that of your voices and speech; "Knowing" of what you conceal of your evil speech and words to those to whom you conceal it and do not speak it publicly; He counts all of that against you, until He recompenses you for all of it with your recompense, the evildoer for his evil and the doer of good for his good. [[See the explanation of "samī'" and "ʿalīm" in the indices of linguistic terms in earlier sections.]]

Commentary on the interpretation of His saying: ﴿If you disclose good or conceal it, or pardon an evil, then indeed Allah is ever Pardoning and Competent.﴾ (4:149)

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, may His praise be exalted, ﴿If you disclose good﴾ (O people), ﴿good﴾ means: if you speak kindly to those who have done good to you, and display that as thanks from you for the good that came from them toward you (see the explanation of "al-Ibda'" (disclosure) in what has preceded, 5:582). ﴿Or conceal it﴾ means: or you leave off displaying that and do not reveal it (see the explanation of "al-Ikhfa'" (concealment) in what has preceded, 5:582). ﴿Or pardon an evil﴾ means: or you overlook the one who has wronged you for his wrong, and do not openly speak to him with evil speech, which I had permitted you to voice openly to him (see the explanation of "'afa" and "'afw" (pardon) in what has preceded, 2:503; 3:371; 7:215, 327; 8:426; 9:102. In the printed and manuscript editions: "He forgives them those who disobey Him," and the correct reading is to omit "for them," since it has no place here). ﴿Then indeed Allah is ever Pardoning﴾ means: He has never ceased to be one who pardons His creatures, forgiving those who disobey Him and oppose His command. ﴿Competent﴾ means: One who has the power to take vengeance upon them (see the explanation of "Qadir" (Competent) in what has preceded, p. 298, note 1, and the references there).

What is meant by this is that Allah has never ceased to be one who pardons His servants, even while He is capable of punishing them for their disobedience to Him.

That is, you too, O people, should pardon the one who wrongs you, and not openly speak evil to him, even if you are able to harm him, just as your Lord pardons you despite His ability to punish you, while you disobey Him and oppose His command.

* *

In His saying, may His praise be exalted: ﴿If you disclose good, or conceal it, or pardon an evil, then indeed Allah is ever Pardoning and Competent,﴾ there is clear evidence that the interpretation of His saying ﴿Allah does not love the public mention of evil speech except by one who has been wronged﴾ differs from the interpretation given by Zayd ibn Aslam (see the two reports nos. 10763 and 10764), who claimed that its meaning is: Allah does not love the public mention of evil speech toward the hypocrites, except toward one who persists in his hypocrisy, for then there is no harm in speaking openly evil to him. This is because He, may His praise be exalted, said immediately afterward: ﴿If you disclose good, or conceal it, or pardon an evil﴾; and it is understood that Allah, may His praise be exalted, did not command the believers to pardon the hypocrites for their hypocrisy, nor did He forbid them from calling by the name "hypocrite" those among them who openly displayed hypocrisy. Rather, pardoning that has no sound meaning, because "pardon" as understood is only the releasing by a person of a right he holds against another. Calling the hypocrite by his name is not a right held against him, so that he would be commanded to pardon it; it is simply his name. And a command to pardon the naming of a thing by its own name is not an understood command.

The interpretation of His saying, may His majesty be exalted: "Indeed, those who disbelieve in Allah and His messengers and wish to differentiate between Allah and His messengers and say, 'We believe in some and disbelieve in others,' and wish to adopt a way in between." (150) "Those are the disbelievers in truth. And We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment." (151)

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: He means by His saying, may His majesty be exalted, "Indeed, those who disbelieve in Allah and His messengers" – from among the Jews and the Christians – "and wish to differentiate between Allah and His messengers," by denying the messengers of Allah whom He sent to His creation with His revelation, and claiming that they had fabricated lies against their Lord. That is the meaning of their wish to differentiate between Allah and His messengers: by attributing to them lying and fabrication against Allah, and making false accusations against them. "And say, 'We believe in some and disbelieve in others'," meaning: they say, "We affirm this and deny that," as the Jews did in denying 'Isa and Muhammad, may Allah bless them both and grant them peace, and affirming Musa and the other prophets before him according to their claim. And as the Christians did in denying Muhammad ﷺ and affirming 'Isa and the other prophets before him according to their claim. "And wish to adopt a way in between" – he says: those who differentiate between Allah and His messengers, who claim that they believe in some and disbelieve in others, wish to adopt, amid the folds of their saying, "We believe in some of the prophets and disbelieve in others," "a way" – meaning a path to the misguidance they have invented and the innovation they have originated, calling the ignorant people among mankind to it. [Editor's note: see the explanation of "al-sabil" in the earlier indexes of language.]

Then He, may His majesty be exalted, said to His servants, warning them of their misguidance and disbelief: "Those are the disbelievers in truth," meaning: O people, those whose description I have set forth for you are the people of disbelief in Me, deserving of My punishment and of eternal abiding in My Fire, in truth. So be certain of this, and let not their claim of lying, and their pretension that they affirm what they claim to affirm of the books and messengers, cause you doubt regarding their affair, for in their claims they are liars. This is because the one who believes in the books and messengers is the one who affirms all that is in the Book he claims to affirm, and what the Messenger brought that he claims to believe in. As for one who affirms some of that and denies some of it, he is a denier of the prophethood of whoever he denies some of what he brought, and whoever denies the prophethood of a prophet has denied him. These people who denied the prophethood of some of the prophets, and claimed that they affirm some, are deniers of those they claimed to believe in, due to their denial of some of what came to them from their Lord. So they, with respect to Allah and His messengers – those whom they claim to affirm and those whom they claim to deny – are disbelievers, and they are the ones who deny the oneness of Allah and the prophethood of His prophets in the truest sense of denial, and who deny that in the truest sense of denial. So beware of being deceived by them and by their innovation, for We have indeed prepared for them a humiliating punishment.

* *

As for His saying, "And We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment," it means: "And We have prepared" for whoever denies Allah and His Messenger with the denial of these people you have been described, O people, their affair from among the People of the Book, and for others among the rest of the kinds of disbelievers [see the explanation of "a'tadda" earlier, 8:103, 355] – "a punishment," in the Hereafter – "humiliating," meaning: it humiliates the one punished by it through his eternal abiding therein. [See the explanation of "muhin" earlier, p. 163, footnote 4, and the references there.]

* *

The people of interpretation have said what we have said regarding the interpretation of that.

Those who said that:

10765 – Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, he said: Yazid narrated to us, he said: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: "Indeed, those who disbelieve in Allah and His messengers and wish to differentiate between Allah and His messengers and say, 'We believe in some and disbelieve in others,' and wish to adopt a way in between. Those are the disbelievers in truth. And We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment." Those are the enemies of Allah, the Jews and the Christians. The Jews believed in the Torah and Musa, and disbelieved in the Gospel and 'Isa. The Christians believed in the Gospel and 'Isa, and disbelieved in the Qur'an and Muhammad ﷺ. They adopted Judaism and Christianity, two innovations that are not from Allah, and abandoned Islam, which is the religion of Allah with which He sent His messengers.

10766 – Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to us, he said: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, he said: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "Indeed, those who disbelieve in Allah and His messengers and wish to differentiate between Allah and His messengers," they say: Muhammad is not a messenger of Allah! And the Jews say: 'Isa is not a messenger of Allah! So they differentiated between Allah and His messengers. "And say, 'We believe in some and disbelieve in others'" – these believe in some and disbelieve in others.

10767 – al-Qasim narrated to us, he said: al-Husayn narrated to us, he said: Hajjaj narrated to me, he said: Ibn Jurayj said regarding His saying: "Indeed, those who disbelieve in Allah and His messengers," up to His saying: "a way in between," he said: The Jews and the Christians. The Jews believed in 'Uzayr and disbelieved in 'Isa, and the Christians believed in 'Isa and disbelieved in 'Uzayr. And they would believe in one prophet and disbelieve in the other. "And wish to adopt a way in between" – he said: a religion by which they worship Allah.

The interpretation of His saying, may His majesty be exalted: "Indeed, those who disbelieve in Allah and His messengers and wish to differentiate between Allah and His messengers and say, 'We believe in some and disbelieve in others,' and wish to adopt a way in between." (150) "Those are the disbelievers in truth. And We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment." (151)

[Editor's note: see the explanation of "al-sabil" in the earlier indexes of language.]

* *

As for His saying, "And We have prepared for the disbelievers a humiliating punishment," it means: "And We have prepared" for whoever denies Allah and His Messenger with the denial of these people you have been described, O people, their affair from among the People of the Book, and for others among the rest of the kinds of disbelievers [see the explanation of "a'tadda" earlier, 8:103, 355] – "a punishment," in the Hereafter – "humiliating," meaning: it humiliates the one punished by it through his eternal abiding therein. [See the explanation of "muhin" earlier, p. 163, footnote 4, and the references there.]

* *

The people of interpretation have said what we have said regarding the interpretation of that.

Those who said that:

10765 – Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, he said: Yazid narrated to us, he said: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: "Indeed, those who disbelieve in Allah and His messengers and wish to differentiate between Allah and His messengers and say, 'We believe in some and disbelieve in others,' and wish to adopt a way in between. 10766 – Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to us, he said: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, he said: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "Indeed, those who disbelieve in Allah and His messengers and wish to differentiate between Allah and His messengers," they say: Muhammad is not a messenger of Allah! And the Jews say: 'Isa is not a messenger of Allah! So they differentiated between Allah and His messengers. "And say, 'We believe in some and disbelieve in others'" – these believe in some and disbelieve in others.

10767 – al-Qasim narrated to us, he said: al-Husayn narrated to us, he said: Hajjaj narrated to me, he said: Ibn Jurayj said regarding His saying: "Indeed, those who disbelieve in Allah and His messengers," up to His saying: "a way in between," he said: The Jews and the Christians. The Jews believed in 'Uzayr and disbelieved in 'Isa, and the Christians believed in 'Isa and disbelieved in 'Uzayr. And they would believe in one prophet and disbelieve in the other. "And wish to adopt a way in between" – he said: a religion by which they worship Allah.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 4, verse 152:

The interpretation of His words: ﴿And those who believe in Allah and His messengers and make no distinction between any of them — those, He will give them their rewards. And Allah is ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾ (4:152).

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: He, may His praise be exalted, means by this: those who affirm the oneness of Allah, and acknowledge the prophethood of all His messengers, and believe them in what they brought them from Allah of the laws of His religion. ﴿And make no distinction between any of them﴾, meaning: they do not deny some of them and affirm others, but rather they acknowledge that everything they brought from their Lord is true. ﴿Those﴾, meaning: these, who have this description, from among the believers in Allah and His messengers. ﴿He will give them﴾, meaning: He will bestow upon them [[See the explanation of "ītā' (giving)" in the earlier indexes of language.]] ﴿their rewards﴾, meaning: their recompense and their reward for their belief in the messengers concerning the oneness of Allah and the laws of His religion, and what came to them from Allah. [[See the explanation of "ajr (reward)" earlier, p. 341, footnote 6, and the references there.]] ﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving﴾, meaning: He forgives those among His creatures who do that what has preceded of their sins, covering it over by His pardon for them and His leaving off punishment for it; for He has never ceased to be Forgiving toward the sins of those among His creatures who turn back to Him penitently. ﴿Merciful﴾, meaning: and He has never ceased to be Merciful to them, by His bounty upon them in guiding them to the path of truth and His granting them success in what frees their necks from the Fire. [[See the explanation of "Ghafur (Forgiving)" and "Rahim (Merciful)" earlier in the indexes of language.]]

Abu Ja'far said: By this, may His praise be exalted, He means: ﴿The People of the Book ask you﴾, O Muhammad, ﴿to bring down to them a Book from heaven﴾. By this He means the People of the Torah among the Jews.

* *

The commentators (ahl al-ta'wil) differed about the "Book" that the Jews asked Muhammad ﷺ to bring down to them from heaven.

Some of them said: They asked him to bring down to them a written book from heaven, just as Moses brought the Children of Israel the Torah written from God.

Those who said this:

10768. Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, regarding ﴿The People of the Book ask you to bring down to them a Book from heaven﴾: The Jews said: "If you are truthful that you are the Messenger of God, then bring us a written book from heaven, just as Moses brought it."

10769. al-Harith narrated to me, saying: Abd al-Aziz narrated to us, saying: Abu Ma'shar narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, who said: Some men from the Jews came to the Messenger of God ﷺ and said: "Moses brought the Tablets from God. So bring us the Tablets from God, and then we will believe you!" So God revealed: ﴿The People of the Book ask you to bring down to them a Book from heaven﴾, up to His words: ﴿and their saying against Mary a great slander﴾.

* *

Others said: Rather, they asked him to bring down to them a book specifically for them.

Those who said this:

10770. Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah regarding His words: ﴿The People of the Book ask you to bring down to them a Book from heaven﴾, meaning: a book, specifically for them, ﴿so they asked Moses for greater than that, and said: Show us God openly﴾.

Others said: Rather, they asked him to bring down books upon specific men among them, commanding them to confirm him and follow him.

Those who said this:

10771. al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, saying: Ibn Juraij said regarding His words: ﴿The People of the Book ask you to bring down to them a Book from heaven﴾: That was because the Jews and the Christians came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "We will not follow you in what you call us to, until you bring us a book from God to so-and-so [[In the manuscript: "from the servant of God, from God to so-and-so"; the printed text is correct, unless the copyist wrote "from God," then changed it to "from God to," and did not strike out the first.]] that you are the Messenger of God, and to so-and-so with a book that you are the Messenger of God!" God, may His praise be exalted, said: ﴿The People of the Book ask you to bring down to them a Book from heaven. So they asked Moses for greater than that, and said: Show us God openly﴾.

Abu Ja'far said: The most correct of these sayings is that it should be said: The People of the Torah asked the Messenger of God ﷺ to ask his Lord to bring down to them a Book from heaven, as a miraculous sign (ayah mu'jizah) that all creation could not match, bearing witness to the Messenger of God ﷺ's truthfulness and commanding them to follow him.

It is permissible that what they asked for was a written book brought down to them from heaven for their community, and it is permissible that it was books addressed to specific individuals. Rather, what is more fitting to the apparent meaning of the recitation is that their request was for the sending down of a single book to their community, because God, in His report about them, mentioned "the Book" in the singular, saying: ﴿The People of the Book ask you to bring down to them a Book from heaven﴾, and did not say "books."

* *

As for His words: ﴿So they asked Moses for greater than that﴾, this is a rebuke from God, may His praise be exalted, to those who asked the Messenger of God ﷺ to bring down to them a Book from heaven, for their asking him for that, and a reproach from Him to them. God says to His Prophet ﷺ: O Muhammad, let their request for that not weigh heavily upon you, for they, because of their ignorance of God, their audacity toward Him, and their deception by His forbearance, if you had brought down to them the Book they asked you to bring down, they would have opposed God's command just as they opposed it after God revived their forefathers from their stupor, so they worshipped the calf and took it as a god to worship besides their Creator and Originator, who showed them of His power and great dominion what He showed them, for they would be nothing other than like their forefathers and predecessors.

* *

Then God recounted from their story and the story of Moses what He recounted. God says: ﴿So they asked Moses for greater than that﴾, meaning: The forefathers of these Jews and their predecessors asked Moses, peace be upon him, for something greater than what they asked you of bringing down a book to them from heaven. They said to him: ﴿Show us God openly﴾, that is: visibly, so that we may see Him and look at Him.

* *

We have already addressed the meaning of "openly" (jahrah), with the transmitted reports and evidences for the correctness of what we said about its meaning earlier, in a way that makes repeating it in this place unnecessary. [[See the explanation of "jahrah" above, 2:80–82.]]

* *

It has been reported from Ibn Abbas that he used to say about this, that:

10772. al-Harith narrated to me, saying: Abu Ubayd narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to us, from Harun ibn Musa, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Ishaq, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Mu'awiyah, from Ibn Abbas regarding this verse, he said: When they saw Him, they had seen Him. They only said "openly": ﴿Show us God.﴾ He said: It is advanced and delayed (muqaddam wa-mu'akhkhar).

* *

Ibn Abbas interpreted it as meaning that their asking Moses was openly (jahrah). [[This saying attributed to Ibn Abbas has not appeared before in the commentary on the verse in Surah al-Baqarah, 2:80–82, and this is one of the proofs that this tafsir has been abridged.]]

* *

As for His words: ﴿Then the thunderbolt seized them﴾, He means: ﴿they were struck﴾ (fa-su'iqu) ﴿for their wrongdoing﴾, against themselves. Their wrongdoing against themselves was their asking Moses to show them their Lord openly, because that was something they had no right to ask.

* *

We have already explained the meaning of "thunderbolt" (al-sa'iqah) earlier, with the disagreement of the commentators about its interpretation and the evidence for the most correct of what has been said about it. [[See the explanation of "al-sa'iqah" above, 2:82–84.]]

* *

As for His words: ﴿Then they took the calf﴾, He means: then they took, these who asked Moses what they asked of seeing their Lord openly, after God had revived them and raised them from their stupor, the calf into which the Samiri had cast what he cast of the handful he had grasped from the hoofprint of Gabriel, peace be upon him, as a god they worshipped besides God. [[The context of this passage: "Then these took ... the calf ... as a god ..."]]

* *

We have already discussed the reason for which they took the calf, and how their affair and his affair stood, earlier, sufficiently. [[See above, 2:63–68.]]

* *

His words: ﴿after the clear signs had come to them﴾ mean: after the clear signs from God and the manifest proofs had come to these who asked Moses what they asked, that they would not see God visibly and plainly.

The "clear signs" (al-bayyinat) are only meant as signs that make clear that they would not see God in their lifetime in this world openly. [[See the explanation of "al-bayyinat" above, 7:450, note 2, and the references there.]] Those clear signs for them that this was so were: God's striking them with thunder when they asked Moses to show them their Lord openly, then His reviving them after their death, together with the rest of the signs God showed them as proof of that.

* *

God says, denouncing their act to them and clarifying for His servants their ignorance and deficiency of intellect and forbearance: Then they affirmed to the calf that it was their god, while they saw it with their own eyes and looked at it plainly, after their Lord had shown them the clear signs that He showed them: that they would not see their Lord openly and visibly in their lifetime in this world. So they devoted themselves to worshipping it, confirming its divinity!!

* *

As for His words: ﴿Then We pardoned that﴾, He says: We pardoned those who worshipped the calf for their worship of it, [[See the explanation of "al-'afw" above, p. 351, note 2, and the references there.]] and those among them who believed it was their god, after what God had shown them of the signs that they would not see their Lord in their lifetime, for their belief in that, [[The context: "We pardoned the worshippers of the calf ... for their belief in that."]] through the repentance they repented to their Lord by killing themselves, and their patience in that according to their Lord's command. ﴿And We gave Moses a manifest authority﴾: He says: And We gave Moses a proof that makes clear his truthfulness and the reality of his prophethood. [[In the printed edition: "and the reality of his prophethood" (wa-haqiyyah nubuwwatih), which departs from the manuscript's wording, the editor supposing it an error; we have noted similar action of his earlier, p. 336, note 4, and what comes shortly after, p. 363, note 2.]] That proof is the clear signs that God gave him. [[See the explanation of "al-itha'" (giving) above in the language indices, and the explanation of "al-sultan" above, 7:279 / 9:336, 337, and the explanation of "mubin" (manifest) above, p. 336, note 3, and the references there.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 4, verse 154:

The interpretation of His words: ﴿And We raised over them the mount (al-Tur) for their covenant, and We said to them, "Enter the gate prostrating," and We said to them, "Do not transgress in the Sabbath," and We took from them a solemn covenant﴾ [4:154].

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, "And We raised over them the mount (al-Tur)," He means: the mountain [see the explanation of "al-Tur" above, 2:157-159]. That was when they refused to act upon what was in the Torah and to accept what Musa had brought them therein. "For their covenant" means: because they had given God their pledge and covenant that they would act upon what is in the Torah [see the explanation of "covenant" (mithaq) above: 41, 44, footnote 1, and the references there]. "And We said to them, 'Enter the gate prostrating,'" means the gate of Hittah, when they were commanded to enter through it prostrating, but they entered crawling on their backsides [see the explanation of "Enter the gate prostrating and say: Hittah" above, 2:103-109].

"And We said to them, 'Do not transgress in the Sabbath,'" by His words, "Do not transgress in the Sabbath," He means: do not go beyond, on the day of Sabbath, what has been permitted to you to what has not been permitted to you [see the explanation of "the Sabbath" and "their transgression in the Sabbath" above, 2:166-174], as related:

10773. Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His words, "And We said to them, 'Enter the gate prostrating,'" he said: We used to hear that it is a gate of the gates of Bayt al-Maqdis. [This report is not mentioned in the explanation of "the gate" above, 2:103-109, and it is one of the proofs of Abu Ja'far's abridgment of his tafsir and his method of abridging.]

* *

"And We said to them, 'Do not transgress in the Sabbath,'" they were commanded not to eat fish on the day of Sabbath nor to approach them, and all else was made lawful for them. [See the explanation of "the Sabbath" and "their transgression in the Sabbath" above, 2:166-174.]

* *

The readers differed regarding the recitation of this.

The majority of the readers of the Muslim cities recited it: ﴿لا تَعْدُوا فِي السَّبْتِ﴾ ("do not transgress"), with the "ayn" lightened, from the saying of the speaker, "I transgressed in the matter" (ʿadawtu fi al-amr), when one goes beyond the truth regarding it: "a'du, ʿadwan, ʿudwan, ʿudwanan, ʿadaa'an." [See the explanation of "ʿadā" above, 2:142, 167, 307; 3:573, 582; 7:117, and the references there.

In the printed edition, "wa-ʿadawu" (with the ʿayn and dal vowelled and the waw doubled) has been dropped here, though it is present in the manuscript.]

* *

Some of the readers of Madinah recited it: ﴿وَقُلْنَا لَهُمْ لا تَعْدُّوا﴾ with the "ayn" sukun and the "dal" doubled, combining two sukun letters, meaning: ta'taduu, then the "ta" is assimilated into the "dal," so it becomes a doubled, vowelled "dal," just as one who recited ﴿أَمْ مَنْ لا يَهْدِّي﴾ [Surah Yunus: 35] with the "ha" sukun.

* *

His words, "And We took from them a solemn covenant," mean: a firm, strong pact, that they would act upon what God commanded them and refrain from what God forbade them, of what is mentioned in this verse and of what is in the Torah. [See the explanation of "covenant" (mithaq) above, p. 361, footnote 2; and the explanation of "solemn" (ghalith) above, 8:127.]

* *

We have already explained, earlier, the cause for which they were commanded to enter the gate prostrating, what occurred in their matter in that and their account and story, and the story of the Sabbath and their transgression in it, in a manner that makes repeating it in this place unnecessary. [See the two preceding footnotes, p. 361, footnotes 3 and 4.]

Commentary on the interpretation of His words: ﴿So for their breaking of their covenant, and their disbelief in the signs of Allah, and their killing of the prophets without right, and their saying, "Our hearts are uncovered," [But] Allah has sealed them for their disbelief, so they believe not, except a few﴾ [4:155].

Abu Ja'far said: He, may His praise be exalted, means: So for the breaking by these people whose description I have given, from the People of the Book, "their covenant," meaning: their pledges which they made with Allah that they would act by what is in the Torah (see the explanation of "covenant" earlier, p. 362, footnote 2), "and their disbelief in the signs of Allah," meaning: their denial of the signs of Allah and His proofs, by which He argued against them concerning the truthfulness of His prophets and messengers (see the explanation of "signs" in the earlier word index, root ʼ-y-y), and the reality of what they brought to them from Him (in the printed edition: "wa-haqiyat ma jaʼuhum bihi," instead of what is in the manuscript; and see the earlier footnote, p. 360, footnote 2), "and their killing of the prophets without right," meaning: and by their killing the prophets after the proof of their prophethood had been established against them, "without right," meaning: without any entitlement on their part to that for a grave sin they had committed, nor any wrongdoing for which killing was deserved (see the explanation of "killing the prophets without right" earlier, 7:116, 117, 446), "and their saying, 'Our hearts are uncovered'," meaning: and by their saying "our hearts are uncovered," that is, they say: there are veils and coverings over them against what you call us to, so we do not understand what you say nor comprehend it.

* *

We have already explained the meaning of "uncovered" (ghulf), and mentioned the reports concerning it earlier (see the explanation of "ghulf" earlier, 2:324–328).

* *

"[But] Allah has sealed them for their disbelief," He, may His praise be exalted, says: They lied in their saying "our hearts are uncovered"; they are not uncovered, nor are there coverings over them, but Allah, may His praise be exalted, placed a seal upon them for their disbelief in Allah.

* *

We have already explained the nature of "the sealing of the heart" earlier, in a way that makes repeating it unnecessary. (The word "ṭabʻ" (sealing) has not appeared in this form in a verse before this one, but it was forgotten; what has passed is its equivalent, "Allah has set a seal upon their hearts" (khatm), and "khatm" is "ṭabʻ.")

* *

"So they believe not, except a few," He says: So these people whose description Allah has given do not believe, because He has sealed their hearts, so that they would affirm Allah and His messengers and what came to them from Allah, except a little faith, meaning: a little affirmation. It became "a little" because they did not affirm what Allah commanded them, but they affirmed some prophets and some books and denied others. Their affirmation of what they affirmed was therefore small, because even though they affirmed it in one respect, they denied it in another respect—namely, in their denial of those prophets they denied and of what they brought of the books of Allah—whereas the messengers of Allah confirm one another, and every prophet commanded his community accordingly, and likewise the books of Allah confirm one another and verify one another. So whoever denies some of them denies all of them, by his rejection of what the book he acknowledges as true confirms. Hence their faith in what they believed was small. (The explanation of "few" in the verses to which we have referred is better than what is here.)

* *

The people of interpretation have said similarly to what we have said.

Those who said so:

10774. Bishr ibn Mu'adh related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, concerning His words "So for their breaking of their covenant," meaning: For their breaking of their covenant, We cursed them. "And their saying, 'Our hearts are uncovered'," meaning: they do not understand. "[But] Allah has sealed them for their disbelief," and He cursed them when they did that.

* *

There was disagreement concerning the meaning of His words "So for their breaking..." (the verse), whether it is connected to what precedes it in speech, or is separate from it. (See also the addition of "mā" in His words "fa-bimā naqḍihim mīthāqahum," earlier, 7:340. Abu Ja'far's omission of explaining this here is one of the indications of his method of abridging this tafsir.)

Some said: It is separate from what precedes it, and its meaning is: For their breaking of their covenant, their disbelief in the signs of Allah, their killing of the prophets without right, and their saying "our hearts are uncovered"—Allah sealed them for their disbelief and their cursing. (In the printed edition: "[But] Allah has sealed them," as in the verse, which does not work; the correct reading is what is in the manuscript.)

Those who said so:

10775. Bishr ibn Mu'adh related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, concerning "they believe not, except a few": when the people abandoned the command of Allah, killed His messengers, disbelieved in His signs, and broke the covenant that was taken from them, Allah sealed them for their disbelief and their cursing.

* *

Others said: Rather, it is connected to what precedes it. They said: The meaning of the speech is: "Then the thunderbolt seized them for their wrongdoing"—for their breaking of their covenant, their disbelief in the signs of Allah, their killing of the prophets without right, and such and such, the thunderbolt seized them. They said: The speech follows one part of it from another, and its meaning refers back to its beginning. The explanation of their "wrongdoing" for which the thunderbolt seized them is by what He, may He be exalted, explained of their breaking the covenant, their killing of the prophets, and the rest of their affairs in which they wronged themselves.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The correct view on this is that His words "So for their breaking of their covenant" and what follows are separate in meaning from what precedes them, and that the meaning of the speech is: For their breaking of their covenant, their disbelief in the signs of Allah, and such and such, We cursed them and were wrathful with them. The words "We cursed them" are omitted, because of the indication of His words "[But] Allah has sealed them for their disbelief," which points to that meaning, since whoever has a seal placed upon his heart has been cursed and has incurred wrath.

We said that this is more correct because the people seized by the thunderbolt were in the time of Moses, whereas those who killed the prophets, and those who accused Mary of the great slander and said "We killed the Messiah," came long after Moses. Those who accused Mary of the great slander did not live to see the time of Moses, nor did those of his people who were struck by the thunderbolt.

Since that is so, it is known that those seized by the thunderbolt were not seized as punishment for their accusing Mary of the great slander, nor for their saying "We killed the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary." Since that is so, it is clear that the people who made this statement were not those punished with the thunderbolt. And since that is so, it is clear that the meaning of His words "So for their breaking of their covenant" is separate from the meaning of His words "Then the thunderbolt seized them for their wrongdoing."

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿And for their disbelief and their speaking against Mary a tremendous slander﴾ (4:156).

Abu Ja'far said: Thereby He, mighty is His praise, means: And for the disbelief of these people whose description He has given, and their speaking against Mary a tremendous slander, meaning: by their fabrication against her and their accusing her of fornication. This is the "tremendous slander," because they accused her of that, and she was innocent of what they accused her of, without any proof or evidence; so they slandered her with false speech. [See the explanation of "slander" (buhtan) above: 5:432 / 8:124 / 9:197.]

The scholars of interpretation have said something similar to what we have said.

Those who said that:

10776 - Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abdullah ibn Salih related to us, saying: Mu'awiyah ibn Salih related to me, from Ali ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn Abbas: "And their speaking against Mary a tremendous slander," meaning: they accused her of fornication.

10777 - Muhammad ibn al-Husayn related to us, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi regarding His saying: "And their speaking against Mary a tremendous slander," when they slandered her with fornication.

10778 - Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq related to us, saying: Ya'la ibn Ubayd related to us, from Juwaybir regarding His saying: "And their speaking against Mary a tremendous slander," he said: They said: "She committed fornication."

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 4, verse 157 (part 1 of 2)**

On the interpretation of His words: ﴿And for their saying, "Indeed, we killed the Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, the messenger of Allah"; and they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him, but it was made to appear to them so﴾.

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: By this, may His majesty be exalted, He means: "And for their saying, 'Indeed, we killed the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, the messenger of Allah.'" Then Allah refuted them in their claim, saying: "And they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him, but it was made to appear to them so," meaning: they did not kill Jesus, nor did they crucify him, but it was made to appear to them so.

* * *

The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) differed about the nature of the resemblance (al-tashbih) that was made to appear to the Jews regarding the matter of Jesus.

Some of them said: When the Jews surrounded him and his companions, they encircled them while they could not identify Jesus by his person. That was because they had all been transformed into the likeness of Jesus, so those who wanted to kill Jesus could not distinguish Jesus from the others. Then one of those who were in the house with Jesus went out to them, and they killed him, thinking he was Jesus.

Mention of those who said this:

10779. Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Ya'qub al-Qummi narrated to us, from Harun ibn Antarah, from Wahb ibn Munabbih, who said: Jesus, with seventeen of the Hawariyyun (the disciples) in a house, was besieged, and they surrounded them. When they entered upon them, Allah gave all of them the form of Jesus. They said to them: "You have bewitched us! Either you produce Jesus for us, or we will kill all of you!" Jesus said to his companions: "Who among you will sell himself today for Paradise?" A man among them said: "I will!" So he went out to them and said: "I am Jesus," while Allah had given him the form of Jesus. So they seized him, killed him, and crucified him. From that, it was made to appear to them so, and they thought they had killed Jesus. The Christians also thought likewise, that it was Jesus. And Allah raised Jesus up that same day.

* * *

Other than this statement, a different account has been transmitted from Wahb ibn Munabbih, namely what follows:

10780. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Isma'il ibn Abd al-Karim narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Samad ibn Ma'qil narrated to me that he heard Wahb say: When Allah informed Jesus, son of Mary, peace be upon him, that he was going out of this world, he was distressed by death and it weighed heavily upon him. So he summoned the Hawariyyun and prepared food for them, [in the printed edition "wa-sana'a" with a waw, and I have kept what is in the manuscript and in al-Tarikh (of al-Tabari)]. He said: "Attend me tonight, for I have a need of you." When they gathered to him at night, he fed them, and then stood serving them. When they had finished eating, he began to wash their hands and to make them perform ablution with his own hand, and he wiped their hands with his garments. They were overwhelmed by this and disliked it. He said: "Whoever rejects anything I do tonight, is not of me, and I am not of him!" So they accepted it. When he had finished that, he said: "As for what I have done with you tonight, serving you at the meal and washing your hands with my hand, let there be an example in me for you. For you see that I am the best of you. So let none of you exalt himself over another, and let each of you give himself to the other, as I have given myself to you. As for my need, for which I sought your help: pray to Allah for me and strive in supplication, that He may delay my term." When they set themselves to supplicate and intended to exert themselves, sleep overcame them so that they could not make supplication. He kept waking them and saying: "Glory be to Allah! Will you not endure for me one night, in which you help me?" They said: "By Allah, we do not know what is wrong with us! We used to stay up late talking and talk much, and tonight we cannot bear talking, and whenever we want to supplicate, something comes between us and it!" He said: "The shepherd will be taken away and the sheep will scatter!" And he kept saying words of this sort, lamenting himself. Then he said: "Truly, one of you will disbelieve in me before the rooster crows three times, and one of you will sell me for a small sum of money, and will consume my price!" So they went out and scattered. The Jews were seeking him, and they seized Simon, one of the Hawariyyun, and said: "This one is among his companions!" He denied it and said: "I am not his companion!" So they left him. Then others seized him, and he denied it likewise. Then he heard the crowing of a rooster and wept, and it grieved him. When morning came, one of the Hawariyyun went to the Jews and said: "What will you give me if I show you the Messiah?" They set for him thirty dirhams, so he took them and showed them where he was. Jesus had been made to appear to them otherwise before that. So they seized him, secured him, and bound him with a rope. They began to lead him, saying to him: "You used to give life to the dead, drive away the devil, and heal the madman. Will you not save yourself from this rope?!" They spat on him and threw thorns upon him, until they brought him to the wood on which they intended to crucify him. Then Allah raised him to Himself, and they crucified what had been made to appear to them, and it remained for seven [days].

= Then his mother and the woman whom Jesus had healed, whom Allah had cured of madness, came weeping to where the crucified one was [in the printed edition "haythu kana al-maslub"; in al-Tarikh: "inda al-maslub"; in the manuscript "haythu" is undotted with a ṭa' written over it, as though the copyist regarded it as an error, since "haythu" is rarely prefixed to a singular noun; but there are many examples of its use with a singular noun, including the line of the poet: "We gave the death to Ma'qil by the sword / and there was among them where the turbans were wound (haythu li al-'amā'im)"]. Jesus came to them and said: "Why are you weeping?" They said: "Over you!" He said: "Indeed, Allah has raised me up to Him, and nothing but good has befallen me. This is a thing that was made to appear to them so. So command the Hawariyyun to bring me to such and such a place." They brought him to that place, eleven of them. They missed the one who had sold him and had shown the Jews where he was, so they asked his companions about him. They said: "He regretted what he had done, so he hanged himself and killed himself." He said: "If he had repented, Allah would have accepted his repentance!" Then he asked them about a boy who followed them, called Yuhanna [in al-Tarikh: "called Yahya"]. He said: "He is with you. Go, for each one of you will wake up speaking the language of a people, so let him warn them and invite them." [The report 10780: Abu Ja'far narrated it in al-Tarikh 2: 22, 23.]

* * *

Others said: Rather, Jesus asked those who were with him in the house that one of them should have his likeness cast upon him. A man volunteered for that, and his likeness was cast upon him, and that man was killed, while Jesus son of Mary, peace be upon him, was raised.

Mention of those who said this:

10781. Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, concerning His words: "Indeed, we killed the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, the messenger of Allah, and they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him" to His words: "And Allah is ever Mighty and Wise." Those were the enemies of Allah, the Jews. They conspired to kill Jesus son of Mary, the messenger of Allah, and they claimed that they had killed him and crucified him. [In the printed edition: "ishtahiru bi-qatl Isa", which has no meaning here; in the manuscript the letters are not clear, and the correct reading is what I have given.] It was mentioned to us that the Prophet of Allah, Jesus son of Mary, said to his companions: "Which of you will have my likeness cast upon him, for he will be killed?" A man among his companions said: "I, O Prophet of Allah!" So that man was killed, and Allah protected His prophet and raised him to Himself.

10782. Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, concerning His words: "And they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him, but it was made to appear to them so." He said: His likeness was cast upon a man of the Hawariyyun, and he was killed. Jesus son of Mary had presented this matter to them, saying: "Which of you will have my likeness cast upon him, and he will have Paradise?" A man said: "Upon me!"

10783. Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, that the Children of Israel besieged Jesus and nineteen men of the Hawariyyun in a house. Jesus said to his companions: "Who will take my form, to be killed, and have Paradise?" A man among them took it, and Jesus was taken up to heaven. When the Hawariyyun came out, they saw them as nineteen, and they informed them that Jesus, peace be upon him, had been taken up to heaven. They began to count the people and found them lacking one man from the number. They saw the form of Jesus among them, so they doubted about him. On that basis, they killed the man, thinking he was Jesus, and crucified him. That is the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted: "And they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him, but it was made to appear to them so," to His words: "And Allah is ever Mighty and Wise."

10784. Al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from al-Qasim ibn Abi Bazzah: that Jesus son of Mary said: "Which of you will have my likeness cast upon him and be killed in my place?" A man among his companions said: "I, O Messenger of Allah!" So his likeness was cast upon him, and they killed him. That is His saying: "And they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him, but it was made to appear to them so."

10785. Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, who said: The name of the king of the Children of Israel who was sent to Jesus to kill him was a man among them called Dawud. When they had resolved upon that against him, no servant of Allah was ever terrified by death, as was reported to me, as he was terrified by it, and he did not grieve over it as he grieved. He did not cease supplicating Allah to turn it away from him, until he would say, as they claim: "O Allah, if You are going to turn this cup away from anyone of Your creation, then turn it away from me!" And his skin would sweat blood from the anguish of that. He entered the place into which they had resolved to enter upon him to kill him, he and his companions, who were thirteen with Jesus. When he became certain that they were entering upon him, he said to his companions among the Hawariyyun [the saying of the Messiah to his companions among the Hawariyyun will come in the paragraph that follows the next paragraph, namely his words: "O company of the Hawariyyun, which of you loves to be my companion in Paradise?" Between the two statements is a digression mentioning the number of the Hawariyyun]. They were twelve men: Titrus (Peter), Ya'qub ibn Zabdi (James son of Zebedee), Yuhanis, the brother of Ya'qub (John), Andarayas (Andrew), Filibus (Philip), Barthulama (Bartholomew), Matta (Matthew), Tuma (Thomas), Ya'qub ibn Halfa (James son of Alphaeus), Taddaus (Thaddeus), Qanaya (Simon the Zealot), and Yudas Zakariyya Yutha (Judas Iscariot). [The editor's note: I will mention these names as they appear in the books of the people, in order here, from the tenth chapter of the Gospel of Matthew: Butrus (Peter), Ya'qub ibn Zabdi (James son of Zebedee), Yuhanna (John) the brother of Ya'qub, Andarawas (Andrew) the brother of Butrus, Filibus (Philip), Burthulamawus (Bartholomew), Matta (Matthew), Tuma (Thomas), Ya'qub ibn Halfi (James son of Alphaeus), Lubawus, called Tiddawus (Thaddeus), Sim'an al-Qanawi (Simon the Canaanite), and Yahudha al-Askhariyuti (Judas Iscariot).]

= Ibn Humayd said, Salamah said, Ibn Ishaq said: Among them, as was reported to me, was a man named Sarjas, so they were thirteen men besides Jesus. The Christians deny him, and that is because he is the one whose likeness was made to appear to the Jews in place of Jesus. He said: I do not know whether he was one of these twelve, or whether he was a thirteenth. They denied him when they acknowledged to the Jews the crucifixion of Jesus, and disbelieved in what Muhammad ﷺ brought of information about him. If they were thirteen, then when they entered the place, they entered with Jesus as fourteen; and if they were twelve, then when they entered the place, they entered with Jesus as thirteen.

= Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, who said: A man who had been a Christian and became Muslim narrated to me that when Jesus received from Allah the words: "Indeed, I will take you up to Me," he said: "O company of the Hawariyyun, which of you loves to be my companion in Paradise, on condition that he be made to appear to the people in my form, and they kill him in my place?" Sarjas said: "I, O Spirit of Allah!" He said: "Then sit in my place." So he sat in it, and Jesus, may Allah's blessings be upon him, was raised. They entered upon him and seized him and crucified him. He was the one they crucified, and it was made to appear to them as him. Their number when they entered with Jesus was known; they had seen them and counted their number. When they entered upon him to seize him, they found Jesus, as they saw it, and his companions, but they missed one man from the number. He was the one about whom they disagreed. They did not recognize Jesus until they offered Yudas Zakariyya Yutha thirty dirhams on condition that he show them him and identify him for them. He said to them: "When you enter upon him, I will kiss him, and he is the one I will kiss, so seize him." When they entered upon him, Jesus having been raised, Sarjas appeared to them in the form of Jesus, and they did not doubt that he was Jesus. So he fell upon him and kissed him, and they seized him and crucified him. Then Yudas Zakariyya Yutha regretted what he had done, and hanged himself with a rope until he killed himself. He is cursed among the Christians, and he had been one of those counted among his companions. Some Christians claim that Yudas Zakariyya Yutha was the one whose likeness was made to appear to them, so they crucified him while he said: "I am not your companion! I am the one who showed you him!" And Allah knows best which of these was the case.

10786. Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, saying: Ibn Jurayj said: It has reached us that Jesus son of Mary said to his companions: "Which of you volunteers to have my likeness cast upon him and be killed?" A man among his companions said: "I, O Prophet of Allah." So his likeness was cast upon him and he was killed, and Allah raised His prophet to Himself.

10787. Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to us, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, concerning His words: "but it was made to appear to them so," who said: They crucified a man other than Jesus, supposing him to be him.

10788. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "But it was made to appear to them so," and he mentioned something similar. [In the printed edition: "fa-dhakara mithlahu."]

10789. Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, who said: They crucified a man whom they made to resemble Jesus, supposing him to be him, and Allah raised Jesus to Himself alive.

* * *

Abu Ja'far said: The most correct of these views is one of the two sayings we have mentioned from Wahb ibn Munabbih [this is the report numbered 10779]: that the likeness of Jesus was cast upon all of those who were in the house with Jesus when he and they were surrounded, without Jesus having asked them to do so. This was so that Allah might humiliate the Jews through it, rescue His prophet, peace be upon him, from the harm of what they intended for him of killing, and test through it whomever He wills among His servants with regard to what they say about Jesus, and the truthfulness of the report about his affair. Or: the saying that Abd al-Samad transmitted from him [this is the report numbered 10780; in the manuscript it read "alladhi rawahu Abd al-Aziz 'anhu," but among the transmitters from Ibn Munabbih previously mentioned there is no "Abd al-Aziz," only "Abd al-Samad ibn Ma'qil," and this is probably a slip by the copyist and a hasty error].

We said that this is the more correct of the two views because those among the Hawariyyun who witnessed Jesus, had they been in a state in which Jesus was raised and his likeness was cast upon the one on whom it was cast, would have witnessed him being raised up from among them, and they would have ascertained the one on whom his likeness was cast, and they would have seen him transformed in his form, after the form that was his own, in their presence. The matter of Jesus and the matter of the one on whom his likeness was cast would not have been hidden from them, along with their witnessing all of that, and it would not have been confused or made obscure to them, even if it was obscure to others of their enemies among the Jews that the one killed and crucified was other than Jesus, and that Jesus had been raised up from among them alive.

And how could it be that this was obscure to them, when they had heard from Jesus his statement: "Whoever has my likeness cast upon him, and he will be my companion in Paradise," if he said that to them, and they heard the answer of one who responded among them: "I," and they witnessed the transformation of the responder into the form of Jesus immediately after his answer? Rather, that was, if Allah wills, in the manner described by Wahb ibn Munabbih: either the people who were with Jesus in the house from which he was raised, among his disciples, were all transformed by Allah into the form of Jesus when Allah willed to raise him, so that they could not establish, by identifying the person, Jesus as distinct from the others, because the forms of all of them were alike; so the Jews killed whichever of them they killed, seeing him in the form of Jesus and supposing him to be him, because they had known Jesus before that. And those who were in the house with Jesus supposed what the Jews supposed, because they could not distinguish the person of Jesus from the person of another who was with him in the house, because his person and the person of the other were alike. So they all agreed, that is, the Jews and the Christians [in the printed edition: "a'ni" (I mean); I have kept what is in the manuscript], on account of this, that the one killed was Jesus, when he was not, but it was made to appear to them so, as Allah, may His majesty be exalted, said: "And they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him, but it was made to appear to them so."

Or the matter may have been as related by ʿAbd al-Ṣamad ibn Maʿqil, from Wahb ibn Munabbih: that the people who were with ʿIsa in the house dispersed from him before the Jews entered upon him, and ʿIsa remained, and his likeness was cast upon one of his companions who was in the house after the people had dispersed, other than ʿIsa and other than the one upon whom his likeness was cast. Then ʿIsa was raised, and the one who had been transformed into the form of ʿIsa, from among his companions, was killed. His companions and the Jews thought that the one who was killed and crucified was ʿIsa, because of the resemblance they saw in him to ʿIsa, and because the matter of ʿIsa was hidden from them. For his being raised and the slain one's being transformed into his form occurred after his companions had dispersed from him. They had heard ʿIsa at night lamenting his own soul and grieving over what he thought was about to befall him of death, so they related what they had held to be true, while the reality with God was contrary to what they related. Thus those among his disciples who related that should not be deemed liars, since they related what was true to them outwardly, [[In the printed edition: "aw ḥakaw", and in the manuscript: "idhā ḥakaw"; the correct reading is what is adopted here.]] even though the matter was in reality with God contrary to what they related. [[In the manuscript: "wa-in kāna al-amr ʿinda Allāh", with the second "kāna" omitted; the copyist of the manuscript supplied it in the margin of the copy.]]

* *

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿And indeed those who differed concerning it are surely in doubt about it. They have no knowledge of it, except the following of assumption. And they did not kill him for certain﴾ (4:157)

Abu Jaʿfar (al-Tabari) said: By His saying, may His praise be exalted, "And indeed those who differed concerning it," He means the Jews who surrounded ʿIsa and his companions when they wanted to kill him. This is because they had known the number of those in the house before they entered, as has been reported. When they entered upon them, they found one of them missing, so the matter of ʿIsa became confused for them due to their missing one of the number they had counted, and they killed whomever they killed, in doubt about the matter of ʿIsa.

This interpretation accords with the view of the one who said: the disciples did not part from ʿIsa until he was raised and the Jews entered upon them.

As for its interpretation according to the view of the one who said: they dispersed from him during the night, then it means: "And indeed those who differed" concerning ʿIsa, whether he is the one who remained in the house among them after the departure of those who had left from the number that had been in it, or not, "are surely in doubt about it," meaning: about the one who was killed, because they had counted, when they entered the house, a number greater than those who had left it and those who were found in it, so they doubted about the one they had killed: was he ʿIsa or not, on account of their missing those of the number they had counted. But they said, "We have killed ʿIsa," because the one killed resembled ʿIsa in form. God, may His praise be exalted, says: "They have no knowledge of it," meaning: they killed whomever they killed in doubt and difference concerning him, whether he was ʿIsa or someone else, without having any knowledge of who he was they killed, whether he was ʿIsa or other than him. "Except the following of assumption," meaning, may His praise be exalted: they had no knowledge of the one they killed, but they followed their assumption and killed him, assuming that he was ʿIsa and that he was the one they wanted to kill, and he was not. "And they did not kill him for certain": they did not kill—this which they followed in the one they killed, whom they supposed to be ʿIsa—for certain that he was ʿIsa nor that he was other than him, but they were in assumption and uncertainty about him.

* *

This is like a man saying to another, "I did not kill this matter with knowledge, and I did not kill it for certain," when he speaks of it by assumption without certain knowledge. The pronoun in His saying "and they did not kill him" refers to "the assumption."

[[See al-Farra's Maʿani al-Qur'an 1: 294.]]

* *

And the people of interpretation have said things similar to what we have said.

Those who said that:

10790. Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: ʿAbd Allah ibn Salih related to us, saying: Muʿawiya ibn Salih related to me, from ʿAli ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: "And they did not kill him for certain," he said: meaning they did not kill their assumption for certain.

10791. Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq related to us, saying: Yaʿla ibn ʿUbayd related to us, from Juwaybir regarding His saying: "And they did not kill him for certain," he said: they did not kill their assumption for certain.

And al-Suddi said regarding that:

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 4, verse 158:

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿Nay, Allah raised him up to Himself; and Allah is ever Mighty, Wise﴾ (4:158)

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: As for His saying, exalted is His praise, "Nay, Allah raised him up to Himself," it means: Nay, Allah raised the Messiah up to Himself. That is, they did not kill him and they did not crucify him, but Allah raised him up to Himself and purified him from those who disbelieved.

* *

We have already explained how Allah's raising of him to Himself took place in the past, and we mentioned the disagreement of those who differ on this and the correct statement on it with the evidences that testify to its soundness, in a way that makes repeating it unnecessary. [[See what preceded, 6: 455-460.]]

* *

As for His saying, "and Allah is ever Mighty, Wise," it means: Allah has never ceased to take vengeance on His enemies, as He took vengeance on those whom the thunderbolt seized for their wrongdoing, and as He cursed those whose story He related in His saying, "For their breaking of their covenant and their disbelief in the signs of Allah" [[See the explanation of "ʿAzīz" and "ʿIzzah" in what preceded, p. 319, note 5, and the references there.]] = "Wise," that is, possessed of wisdom in His management and in His disposing of His creation by His decree. [[See the explanation of "Ḥakīm" in the language indexes of what preceded.]] It means: Beware, O you who question Muhammad, lest He send down upon you a Book from heaven, lest My punishment descend upon you as it descended upon your predecessors who did as you did, in their denial of My messengers and their slander against My friends. And indeed:

[[The report 10793: I do not know a biography of "Muhammad ibn Ishaq ibn Abi Sarah al-Ru'asi," nor have I found any mention of him in the books available to me, and I fear that his name may contain an error or a misreading. Ibn ʿAbbas's statement in explaining the verse, "the meaning of that is that He is so," intends that Allah has always been and never ceased to be Mighty and Wise.
